levels.title: Kindergarten to Grade 2
levels.description: Playful, concrete mathematics: collections, counting, shapes, patterns and simple actions that can be done and undone. Ideas are met through objects, pictures and talk, never through formal notation.

levels.title: Grades 3 to 5
levels.description: Whole-number arithmetic, fractions, measurement and the first language of sets. Learners begin to explain why a method works, not only how to use it.

levels.title: Grades 6 to 8
levels.description: Integers, rational numbers, functions as mappings, equations and proportional reasoning. Set notation, quantifiers and equivalence relations prepare the ground for proof.

levels.title: Grades 9 to 12
levels.description: Algebra, geometry, trigonometry, logic and proof, countability and introductory calculus. Composition, structure-preserving maps and a first universal property preview the language of higher mathematics.

levels.title: Early undergraduate
levels.description: Calculus I–III, linear algebra, differential equations, probability and statistics, first-order logic and a first course in algebraic structures and categories.

levels.title: Advanced undergraduate
levels.description: Real and complex analysis, abstract algebra, topology, number theory, axiomatic set theory, computability and core category theory through the Yoneda lemma.

levels.title: First-year graduate
levels.description: Measure theory, functional analysis, graduate algebra and topology, logic and category theory. Graduate programmes differ, so this level is organised as specialisation pathways rather than a single required syllabus.

levels.title: Research pathways
levels.description: Optional advanced directions and research skills: higher and derived categories, homotopy type theory, quiver representations, large cardinals, formalising published mathematics and research ethics. Established results are distinguished from open questions.

subjects.title: Foundations
subjects.description: Collections, sets, logic and proof, growing into axiomatic set theory, model theory, proof theory and type theory. This lane is where mathematics examines its own language and assumptions.

subjects.title: Number
subjects.description: From counting and place value through integers, rationals, reals and complex numbers to congruences and number theory.

subjects.title: Algebra
subjects.description: School algebra, then linear algebra and abstract algebra (groups, rings, fields, modules), leading to homological algebra and representation theory.

subjects.title: Geometry & Topology
subjects.description: Shapes, measurement, transformations and Euclidean geometry, trigonometry, then topology, differential geometry and algebraic geometry.

subjects.title: Analysis
subjects.description: Approximation, rates of change and functions of a real variable, then calculus, real and complex analysis, differential equations, measure theory and functional analysis.

subjects.title: Discrete Mathematics
subjects.description: Systematic counting, combinatorics, recurrences and graph theory, from puzzles with dots and lines to the probabilistic method.

subjects.title: Probability & Statistics
subjects.description: Data, chance and variability, then probability theory, statistical inference, Markov chains and measure-theoretic stochastic processes.

subjects.title: Category Theory
subjects.description: Early precursors (doing, undoing and chaining actions), then composition, structure-preserving maps, universal properties, categories, functors, adjunctions and Yoneda, reaching monoidal, abelian, higher and derived categories.

subjects.title: Computation
subjects.description: Algorithms, programming for mathematics, numerical methods, computability and complexity, lambda calculus, formal methods and machine-checked proof in Lean.

subjects.title: Applied Mathematics
subjects.description: Mathematics in use: codes and cryptography, modelling, mechanics and mathematical physics, information theory, optimisation and mathematical biology.

topics.title: Collections
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Grouping objects into collections, deciding what belongs, sorting by a rule, comparing collections, meeting the collection with nothing in it, and counting members.

discoveries.note: A collection can itself be a member of another collection, like a box inside a box. Pushing this to 'the collection of all collections that are not members of themselves' leads to Russell's paradox.
Sorting by a rule so that every object lands in exactly one group is the seed of a partition; partitions correspond exactly to equivalence relations.

objectives: Sort objects into collections using a stated rule, and describe the rule someone else used.
Decide whether a given object is a member of a collection.
Explain that two collections are the same exactly when they have the same members, however they are arranged or listed.
Recognise the empty collection and count the members of small collections.
definitions: A collection is a group of things considered together; the things in it are its members.
Two collections are equal when every member of each one is also a member of the other.
The empty collection is the collection with no members.
Sorting (classification) places objects into collections according to a rule, such as colour or shape.
keyResults: Rearranging the members, or listing them in a different order, does not change a collection.
Naming the same member twice does not add a new member.
Counting the members of a collection gives the same answer whatever order we count them in.
There is only one empty collection: any two collections with no members have exactly the same members.
misconceptions: Thinking a collection changes when its members are moved around or listed in a different order.
Believing that a collection with nothing in it is not a collection at all.
Confusing a box that contains an empty box with an empty box: the first one has one member.
Thinking an object can belong to only one collection (the same toy can be in 'red things' and in 'round things').

references.title: Naive Set Theory
references.author: Paul R. Halmos
references.note: Background for educators, not for children.

topics.title: Counting
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: Counting a collection by matching each member with exactly one number word, knowing that the last number said tells how many, and comparing collections by counting or by pairing.

discoveries.note: Pairing members one-to-one, rather than counting, is how mathematicians compare the sizes of infinite collections.

objectives: Count a collection of up to about 100 objects, saying exactly one number word for each object.
Explain that the last number word said tells how many objects there are, whatever order they were counted in.
Compare two collections by pairing their members one-to-one and by counting.
definitions: Counting matches each member of a collection with exactly one number word, in order, without skipping or repeating.
Two collections have the same number of members when their members can be paired up exactly, with none left over.
Zero is the number of members of the empty collection.
keyResults: The number of members does not depend on the order of counting or on how the objects are arranged.
If the members of two collections can be paired with none left over, counting them gives the same number.
Every counting number has a next one, so there is no largest counting number.
misconceptions: Thinking that spreading objects out makes more of them.
Counting an object twice, or skipping one, when the objects are not in a line.
Believing the last number word names only the last object rather than the size of the whole collection.

references.title: Understanding Numbers in Elementary School Mathematics
references.author: Hung-Hsi Wu

topics.title: Addition, subtraction and place value to 100
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: Adding as putting together and subtracting as taking away or comparing, the meaning of the equals sign, and place value in tens and ones up to 100.

discoveries.note: 'Add 3' and 'take away 3' are actions that undo each other.
Can we take 5 away from 3? Extending the whole numbers to the integers makes every subtraction possible.

objectives: Add and subtract within 20 fluently, and within 100 using tens and ones.
Explain that the equals sign means 'has the same value as', so that 7 = 3 + 4 and 3 + 4 = 4 + 3 are both true.
Represent two-digit numbers as tens and ones and use this to compare them.
definitions: Addition combines two collections with no members in common; a + b is the number of members of the combined collection.
Subtraction a − b (with b ≤ a) is the number left when b members are taken from a collection of a members, or the difference between two amounts.
In a two-digit numeral, the left digit counts tens and the right digit counts ones.
keyResults: Addition is commutative and associative: a + b = b + a and (a + b) + c = a + (b + c).
Subtraction undoes addition: (a + b) − b = a.
Adding zero changes nothing.
misconceptions: Reading '=' as 'the answer comes next', so that 7 = 3 + 4 seems wrong.
Thinking subtraction is commutative, for example that 3 − 5 = 5 − 3.
Reading 52 as 'five and two' rather than five tens and two ones.

references.title: Understanding Numbers in Elementary School Mathematics
references.author: Hung-Hsi Wu

topics.title: Patterns
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Repeating and growing patterns with shapes, sounds, movements and numbers: finding the unit that repeats, predicting what comes next and describing the rule.

discoveries.note: Which colour is the 100th bead in a red–blue–green pattern? The answer depends only on the remainder when 100 is divided by 3.
Growing patterns lead to rules such as 'the n-th term is 2 × n', the first algebraic expressions.

objectives: Copy, extend and create repeating patterns such as red, blue, red, blue, … and identify the unit that repeats.
Extend simple growing patterns such as 2, 4, 6, 8, … and describe the rule in words.
Predict an item further along a repeating pattern without drawing every step.
definitions: A repeating pattern is made by repeating the same unit again and again.
A growing pattern changes by the same rule at each step, such as 'add 2'.
keyResults: In a repeating pattern whose unit has k items, the item k places further on is always the same.
The first few items do not always decide a pattern: 1, 2, 4 could continue with 8 (doubling) or with 7 (add 1, then 2, then 3), so the rule must be stated.
misconceptions: Thinking a pattern must continue the way you first guessed.
Confusing the repeating unit with a single item of the pattern.

topics.title: Shapes
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: Recognising, naming, sorting and building two- and three-dimensional shapes by their attributes, such as number of sides and corners and whether faces are flat or curved.

discoveries.note: Sorting shapes into overlapping groups, such as 'four-sided' and 'red', leads to Venn diagrams.

objectives: Name and describe circles, triangles, squares, rectangles, cubes, cylinders, cones and spheres, whatever their size or orientation.
Sort shapes by attributes such as the number of sides or corners, and explain the sorting rule.
Compose larger shapes from smaller ones and decompose shapes into parts.
definitions: A triangle is a closed flat shape with three straight sides.
A side is a straight edge of a flat shape; a corner (vertex) is where two sides meet.
A square is a rectangle whose four sides all have the same length.
keyResults: Turning or moving a shape does not change what shape it is.
Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square.
misconceptions: Thinking a square turned onto a corner is no longer a square.
Believing a triangle must have a flat bottom or equal sides.
Treating colour or size as part of what makes a shape a triangle or a square.

topics.title: Measuring length and time
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: Comparing and ordering objects by length, measuring with non-standard and standard units, and telling time to the hour and half hour.

discoveries.note: Lengths that fall between whole units lead to fractions of a unit.
Every physical measurement is an approximation, accurate only to some precision.

objectives: Compare and order objects by length, directly and by using a third object.
Measure lengths by laying copies of a unit end to end without gaps or overlaps, and then with a ruler.
Tell and write time to the hour and half hour on analogue and digital clocks.
definitions: A unit is a fixed amount used for measuring, such as a centimetre or the length of a paper clip.
The length of an object is the number of units that fit along it end to end.
keyResults: Measuring the same length with a smaller unit gives a larger number.
If A is longer than B and B is longer than C, then A is longer than C.
misconceptions: Starting to measure from 1 on a ruler instead of from 0.
Leaving gaps or overlaps between units.
Thinking a string becomes shorter when it is bent.

topics.title: Data, tallies and picture graphs
topics.subject: probability
topics.summary: Asking questions, collecting data by counting, sorting answers into categories, recording with tally marks, and showing results in picture graphs.

discoveries.note: Later, data are summarised by averages and by measures of spread.

objectives: Collect answers to a simple question and sort them into categories.
Record counts with tally marks and show them in a picture graph or block graph.
Answer 'how many more' and 'which is most' questions from a graph.
definitions: Data are pieces of information collected to answer a question.
A tally mark records one item; tallies are grouped in fives to make counting easier.
A picture graph uses one picture for each item, or for a fixed number of items.
keyResults: If every answer goes into exactly one category, the category totals add up to the number of answers collected.
Comparing categories by the length of a row of pictures is reliable only when the pictures are the same size and evenly spaced.
misconceptions: Comparing rows of pictures of different sizes by their length.
Counting one answer in two categories.

topics.title: Doing and undoing
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Actions that change things (turning a card, adding a block, walking two steps forward), the action of doing nothing, and actions that can or cannot be undone, explored through play without any special vocabulary.

discoveries.note: Much later, actions become functions, doing nothing becomes the identity function, and undoing becomes taking an inverse function.
Collections of actions that can be combined and that can all be undone are studied in group theory.

objectives: Describe the effect of an action on an object, such as 'turn the arrow a quarter turn'.
Find the action that undoes a given action, and notice actions that cannot be undone, such as cracking an egg.
Recognise 'doing nothing' as an action that leaves everything as it was.
definitions: An action changes an object or a situation, possibly leaving it the same.
One action undoes another if doing the first and then the second puts everything back as it was.
Doing nothing is the action that leaves every object unchanged.
keyResults: 'Take 3 steps forward' is undone by 'take 3 steps back'.
Some actions, such as mixing two paints, cannot be undone.
Doing nothing and then doing an action has the same effect as just doing the action.
misconceptions: Thinking every action can be undone.
Believing that 'doing nothing' is not something we can talk about as an action.
Thinking that an action is always undone by doing it again; this works for flipping a card but not for walking forward.

topics.title: Following and giving precise instructions
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: Algorithms as step-by-step instructions: following directions on a grid, giving instructions to a friend or a floor robot, and finding and fixing mistakes ('bugs') in a sequence of steps.

discoveries.note: A list of instructions is a chain of actions carried out one after another.

objectives: Follow a sequence of movement instructions on a grid and predict where it ends.
Write a sequence of instructions to reach a target, and test it.
Find and fix a mistake in a sequence of instructions.
definitions: An algorithm is a precise list of steps that can be followed to complete a task.
A bug is a mistake in an algorithm that makes it do something unintended.
keyResults: Changing the order of the steps can change the result.
Instructions must be precise enough to be followed without guessing.
misconceptions: Thinking a robot or computer 'knows what you mean' when instructions are vague.
Believing there is only one correct algorithm for a task.

references.title: Computer Science Unplugged
references.author: Tim Bell, Ian H. Witten and Mike Fellows

topics.title: Sets
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Finite sets and their language: membership, subsets, union, intersection, complement, the empty set, Venn diagrams, a first look at set-builder notation, ordered pairs, Cartesian products and counting elements.

discoveries.note: Sets can have sets as elements, and {∅} ≠ ∅. Allowing every property to define a set leads to Russell's paradox.
Nesting alone builds numbers: von Neumann's construction 0 = ∅, 1 = {∅}, 2 = {∅, {∅}}, … defines the natural numbers inside axiomatic set theory.
Matching elements one-to-one compares the sizes of finite sets; the same idea applied to infinite sets shows that some infinite sets are strictly larger than others.
Cardinal numbers extend 'number of elements' from finite sets to all sets.
The Cartesian product, met here as a set of ordered pairs, can also be characterised by how functions into it behave.

objectives: Use x ∈ A, A ⊆ B and brace notation to describe finite sets, including the empty set ∅.
Compute unions, intersections and complements (relative to a stated universe) of finite sets and show them on Venn diagrams.
Form ordered pairs and Cartesian products A × B, and explain why (a, b) differs from {a, b}.
Count elements of finite sets, using |A × B| = |A|·|B| and |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|.
definitions: A set is a collection of distinct objects, its elements; x ∈ A means x is an element of A.
A ⊆ B (A is a subset of B) means every element of A is an element of B.
A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B} and A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}; the complement of A in a universe U is {x ∈ U : x ∉ A}.
The empty set ∅ is the set with no elements.

An ordered pair (a, b) has a first entry a and a second entry b, and (a, b) = (c, d) exactly when a = c and b = d. The Cartesian product A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B.
The cardinality |A| of a finite set A is the number of its elements.
keyResults: Two sets are equal exactly when they have the same elements (extensionality); order and repetition in a list do not matter.
∅ ⊆ A and A ⊆ A for every set A.
|A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| for finite sets A and B.
|A × B| = |A|·|B| for finite sets A and B.
A finite set with n elements has exactly 2ⁿ subsets.
misconceptions: Thinking ∅ and {∅} are the same set: {∅} has exactly one element.
Reading 'or' in a union as 'one but not both'; mathematical 'or' is inclusive.
Assuming (a, b) = (b, a); this holds only when a = b.
Taking a complement without saying which universe it is taken in.

topics.title: True, false, and, or, not
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Statements that are either true or false, combining them with and, or and not, and testing general claims with examples and counterexamples.

discoveries.note: Is every true statement about whole numbers provable? Gödel showed that any consistent, effectively axiomatised theory containing enough arithmetic leaves some true arithmetic statements unprovable.

objectives: Decide whether a simple mathematical statement is true or false and justify the answer.
Combine statements with and, or and not, reading 'or' inclusively.
Use a single counterexample to refute an 'every…' claim, and explain why examples alone cannot prove one.
definitions: A statement is a sentence that is either true or false.
'P and Q' is true when both are true; 'P or Q' is true when at least one is true; 'not P' is true exactly when P is false.
A counterexample to 'every x has property P' is a particular x that does not have property P.
keyResults: One counterexample is enough to show that a general claim is false.
Checking many examples can support a general claim but does not prove it.
misconceptions: Believing that several confirming examples prove a statement about all numbers.
Reading 'or' as exclusive.
Thinking the opposite of 'all are' is 'none are'; it is 'at least one is not'.

topics.title: Whole-number arithmetic
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: Multiplication and division of whole numbers, division with remainder, the commutative, associative and distributive laws, and why the standard written algorithms work.

discoveries.note: The laws that make arithmetic work (commutative, associative, distributive) later become the axioms of a ring.

objectives: Multiply and divide multi-digit whole numbers, explaining each step of the algorithms through place value and the distributive law.
Divide with remainder, writing a = qb + r with 0 ≤ r < b.
Use the commutative, associative and distributive laws to calculate flexibly, for example 7 × 98 = 7 × 100 − 7 × 2.
definitions: a × b is the total number of objects in a equal groups of b, or the number of cells in an a-by-b array.
Division with remainder: for whole numbers a and b with b > 0, there are unique whole numbers q and r with a = qb + r and 0 ≤ r < b.
The distributive law: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c.
keyResults: Multiplication is commutative and associative and distributes over addition.
The quotient and remainder in division with remainder are unique.
Division by zero is undefined: for instance, no number q satisfies q × 0 = 5.
misconceptions: Believing multiplication always makes a number bigger (false for 0 and 1, and later for fractions less than 1).
Allowing a remainder as large as, or larger than, the divisor.
Treating 'carrying' as a trick rather than as regrouping ten ones into one ten.

references.title: Understanding Numbers in Elementary School Mathematics
references.author: Hung-Hsi Wu

topics.title: Fractions and decimals
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: Fractions as numbers on the number line, equivalent fractions, comparing and adding fractions, and decimals as fractions whose denominators are powers of ten.

discoveries.note: Some numbers, such as √2, cannot be written as fractions at all.

objectives: Place fractions on a number line and explain a/b as a copies of 1/b.
Generate equivalent fractions and use them to compare, add and subtract fractions.
Convert between decimals with up to three places and fractions with denominators 10, 100 and 1000.
Multiply a fraction by a whole number.
definitions: For a whole number b > 0, 1/b is the length of each part when the unit interval is cut into b equal parts, and a/b is the length of a such parts.
a/b and c/d are equivalent (equal as numbers) when ad = bc.
A decimal such as 0.37 means 37/100.
keyResults: a/b = (na)/(nb) for every whole number n > 0.
a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/(bd).
A fraction in lowest terms has a terminating decimal expansion exactly when its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5.
misconceptions: Adding numerators and denominators: 1/2 + 1/3 is not 2/5.
Thinking a larger denominator means a larger fraction.
Believing 0.25 > 0.3 because 25 > 3.
Thinking fractions are only parts of shapes rather than numbers.

references.title: Understanding Numbers in Elementary School Mathematics
references.author: Hung-Hsi Wu

topics.title: Factors, multiples and primes
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: Factors and multiples, divisibility tests, prime and composite numbers, and writing numbers as products of primes.

discoveries.note: RSA encryption relies on the belief, widely held but not proved, that factoring very large numbers is computationally hard.
Unique factorisation can fail in other number systems: in ℤ[√−5], 6 = 2 · 3 = (1 + √−5)(1 − √−5).

objectives: List the factors of numbers up to 100 and find common factors and common multiples.
Classify numbers as prime or composite and use the sieve of Eratosthenes.
Write a whole number as a product of primes using a factor tree, and explain the divisibility tests for 2, 3, 5, 9 and 10.
definitions: b is a factor of a, and a is a multiple of b, if a = b × k for some whole number k.
A prime is a whole number greater than 1 whose only factors are 1 and itself; a composite number is a whole number greater than 1 that is not prime.
keyResults: Every whole number greater than 1 is a prime or a product of primes, and the product is unique apart from order (the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, proved later).
A number is divisible by 3 (or by 9) exactly when the sum of its digits is.
1 is neither prime nor composite.
misconceptions: Thinking 1 is prime.
Believing all odd numbers are prime, although 9 = 3 × 3.
Confusing factors with multiples.

topics.title: Expressions, unknowns and rules
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Numerical expressions and the order of operations, finding unknown numbers in equations such as 3 × □ = 24, and describing input–output rules.

discoveries.note: 'Multiply by 3, then add 1' is a chain of actions; to undo it, subtract 1 first and then divide by 3.

objectives: Evaluate expressions using brackets and the conventional order of operations.
Find the unknown in equations such as 3 × □ = 24 or □ + 17 = 40, explaining the method with inverse operations.
Describe input–output rules in words and with expressions such as 2 × n + 1, and complete tables from a rule.
definitions: An expression is a combination of numbers and operations, possibly with brackets, that names a number.
An equation states that two expressions have the same value.
An unknown is a number, shown by a box or a letter, whose value we are asked to find.
keyResults: Brackets group operations; without them, multiplication and division are carried out before addition and subtraction.
Adding a number is undone by subtracting it, and multiplying by a non-zero number is undone by dividing by it.
misconceptions: Working strictly left to right, so that 2 + 3 × 4 is taken to be 20.
Thinking an equation must have 'the answer' on the right of the equals sign.
Believing a letter stands for an object ('a for apples') rather than for a number.

topics.title: Area, perimeter and angles
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: Area as the number of unit squares that cover a shape, perimeter as the distance around it, area of rectangles, first volumes, and angles as amounts of turn measured in degrees.

discoveries.note: Which sets of points have an area at all? Measure theory answers this; with the axiom of choice, some sets cannot be given a countably additive area that is unchanged by sliding them.

objectives: Find areas by counting unit squares and by multiplying length by width, and compute perimeters.
Show that shapes with the same perimeter can have different areas, and vice versa.
Measure and draw angles in degrees, and classify triangles and quadrilaterals by their sides and angles.
Find the volume of a rectangular box by counting unit cubes.
definitions: Area is the amount of surface a shape covers, measured in square units.
Perimeter is the total length of the boundary of a shape.
An angle is the amount of turn between two rays from a common point; a full turn is 360°.
keyResults: The area of a rectangle is length × width.
The angles of a triangle in the plane add up to 180°.
The volume of a rectangular box is length × width × height.
misconceptions: Confusing area with perimeter.
Thinking an angle gets bigger when its arms are drawn longer.
Believing that shapes with equal perimeters must have equal areas.

topics.title: Symmetry: slides, turns and flips
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: Line and rotational symmetry, and moving shapes by slides (translations), turns (rotations) and flips (reflections), including doing one move after another and undoing a move.

discoveries.note: The symmetries of a shape can be combined and undone; together they form a group, such as the 8-element dihedral group of a square.
Doing one move after another, and undoing a move, are early examples of composing and reversing actions.

objectives: Identify lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry of shapes.
Perform slides, turns and flips on a grid and describe them precisely.
Find a move that undoes a given move, and explore what happens when two flips are done one after the other.
definitions: A line of symmetry divides a shape into two mirror-image halves.
A shape has rotational symmetry of order n if exactly n turns within one full revolution (including the full turn) leave it looking the same.
A slide moves every point the same distance in the same direction; a turn rotates about a fixed point; a flip reflects in a line.
keyResults: A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order n.
Slides, turns and flips do not change lengths or angles.
Flipping twice in the same line returns every point to where it started.
Two flips in parallel lines give a slide, and two flips in crossing lines give a turn about the crossing point.
misconceptions: Thinking the diagonals of every rectangle are lines of symmetry; this is true only for squares.
Believing a flip and a half turn always have the same effect.

topics.title: Estimation and rounding
topics.subject: analysis
topics.summary: Rounding to the nearest ten, hundred or tenth, estimating sums and products, and judging how far an estimate might be from the exact answer.

discoveries.note: Approximating more and more closely, with an error that can be made as small as we like, is the idea behind limits.
Computers round almost every non-integer calculation; numerical analysis tracks how such errors grow.

objectives: Round whole numbers and decimals to a given place, and explain the convention for halfway cases.
Estimate sums, differences and products before calculating, and use estimates to check answers.
Give lower and upper bounds for a quantity, such as 'between 300 and 400'.
definitions: Rounding replaces a number by a nearby simpler number, such as the nearest multiple of 10.
An estimate is an approximate value; its error is the difference between the estimate and the exact value.
A lower bound and an upper bound are numbers known to be at most and at least the quantity.
keyResults: Rounding a whole number to the nearest ten changes it by at most 5.
Rounding errors can accumulate: rounding many numbers before adding can be further off than rounding the total once.
misconceptions: Thinking an estimate is a wild guess rather than a reasoned approximation.
Believing that rounding at every step of a calculation never changes the final rounded answer.

topics.title: Systematic listing and counting
topics.subject: discrete
topics.summary: Finding all possibilities in an organised way (outfits, routes, arrangements, handshakes) using lists, tables and tree diagrams, and checking that nothing is missed or counted twice.

discoveries.note: Systematic counting grows into permutations, combinations and the binomial theorem.

objectives: List all combinations in small problems, such as outfits from 3 shirts and 2 pairs of trousers, using a table or tree diagram.
Explain how an organised list guarantees that no possibility is missed or repeated.
Discover that 3 shirts and 2 pairs of trousers give 3 × 2 outfits, and generalise.
definitions: A tree diagram shows each choice as a branch, so that each path from the start to an end is one possibility.
keyResults: If a first choice can be made in m ways and a second in n ways, there are m × n combined choices.
Three different objects can be arranged in a row in exactly 6 ways.
misconceptions: Counting the same possibility twice when order does not matter, as with handshakes.
Stopping when no new possibility comes to mind, instead of using a system.

topics.title: Dots and lines: networks and puzzles
topics.subject: discrete
topics.summary: Networks of dots joined by lines: tracing figures without lifting the pencil, finding routes, and counting how many lines meet at each dot.

discoveries.note: Finding shortest routes in huge networks, such as road maps, uses efficient algorithms such as Dijkstra's.

objectives: Decide by experiment which figures can be traced in one stroke without retracing a line.
Count the line ends at each dot and notice the pattern behind traceable figures.
Find shortest routes in a small road network with distances marked.
definitions: A network (graph) is a collection of dots (vertices) with lines (edges) joining some pairs of them.
The degree of a dot is the number of line ends at it.
keyResults: The degrees of all the dots add up to an even number: twice the number of lines.
A connected figure can be traced in one stroke exactly when it has either no dots or exactly two dots of odd degree.
misconceptions: Thinking whether a figure can be traced depends on its overall shape rather than on the degrees of its dots.
Believing the shortest route is always the one with the fewest roads.

topics.title: Data displays and the mean as a fair share
topics.subject: probability
topics.summary: Bar graphs, line plots and tables with scales; reading and comparing displays; spotting misleading graphs; and the mean as a fair share.

discoveries.note: A sample can look different from the whole population; statistics asks how different it is likely to be.

objectives: Draw and read bar graphs with scales and line plots, including measurements in fractions of a unit.
Answer comparison questions from displays and recognise misleading scales.
Interpret the mean as the amount each person would get if the total were shared equally.
definitions: A bar graph shows each category as a bar whose length represents its count or amount.
A scale states how many items each unit of length on an axis represents.
The mean of a list of numbers is their sum divided by how many numbers there are.
keyResults: A bar graph whose axis does not start at zero can exaggerate differences.
The mean multiplied by the number of values equals the total.
misconceptions: Reading bar heights without checking the scale.
Thinking the mean must be one of the data values.

topics.title: One thing after another
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Doing one action and then another: chains of actions on shapes, numbers and objects, how the order can matter, how to undo a chain by undoing its steps in reverse order, and arrow pictures showing how one thing leads to another.

discoveries.note: Chaining actions becomes composition of functions g ∘ f, and undoing a chain becomes the rule (g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹.
The socks-and-shoes rule (gh)⁻¹ = h⁻¹g⁻¹ holds in every group.

objectives: Carry out chains of actions such as 'add 5, then double' and predict their results.
Find examples where swapping the order of two actions changes the result, and examples where it does not.
Undo a chain of actions by undoing its steps in reverse order, as with socks and shoes.
Draw arrow pictures showing how objects are related or transformed, and follow paths of arrows.
definitions: Chaining two actions means doing the first and then doing the second to the result.
An arrow picture shows objects as dots and actions or relationships as arrows from one dot to another.
keyResults: 'Add 5, then double' and 'double, then add 5' usually give different results.
To undo 'put on socks, then put on shoes', take off the shoes first and then the socks.
Doing 'turn a quarter turn' four times in a row has the same effect as doing nothing.
misconceptions: Assuming the order of two actions never matters.
Undoing a chain by undoing its steps in the original order.

topics.title: Repetition and decisions
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: Repeating steps with loops, making decisions with if–then rules, and algorithms for arithmetic such as column addition, in unplugged activities and simple block-based programs.

discoveries.note: Can we always tell whether a program will stop? No algorithm can decide this for every program: the halting problem is undecidable.

objectives: Use a loop to shorten a sequence of repeated instructions, such as drawing a square.
Write if–then rules for sorting objects or playing a simple game.
Explain the written algorithm for column addition as a loop over place values with a carry.
definitions: A loop repeats a block of instructions a fixed number of times or until a condition holds.
A condition is a statement that is true or false, used to decide which instructions to follow.
keyResults: 'Repeat 4 times: move forward, turn right 90°' draws a square.
Column addition works through the digits from right to left, carrying 1 whenever a column sum is 10 or more.
misconceptions: Thinking a loop must run forever or exactly once.
Writing a stopping condition that can never become true, so that the loop never stops.

references.title: Computer Science Unplugged
references.author: Tim Bell, Ian H. Witten and Mike Fellows

topics.title: Secret codes
topics.subject: applied
topics.summary: Hiding messages with simple codes: Caesar shifts on an alphabet wheel, substitution ciphers, breaking codes by counting letter frequencies, and why the alphabet 'wraps around'.

discoveries.note: A Caesar shift is addition modulo 26.
Modern cryptography gets its security from number theory and computational hardness, not from keeping the method secret.

objectives: Encode and decode messages with a Caesar shift using an alphabet wheel.
Break a Caesar cipher by trying every shift, and a simple substitution cipher by counting letter frequencies.
Explain why shifting past Z wraps around to A.
definitions: A cipher is a rule for turning a message into a disguised form and back again.
A Caesar shift replaces each letter by the letter a fixed number of places later in the alphabet, wrapping round from Z to A.
The key is the secret information needed to decode a message, such as the size of the shift.
keyResults: A 26-letter alphabet has only 25 non-trivial Caesar shifts, so the cipher can be broken by trying them all.
A shift forward by k is undone by a shift forward by 26 − k.
In English text some letters, such as E, are much more common than others, which helps to break substitution ciphers.
misconceptions: Thinking a code is secure because the message looks scrambled.
Forgetting to wrap around at the end of the alphabet.

topics.title: Functions
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: A function assigns to each input in its domain exactly one output in its codomain. Arrow diagrams, the set-of-ordered-pairs definition, images, and the properties injective, surjective and bijective.

discoveries.note: A function into a Cartesian product A × B is exactly a pair of functions, one into A and one into B: the first example of a universal property.
Programming languages also have 'functions', but a program function may read input, change state or fail to return, so it need not be a mathematical function.

objectives: Decide whether a rule, table or arrow diagram defines a function from a given domain to a given codomain.
Identify the domain, codomain and image of a function, and explain why the image can be smaller than the codomain.
Describe a function as a set of ordered pairs and classify functions as injective, surjective or bijective.
Count the functions from a finite set A to a finite set B, and the injections when |A| ≤ |B|.
definitions: A function f : A → B assigns to each element a of the domain A exactly one element f(a) of the codomain B.
Formally, a function from A to B is a subset f ⊆ A × B such that for each a ∈ A there is exactly one b ∈ B with (a, b) ∈ f; the domain and codomain are part of the data.
The image of f is the set {f(a) : a ∈ A}, a subset of the codomain.
f is injective if f(a) = f(a′) implies a = a′, surjective if every b ∈ B equals f(a) for some a ∈ A, and bijective if it is both.
keyResults: There are |B|^|A| functions from a finite set A to a finite set B; in particular there is exactly one function from ∅ to any set.
If |A| = m ≤ n = |B|, there are n(n − 1)⋯(n − m + 1) injections from A to B.
For finite sets with |A| = |B|, a function A → B is injective if and only if it is surjective.
A function has an inverse function exactly when it is bijective.
misconceptions: Thinking a function must be given by a formula; any rule assigning exactly one output to each input is a function.
Believing every element of the codomain must be an output; that is surjectivity, not part of the definition.
Thinking a function may not send two different inputs to the same output.
Ignoring the codomain: n ↦ 2n is surjective as a function from ℤ to the even integers, but not as a function from ℤ to ℤ.

references.title: Functions and Graphs
references.author: I. M. Gelfand, E. G. Glagoleva and E. E. Shnol

topics.title: Relations, equivalence relations and partitions
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Relations as sets of ordered pairs, and the special relations (reflexive, symmetric and transitive) that sort a set into non-overlapping classes. 'Same remainder', 'same colour' and 'same shape' are first examples.

discoveries.note: Collapsing each class to a single point gives a quotient set; when the relation respects an operation, the quotient inherits it, giving quotient groups and rings such as ℤ/nℤ.
The quotient map A → A/~ is universal: every function out of A that is constant on equivalence classes factors through it in exactly one way.
Gluing points by an equivalence relation produces quotient spaces, such as a circle from an interval with its endpoints identified.

objectives: Represent a relation on a finite set as a set of ordered pairs, a table and an arrow diagram.
Test a relation for reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity, giving a counterexample whenever a property fails.
Pass between an equivalence relation and the partition formed by its equivalence classes.
definitions: A relation R on a set A is a subset of A × A; we write a R b when (a, b) ∈ R.
R is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive (a R a), symmetric (a R b implies b R a) and transitive (a R b and b R c imply a R c).
The equivalence class of a is [a] = {x ∈ A : x R a}.
A partition of A is a set of non-empty, pairwise disjoint subsets of A whose union is A.
keyResults: The equivalence classes of an equivalence relation on A form a partition of A, and every partition of A comes from exactly one equivalence relation.
Any two equivalence classes are either equal or disjoint.
For n ≥ 1, 'has the same remainder on division by n' is an equivalence relation on ℤ with exactly n classes.
misconceptions: Thinking symmetry and transitivity together imply reflexivity; the argument fails for an element related to nothing.
Treating an equivalence class as a single element instead of a set of elements.
Assuming every relation is symmetric, as 'is less than' shows it need not be.

references.title: How to Prove It: A Structured Approach
references.author: Daniel J. Velleman

topics.title: Set-builder notation, quantifiers and infinite sets
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Describing sets by properties, reading and writing 'for all' and 'there exists', negating quantified statements, and meeting the first infinite sets such as the natural numbers and the even numbers.

discoveries.note: Matching an infinite set one-to-one with ℕ, as with the even numbers, is the starting point of countability.
Quantifiers become part of a precise formal language with explicit rules of inference.

objectives: Read and write sets in set-builder notation, such as {n ∈ ℕ : n is even}.
Translate between everyday sentences and statements using ∀ and ∃, and negate them correctly.
Recognise ℕ, ℤ and the even numbers as infinite sets and explain why no finite list contains all natural numbers.
definitions: {x ∈ A : P(x)} is the set of those elements x of A for which P(x) is true.
∀x ∈ A, P(x) means P(x) holds for every x in A; ∃x ∈ A, P(x) means P(x) holds for at least one x in A.
A set is finite if its elements can be listed as a₁, …, aₙ for some natural number n (n = 0 gives the empty set); otherwise it is infinite.
keyResults: 'Not every x has P' is equivalent to 'some x does not have P', and 'no x has P' is equivalent to 'every x fails P'.
The order of mixed quantifiers matters: in ℕ, ∀x ∃y (y > x) is true but ∃y ∀x (y > x) is false.
ℕ is infinite: given any finite list of natural numbers, one more than the largest is not on the list.
misconceptions: Swapping the order of ∀ and ∃ and expecting the meaning to stay the same.
Thinking a statement about all elements of the empty set must be false; it is vacuously true.
Treating 'infinity' as a very large natural number.

topics.title: Integers
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: The integers ℤ = {…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …} on the number line: additive inverses, the laws of arithmetic, the sign rules with a proof that (−a)(−b) = ab, and why most integers have no multiplicative inverse in ℤ.

discoveries.note: Under addition the integers have an identity (0) and every element has an inverse: they form a group. Under multiplication only 1 and −1 have inverses, so ℤ is a ring but not a field.
(ℤ, +) is the infinite cyclic group, generated by 1.
(ℤ, +, ×) is the prototype of a commutative ring with identity; enlarging it to ℚ gives every non-zero element a multiplicative inverse.
On a clock, adding 12 hours changes nothing: arithmetic with remainders wraps the infinite line of integers into a finite circle.
a ≡ b (mod n) means that n divides a − b; congruence respects addition and multiplication.
Grouping integers by their remainder on division by n splits ℤ into n families, the classes of an equivalence relation.
The integers can be constructed from the natural numbers as equivalence classes of pairs (a, b), thought of as a − b.

objectives: Place integers on the number line and interpret negative numbers as opposites, debts, temperatures below zero or positions left of zero.
Add, subtract and multiply integers, explaining subtraction as adding the additive inverse.
Prove from the distributive law that a · 0 = 0, (−a)b = −(ab) and (−a)(−b) = ab.
Explain why every integer has an additive inverse in ℤ while only 1 and −1 have multiplicative inverses in ℤ.
definitions: The integers are the whole numbers 0, 1, 2, … together with their negatives −1, −2, −3, ….
The additive inverse (opposite) of a is the integer −a with a + (−a) = 0.
Subtraction is defined by a − b = a + (−b).
A multiplicative inverse of a is a number b with ab = 1.
keyResults: Addition and multiplication of integers are commutative and associative, multiplication distributes over addition, 0 is the additive identity and 1 the multiplicative identity.
Every integer has exactly one additive inverse.
a · 0 = 0 and (−a)(−b) = ab for all integers a and b, as consequences of the distributive law.
The only integers with a multiplicative inverse in ℤ are 1 and −1.
ℤ has no zero divisors: if ab = 0 then a = 0 or b = 0.
misconceptions: Reading '−' only as 'negative': −a is positive when a is negative, and '−' can also mean 'subtract' or 'the opposite of'.
Believing (−a)(−b) = ab is an arbitrary convention; it is forced by the distributive law.
Thinking −5 > −2 because 5 > 2.
Assuming every integer has an integer reciprocal.

references.title: Algebra
references.author: I. M. Gelfand and A. Shen

references.title: Understanding Numbers in Elementary School Mathematics
references.author: Hung-Hsi Wu

topics.title: Clock arithmetic: remainders and modular arithmetic
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: Arithmetic on a clock: working with remainders on division by n, addition and multiplication tables modulo n, repeating patterns, and calendar and game puzzles.

discoveries.note: Clock arithmetic becomes the theory of congruences: a ≡ b (mod n) when n divides a − b, an equivalence relation that respects + and ×.
The hours of a 12-hour clock under addition form a cyclic group of order 12.
Fast modular exponentiation is the engine of RSA and Diffie–Hellman key exchange.

objectives: Compute sums and products modulo n using remainders, for example on a 12-hour clock or in a 7-day week.
Build addition and multiplication tables modulo n and look for patterns, such as which remainders have a multiplicative partner.
Explain why the remainder of a sum or product depends only on the remainders of its parts.
definitions: a mod n is the remainder r, with 0 ≤ r < n, when a is divided by n.
Addition modulo n: add as usual and take the remainder on division by n; multiplication modulo n works the same way.
keyResults: (a + b) mod n = ((a mod n) + (b mod n)) mod n, and similarly for multiplication.
A remainder a has a partner b with ab mod n = 1 exactly when a and n have no common factor greater than 1 (proved later with Euclid's algorithm).
Modulo a prime p, every non-zero remainder has such a partner.
misconceptions: Thinking modular arithmetic is only about 12-hour clocks.
Believing that if ab mod n = 0 then a or b must be 0 mod n; in fact 3 × 4 mod 12 = 0.
Forgetting that a remainder must lie between 0 and n − 1.

topics.title: Rational numbers
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: The rational numbers as quotients of integers: arithmetic with negative fractions, reciprocals, terminating and repeating decimals, and density on the number line.

discoveries.note: ℚ is a field: every non-zero element has a multiplicative inverse.
Although the rationals are dense, they can be listed one after another: ℚ is countable.

objectives: Add, subtract, multiply and divide rational numbers, including negative ones.
Explain why every non-zero rational number has a reciprocal, in contrast with the integers.
Convert between fractions and decimals, and show that a fraction's decimal expansion terminates or eventually repeats.
definitions: A rational number is a number a/b with a and b integers and b ≠ 0; a/b = c/d when ad = bc.
The reciprocal of a non-zero rational number a/b is b/a.
keyResults: ℚ is closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division by non-zero numbers.
The decimal expansion of a rational number terminates or eventually repeats, and every such decimal represents a rational number.
Between any two distinct rational numbers there is another, for example their average.
misconceptions: Thinking division always makes smaller; dividing by 1/2 doubles.
Believing 0.999… is less than 1.
Thinking the number line is full once every fraction is placed; √2 is still missing.

topics.title: Ratios, rates and proportional reasoning
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: Ratios, unit rates, percentages and proportional relationships, using tables, double number lines and the constant of proportionality.

discoveries.note: When outcomes are equally likely, a probability is the ratio of favourable outcomes to all outcomes.

objectives: Solve ratio and rate problems using tables, double number lines and unit rates.
Recognise proportional relationships y = kx in tables, graphs and situations, and identify the constant k.
Compute percentages and percentage changes, and explain why a 10% rise followed by a 10% fall does not return to the start.
definitions: A ratio a : b compares two quantities; it is equivalent to ka : kb for every k > 0.
A unit rate is the amount of one quantity per one unit of another.
Quantities x and y are proportional if y = kx for a fixed constant k.
keyResults: The graph of a proportional relationship is a straight line through the origin.
p% of x is (p/100) · x.
Successive percentage changes multiply: a 10% increase and then a 10% decrease give an overall factor of 1.1 × 0.9 = 0.99.
misconceptions: Using additive reasoning ('3 more') where multiplicative reasoning ('3 times as many') is needed.
Thinking every linear relationship is proportional; y = 2x + 1 is not.
Adding successive percentage changes.

topics.title: Variables and algebraic expressions
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Letters as variables standing for numbers, writing and evaluating algebraic expressions, combining like terms, using the distributive law, and the laws of exponents for whole-number powers.

discoveries.note: The rules for manipulating expressions are the laws of a commutative ring, so the same manipulations are valid wherever those laws hold, for example with remainders modulo n.

objectives: Write algebraic expressions for situations and evaluate them for given values, including negative ones.
Simplify expressions by combining like terms, and expand and factorise using the distributive law.
Use the laws of exponents aᵐaⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ and (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ for whole-number exponents.
definitions: A variable is a letter that stands for any number from a given set.
Two expressions are equivalent if they have the same value for every value of their variables.
For a whole number n ≥ 1, aⁿ is the product of n factors each equal to a; a⁰ = 1 for a ≠ 0.
keyResults: a(b + c) = ab + ac for all numbers a, b and c.
aᵐ · aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ and (ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ.
Testing an equivalence with a few values can refute it but cannot prove it.
misconceptions: Writing (a + b)² = a² + b².
Treating 2x and x² as the same.
Believing x must be positive, or that different letters must have different values.

references.title: Algebra
references.author: I. M. Gelfand and A. Shen

topics.title: Linear equations and inequalities
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Solving linear equations and inequalities in one variable by doing the same thing to both sides, checking solutions, and modelling word problems.

discoveries.note: Systems of many linear equations in many unknowns are the starting point of linear algebra.

objectives: Solve linear equations with the variable on both sides, including fractions and negative coefficients.
Recognise equations with exactly one solution, no solution or infinitely many solutions.
Solve linear inequalities, reversing the inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
definitions: A linear equation in x is one that can be written as ax + b = cx + d.
A solution is a value of the variable that makes the equation true.
Two equations are equivalent if they have the same solutions.
keyResults: Adding the same number to both sides, or multiplying both sides by the same non-zero number, gives an equivalent equation.
ax = b has exactly one solution if a ≠ 0, none if a = 0 and b ≠ 0, and every number as a solution if a = b = 0.
Multiplying both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses its direction.
misconceptions: Multiplying both sides by zero, or by an expression that might be zero, and expecting an equivalent equation.
Forgetting to reverse an inequality after multiplying by a negative number.
Applying an operation to only one term on a side of the equation.

references.title: Algebra
references.author: I. M. Gelfand and A. Shen

topics.title: Linear relationships and simultaneous equations
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Lines in the coordinate plane: slope as a constant rate of change, the form y = mx + b, linear functions, and solving pairs of simultaneous linear equations graphically and algebraically.

discoveries.note: Composing two linear functions gives another: applying x ↦ m₂x + b₂ and then x ↦ m₁x + b₁ gives x ↦ m₁m₂x + (m₁b₂ + b₁).

objectives: Compute the slope of a line from two points and interpret it as a rate of change.
Write the equation of a line from its slope and a point, and recognise linear functions in tables, graphs and formulas.
Solve two simultaneous linear equations by substitution, elimination and graphing, and interpret the cases with no solution or infinitely many.
definitions: The slope of the line through (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂), with x₁ ≠ x₂, is (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
A linear function has the form f(x) = mx + b.
A solution of a system of equations satisfies every equation in the system at once.
keyResults: The slope between any two points on a non-vertical line is the same.
Two distinct lines in the plane meet in exactly one point unless they are parallel, that is, have equal slopes or are both vertical.
A system of two linear equations in two unknowns has exactly one solution, no solution, or infinitely many solutions.
misconceptions: Computing slope as 'run over rise'.
Believing every straight-line relationship is proportional.
Giving a vertical line slope zero; its slope is undefined.

references.title: Algebra
references.author: I. M. Gelfand and A. Shen

topics.title: The coordinate plane
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: Locating points with ordered pairs in all four quadrants, distances along grid lines, reflections in the axes, and plotting data and relationships.

discoveries.note: Points of the plane can be added and scaled as vectors, giving the vector space ℝ².

objectives: Plot and read points (x, y) with integer and rational coordinates in all four quadrants.
Find horizontal and vertical distances between points using absolute value.
Reflect points in the axes and describe the effect on their coordinates.
definitions: The coordinate plane is formed by two perpendicular number lines, the x-axis and the y-axis, meeting at the origin (0, 0).
The coordinates (a, b) of a point give its horizontal and vertical positions relative to the origin.
keyResults: Reflecting (a, b) in the x-axis gives (a, −b), and in the y-axis gives (−a, b).
The distance between (a, b) and (c, b) is |a − c|.
Each point of the plane corresponds to exactly one ordered pair of real numbers.
misconceptions: Swapping the coordinates, plotting (3, 2) at (2, 3).
Counting grid lines rather than unit intervals when finding distances.

topics.title: The Pythagorean theorem
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: The relation a² + b² = c² for right triangles, proofs by rearrangement, the converse, square roots, and distances in the coordinate plane.

discoveries.note: A square of side 1 has a diagonal of length √2, which cannot be written as a fraction of whole numbers.

The primitive Pythagorean triples are exactly (m² − n², 2mn, m² + n²), up to swapping the first two, with m > n > 0 coprime and not both odd. For n ≥ 3, xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ has no solutions in positive integers (Fermat's Last Theorem, proved by Wiles in 1995).

objectives: Explain at least one proof of the Pythagorean theorem, such as a rearrangement proof.
Use the theorem and its converse to find missing lengths and to test whether a triangle is right-angled.
Compute the distance between two points in the coordinate plane.
definitions: A right triangle has one angle of 90°; the side opposite it is the hypotenuse.
For x ≥ 0, the square root √x is the non-negative number whose square is x.
keyResults: Pythagorean theorem: in a right triangle with legs a, b and hypotenuse c, a² + b² = c².
Converse: if the sides of a triangle satisfy a² + b² = c², the triangle has a right angle opposite the side c.
The distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²).
There are infinitely many Pythagorean triples, such as (3, 4, 5) and (5, 12, 13).
misconceptions: Applying a² + b² = c² to triangles that are not right-angled.
Taking c to be any side rather than the hypotenuse.
Thinking √(a² + b²) = a + b.

topics.title: Rigid motions, congruence and similarity
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: Translations, rotations, reflections and dilations in the coordinate plane; congruence as the existence of a rigid motion, similarity as a dilation followed by a rigid motion; and composing transformations.

discoveries.note: Isometries are the structure-preserving maps of the plane with its distances: composites and inverses of isometries are again isometries.
Klein's idea: a geometry is the study of the properties left unchanged by a group of transformations.

objectives: Describe translations, rotations by multiples of 90° and reflections in the axes using coordinates.
Decide whether two figures are congruent or similar by finding a sequence of transformations.
Compose transformations and identify the result; for example, two reflections in intersecting lines give a rotation.
definitions: A rigid motion (isometry) is a transformation of the plane that preserves distances.
Two figures are congruent if some rigid motion maps one onto the other.
A dilation with centre O and scale factor k > 0 sends each point P to the point P′ on the ray OP with OP′ = k · OP.
Two figures are similar if a dilation followed by a rigid motion maps one onto the other.
keyResults: Rigid motions preserve lengths and angle measures; dilations preserve angle measures and multiply lengths by k.
The composite of two rigid motions is a rigid motion, and every rigid motion has an inverse that is also a rigid motion.
Under a dilation with scale factor k, areas are multiplied by k².
misconceptions: Thinking similar figures must be the same size, or that any two rectangles are similar.
Believing the order of transformations never matters; a rotation followed by a translation generally differs from the reverse order.

topics.title: Graphs of change
topics.subject: analysis
topics.summary: Reading and sketching graphs that show how one quantity changes with another, such as distance against time, and interpreting steepness as rate of change.

discoveries.note: Shrinking the interval turns an average rate of change into an instantaneous rate: the derivative.

objectives: Interpret distance–time and other real-world graphs, describing where a quantity increases, decreases or stays constant.
Compute average rates of change between two points of a graph or table.
Sketch a graph from a verbal description, and describe a situation from a graph.
definitions: The average rate of change of y between x = a and x = b is (y(b) − y(a))/(b − a).
A graph is increasing on an interval if y gets larger whenever x gets larger within that interval.
keyResults: On a distance–time graph, the slope of a segment is the average speed over that time interval.
A horizontal segment means the quantity is not changing.
Two situations can have the same average rate over an interval but behave differently within it.
misconceptions: Reading a distance–time graph as a picture of the path travelled, such as a hill.
Thinking a steeper graph means a larger quantity rather than a faster change.

topics.title: Counting principles
topics.subject: discrete
topics.summary: The addition and multiplication principles, ordered arrangements (permutations), factorial notation and complementary counting.

discoveries.note: Counting equally likely outcomes gives probabilities.

objectives: Apply the addition and multiplication principles to count outcomes.
Count arrangements of n objects (n!) and ordered selections of k objects from n.
Use complementary counting, for example to count passwords containing at least one digit.
definitions: A permutation is an ordered arrangement of objects.
keyResults: Addition principle: if A and B are disjoint finite sets, |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B|.
Multiplication principle: |A × B| = |A| · |B|.
The number of ordered selections of k objects from n distinct objects is n!/(n − k)!.
misconceptions: Adding where the multiplication principle applies, or multiplying where the addition principle applies.
Counting overlapping cases twice.

topics.title: Statistics: centre, spread and distributions
topics.subject: probability
topics.summary: Statistical questions, distributions of data, measures of centre (mean, median, mode) and spread (range, interquartile range), box plots and histograms.

discoveries.note: Formal statistics models data as random samples and quantifies uncertainty with confidence intervals and tests.

objectives: Distinguish statistical questions, which anticipate variability, from non-statistical ones.
Compute mean, median, mode, range and interquartile range, and choose an appropriate summary.
Draw and compare histograms and box plots of two data sets.
definitions: The median is the middle value of an ordered list, or the mean of the two middle values.
The range is the largest value minus the smallest; the interquartile range is Q₃ − Q₁.
An outlier is a value far from the rest of the data.
keyResults: The median is resistant to outliers; the mean is not.
Two data sets can have the same mean but very different spreads.
misconceptions: Thinking the mean is always the best summary of centre.
Comparing two groups by their centres alone and ignoring spread.

references.title: Statistics
references.author: David Freedman, Robert Pisani and Roger Purves

topics.title: Probability
topics.subject: probability
topics.summary: Probability as a number from 0 to 1, sample spaces of equally likely outcomes, experimental (relative frequency) versus theoretical probability, and simulation.

discoveries.note: Kolmogorov (1933) placed probability on the foundation of measure theory.

objectives: List sample spaces for simple experiments, using tables or tree diagrams for two stages.
Compute probabilities of events with equally likely outcomes as fractions.
Compare theoretical probabilities with relative frequencies from repeated trials or simulations.
definitions: A sample space is the set of possible outcomes of an experiment; an event is a subset of the sample space.
If all outcomes in a finite sample space S are equally likely, the probability of an event A is P(A) = |A|/|S|.
The relative frequency of an event in n trials is the number of times it occurred divided by n.
keyResults: 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1, P(S) = 1, and P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
As the number of independent trials grows, relative frequencies tend to settle near the probability (the law of large numbers, stated informally).
misconceptions: The gambler's fallacy: thinking a fair coin is 'due' to land heads after several tails.
Assuming all outcomes are equally likely, for example all sums of two dice.
Believing a probability of 1/6 means the event happens exactly once in every 6 trials.

topics.title: Function machines in sequence
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Feeding the output of one function into another, the identity function that returns its input unchanged, inverse functions that undo, and tables and arrow diagrams for chained functions.

discoveries.note: Writing 'f, then g' as g ∘ f and proving the laws it obeys (associativity and the identity laws) is the next step.

objectives: Compute the result of applying one function and then another, using tables, arrow diagrams and formulas.
Recognise the identity function on a set and explain why chaining it with any function changes nothing.
Find inverses of simple bijections, such as x ↦ x + 3 or x ↦ 2x on ℚ, and check that they undo the original.
definitions: Applying f : A → B and then g : B → C sends each a in A to g(f(a)) in C.
The identity function on A sends each element of A to itself.
A function g undoes f if g(f(a)) = a for every a in the domain of f.
keyResults: Chaining is possible only when every output of the first function is an allowed input of the second.
Chaining with an identity function, before or after, gives back the original function.
If f and g can both be undone, then 'f, then g' is undone by 'undo g, then undo f'.
misconceptions: Writing the chain 'first f, then g' as f(g(x)).
Thinking every function can be undone; x ↦ x² on ℤ cannot.
Ignoring whether the outputs of the first function lie in the domain of the second.

topics.title: Diagrams where paths agree
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Square diagrams of functions in which the two routes from one corner to the opposite corner give the same result, and how 'preserving an operation' can be expressed by such a square, as when converting units respects adding lengths.

discoveries.note: In category theory, commutative diagrams are the main way of stating equations between composites of morphisms.
Homomorphisms are exactly the maps for which the square comparing 'operate, then map' with 'map, then operate' commutes.

objectives: Check whether the two routes around a square of functions agree for every input.
Express statements such as 'doubling then adding 2 equals adding 1 then doubling' as agreeing paths in a diagram.
Recognise maps that preserve an operation, f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b), such as converting metres to centimetres, as diagrams whose paths agree.
definitions: A diagram of functions shows sets at its corners and functions as arrows between them.
A square diagram commutes when the two routes from the starting corner to the opposite corner give the same output for every input.
keyResults: Converting metres to centimetres, x ↦ 100x, respects addition: 100(a + b) = 100a + 100b.
x ↦ x + 1 does not respect addition: (a + b) + 1 ≠ (a + 1) + (b + 1).
If two commuting squares are placed side by side, the outer rectangle they form also commutes.
misconceptions: Checking that the routes agree for one input and concluding that the diagram commutes.
Thinking a diagram commutes just because all its arrows can be drawn.

topics.title: Programming for mathematics
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: Writing short Python programs that use variables, loops, conditionals and functions to explore mathematics: generating sequences, testing conjectures on many cases, and representing numbers in binary.

discoveries.note: Floating-point rounding, visible in 0.1 + 0.2, is studied systematically in numerical analysis.
Computer experiments suggest conjectures and find counterexamples in research mathematics.

objectives: Write programs with variables, loops, conditionals and functions to compute sums, tables and sequences.
Use a program to test a conjecture on many cases, and explain why this is evidence but not proof.
Convert between decimal and binary representations, by hand and in code.
definitions: A program variable names a stored value that can change while the program runs.
A program function takes inputs (arguments) and returns an output, possibly with other effects.
In base 2, the digits 0 and 1 count ones, twos, fours, eights and so on.
keyResults: Every positive whole number has exactly one binary representation without leading zeros.
Checking a statement for the first million cases is experimental evidence, not a proof.
Floating-point numbers are approximations: in Python, 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluates to False.
misconceptions: Reading '=' in a program (assignment) as mathematical equality.
Believing a program that runs without errors must compute the right answer.
Assuming computer arithmetic with decimals is exact.

topics.title: Check digits and error detection
topics.subject: applied
topics.summary: How ISBNs, bank cards and barcodes catch typing errors with check digits computed by modular arithmetic, and how parity bits protect digital data.

discoveries.note: Error-correcting codes go further and correct errors, and Shannon's noisy-channel theorem limits how efficiently this can be done.

objectives: Compute and verify ISBN-10 and ISBN-13 check digits.
Explain why the ISBN-10 scheme detects every single-digit error and every swap of two adjacent digits.
Add a parity bit to binary data and show that it detects any single flipped bit.
definitions: A check digit is an extra digit computed from the others so that certain errors can be detected.
The digits d₁, …, d₁₀ of an ISBN-10 satisfy 1·d₁ + 2·d₂ + ⋯ + 10·d₁₀ ≡ 0 (mod 11), with X standing for 10.
A parity bit is chosen so that the total number of 1s is even.
keyResults: ISBN-10 detects every single-digit error and every adjacent transposition, because 11 is prime and the weights are distinct and non-zero modulo 11.
ISBN-13, with weights alternating 1 and 3 modulo 10, detects every single-digit error but misses adjacent transpositions of digits that differ by 5.
A single parity bit detects any odd number of flipped bits and no even number.
misconceptions: Thinking a check digit can correct errors; simple check digits only detect them.
Believing every possible error is detected.

topics.title: Propositional logic and truth tables
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Truth tables, implication with its converse and contrapositive, logical equivalence and tautologies: the logic of 'and', 'or', 'not' and 'if…then' made exact.

discoveries.note: Deciding whether a propositional formula is satisfiable (SAT) was the first problem proved NP-complete (Cook–Levin theorem).
In constructive logic and type theory, a proof of P → Q is a method turning proofs of P into proofs of Q, and P ∨ ¬P is not assumed as a law.

objectives: Build truth tables for compound statements and use them to test logical equivalence.
Distinguish an implication from its converse, inverse and contrapositive.
Negate compound and quantified statements, including implications.
definitions: P → Q is false only when P is true and Q is false.
Two formulas are logically equivalent if they have the same truth value under every assignment of truth values to their variables.
A tautology is a formula that is true under every assignment.
keyResults: P → Q is logically equivalent to its contrapositive ¬Q → ¬P, but not to its converse Q → P.
De Morgan's laws: ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q and ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q.
misconceptions: Thinking an implication with a false hypothesis is false; it is true.
Treating the converse of an implication as equivalent to it.
Reading 'if P then Q' as claiming that P causes Q.

references.title: How to Prove It: A Structured Approach
references.author: Daniel J. Velleman

topics.title: Proof: direct, contrapositive, contradiction and induction
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: How mathematicians establish general truths: direct proof, proof by cases, contrapositive, contradiction and mathematical induction, with attention to clear writing and hidden assumptions.

discoveries.note: A proof assistant such as Lean checks every step of a proof mechanically, including the base case and inductive step.
Proofs can themselves be studied as mathematical objects; Gentzen's cut-elimination theorem is a central example.

objectives: Write direct and contrapositive proofs about integers, such as 'if n² is even then n is even'.
Prove a statement by contradiction, for example that there are infinitely many primes.
Prove statements about all natural numbers by ordinary and by strong induction.
Find gaps, circular reasoning and unstated assumptions in a proposed proof.
definitions: A proof is a finite chain of justified steps leading from accepted assumptions to a conclusion.
Induction: if P(0) holds and P(n) implies P(n + 1) for every n, then P(n) holds for every natural number n.
Strong induction: if, for every n, P(k) for all k < n implies P(n), then P(n) holds for every n.
keyResults: Ordinary induction, strong induction and the well-ordering principle for ℕ are interderivable (given the basic properties of ℕ).
1 + 2 + ⋯ + n = n(n + 1)/2 for every natural number n.
There are infinitely many prime numbers (Euclid).
misconceptions: Proving the converse instead of the statement asked for.
Checking the inductive step but forgetting the base case.
Assuming what is to be proved.
Reaching a contradiction from an extra, unjustified assumption and blaming the hypothesis.

references.title: How to Prove It: A Structured Approach
references.author: Daniel J. Velleman

topics.title: Countability and Cantor's diagonal argument
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Comparing infinite sets by bijections: ℕ, ℤ and ℚ are countable, every set is strictly smaller than its power set, and Cantor's diagonal argument shows that the real numbers are uncountable.

discoveries.note: Is there a set strictly larger than ℕ but smaller than ℝ? This is the continuum hypothesis; Gödel (1940) and Cohen (1963) showed that, if ZFC is consistent, it can be neither proved nor refuted in ZFC.
A diagonal idea reappears in Gödel's proof through a self-referential sentence; the resemblance is genuine in spirit, but Gödel's diagonal lemma is a different construction.

objectives: Show that ℤ and ℚ are countable by constructing explicit enumerations or bijections.
Define the power set P(A) and prove Cantor's theorem that no function A → P(A) is surjective.
Reproduce Cantor's diagonal argument that [0, 1) is uncountable, handling numbers with two decimal expansions.
definitions: Sets A and B have the same cardinality if there is a bijection A → B.
A set is countable if it is finite or has the same cardinality as ℕ; otherwise it is uncountable.
The power set P(A) is the set of all subsets of A.
keyResults: ℤ, ℚ and ℕ × ℕ are countable.
A countable union of countable sets is countable (the general statement uses the axiom of countable choice).
Cantor's theorem: for every set A there is no surjection from A onto P(A).
ℝ is uncountable; in fact ℝ and P(ℕ) have the same cardinality.
misconceptions: Thinking a proper subset of an infinite set must be smaller: ℕ and the even numbers have the same cardinality.
Objecting that the diagonal number 'can just be added to the list'; the argument shows that every list misses some number.
Forgetting that 0.4999… = 0.5, which a careful diagonal argument must avoid (for example by never changing a digit to 0 or 9).

references.title: Proofs from THE BOOK
references.author: Martin Aigner and Günter M. Ziegler

topics.title: Russell's paradox and why sets need axioms
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Naive comprehension, the idea that every property defines a set, is inconsistent: the set of all sets that are not members of themselves cannot exist. Axiomatic set theory replaces comprehension with safer principles such as separation.

discoveries.note: Zermelo proposed axioms avoiding the paradox in 1908; with the axiom of replacement (Fraenkel, Skolem) and the axiom of choice these became ZFC.
Russell's own response was a theory of types, which stratifies objects by type; modern type theories descend in part from this idea.

objectives: State the naive comprehension principle and derive Russell's contradiction from it.
Explain how the separation axiom, which only forms {x ∈ A : P(x)} inside an existing set A, blocks the paradox, and deduce that there is no set of all sets.
Distinguish naive set theory, a useful informal language, from axiomatic set theory, a precise theory.
definitions: Naive comprehension: for every property P there is a set {x : P(x)}.
Russell's set is R = {x : x ∉ x}.
Separation: for every set A and property P, {x ∈ A : P(x)} is a set.
keyResults: Naive comprehension is inconsistent: it gives R ∈ R if and only if R ∉ R.
With separation, for any set A the set {x ∈ A : x ∉ x} is not an element of A; hence no set contains every set.
Ordinary mathematics can be carried out in axiomatic set theories such as ZFC that avoid the paradox.
misconceptions: Thinking the paradox shows mathematics is inconsistent; it shows naive comprehension is.
Treating Russell's paradox and the liar paradox as the same argument; they are analogous, not identical.
Believing ZF avoids the paradox by banning x ∈ x. ZF does prove x ∉ x, but from the separate axiom of foundation; the paradox is blocked by restricting comprehension to separation.

topics.title: Real numbers and irrationality
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: The real number line: proofs that √2 and other numbers are irrational, decimal expansions, intervals and absolute value, and an informal statement of completeness.

discoveries.note: A decimal expansion is an infinite series; 0.999… = 1 because its partial sums converge to 1.
