objectives: Prove that √2 is irrational, and generalise to √n for every positive integer n that is not a perfect square.
Describe real numbers by decimal expansions and order them; work with intervals and absolute value.
State informally that every non-empty set of reals that is bounded above has a least upper bound, and give a set of rationals with no least upper bound in ℚ.
definitions: A real number is irrational if it is not rational.
|x| = x if x ≥ 0 and |x| = −x if x < 0; |x − y| is the distance between x and y.
An upper bound of a set S is a number b with s ≤ b for all s ∈ S; the least upper bound (supremum) is the smallest such b.
keyResults: √2 is irrational.
The sum of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational.
Completeness: every non-empty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a least upper bound in ℝ; ℚ does not have this property.
Triangle inequality: |x + y| ≤ |x| + |y|.
misconceptions: Thinking π equals 22/7 or 3.14 exactly.
Believing an infinite decimal that never repeats can be written as a fraction.
Thinking the product of two irrational numbers must be irrational; √2 · √2 = 2.

topics.title: Complex numbers
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: Complex numbers a + bi: arithmetic, the complex plane, modulus and argument, polar form, De Moivre's theorem, roots of unity and the roots of quadratic equations.

discoveries.note: ℂ can be constructed as the quotient ring ℝ[x]/(x² + 1).

objectives: Add, multiply and divide complex numbers and represent them in the complex plane.
Convert between Cartesian and polar forms and interpret multiplication as rotation combined with scaling.
Use De Moivre's theorem to find the n-th roots of unity, and solve quadratics with negative discriminant.
definitions: A complex number is z = a + bi with a and b real and i² = −1; ℂ denotes the set of complex numbers.
The modulus of z = a + bi is |z| = √(a² + b²), and its conjugate is z̄ = a − bi.
Polar form: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), where r = |z| and θ is an argument of z.
keyResults: Multiplying complex numbers multiplies their moduli and adds their arguments.
De Moivre: (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ for every integer n.
There are exactly n complex n-th roots of unity, and they are the vertices of a regular n-gon.
Every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has a complex root (the fundamental theorem of algebra, proved later).
misconceptions: Thinking complex numbers are 'imaginary' in the sense of illegitimate.
Using √(ab) = √a · √b for negative a and b: √(−1) · √(−1) = −1, not √1 = 1.
Believing ℂ can be ordered in a way compatible with its arithmetic, as ℝ can.

topics.title: Divisibility, Euclid's algorithm and unique factorisation
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: Divisibility of integers, greatest common divisors, Euclid's algorithm, Bézout's identity and a proof of the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.

discoveries.note: Euclid's algorithm works in any Euclidean domain, such as polynomials over a field or the Gaussian integers ℤ[i], which therefore also have unique factorisation.
Lamé's theorem: the number of division steps in Euclid's algorithm is at most five times the number of decimal digits of the smaller number.

objectives: Compute gcd(a, b) with Euclid's algorithm and express it as ax + by.
Prove Euclid's lemma: if a prime p divides ab, then p divides a or p divides b.
Prove the existence and uniqueness of prime factorisation.
definitions: a | b means b = ak for some integer k.
gcd(a, b), for a and b not both zero, is the greatest integer dividing both.
Integers a and b are coprime if gcd(a, b) = 1.
keyResults: Bézout: if a and b are not both zero, there are integers x and y with ax + by = gcd(a, b).
Euclid's lemma holds for every prime p.
Fundamental theorem of arithmetic: every integer n > 1 is a product of primes, uniquely apart from order.
Euclid's algorithm terminates because the remainders strictly decrease.
misconceptions: Thinking unique factorisation is obvious; it fails in some number systems and needs proof.
Assuming that if d divides ab then d divides a or b when d is not prime; 4 divides 2 · 2 but not 2.
Confusing the greatest common divisor with the least common multiple.

references.title: An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers
references.author: G. H. Hardy and E. M. Wright

references.title: An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers
references.author: Ivan Niven, Herbert S. Zuckerman and Hugh L. Montgomery

topics.title: Polynomials
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Polynomial expressions and their arithmetic, factorisation, long division, the remainder and factor theorems, and the link between roots and factors.

discoveries.note: Is there a formula with radicals for the roots of every polynomial? For degree five and above there is not (Abel–Ruffini), and Galois theory explains why.
Most roots cannot be written exactly, but they can be approximated to any accuracy, for instance by Newton's method.

objectives: Add, multiply and factorise polynomials, including special products such as a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b).
Divide polynomials and use the remainder theorem: the remainder of p(x) ÷ (x − a) is p(a).
Use the factor theorem to relate roots to linear factors, and bound the number of roots by the degree.
definitions: A polynomial in x is an expression aₙxⁿ + ⋯ + a₁x + a₀; if aₙ ≠ 0 its degree is n.
a is a root of p if p(a) = 0.
keyResults: Division algorithm: for polynomials p and d ≠ 0 with rational (or real) coefficients there are unique q and r with p = qd + r and r = 0 or deg r < deg d.
Factor theorem: x − a divides p(x) if and only if p(a) = 0.
A non-zero polynomial of degree n with real or complex coefficients has at most n roots.
misconceptions: Cancelling terms across a fraction: (x² + 1)/x is not x + 1.
Thinking every polynomial factorises over the integers.
Believing a polynomial of degree n must have exactly n real roots.

references.title: Algebra
references.author: I. M. Gelfand and A. Shen

topics.title: Quadratic equations and functions
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Solving quadratic equations by factorising, completing the square and the quadratic formula; the discriminant; and graphs of quadratic functions as parabolas with a vertex and an axis of symmetry.

discoveries.note: The vertex of a parabola is where its slope is zero, an idea that calculus extends to all differentiable functions.

objectives: Solve quadratic equations by factorising, completing the square and the quadratic formula, and derive the formula.
Use the discriminant to determine the number of real roots.
Sketch y = ax² + bx + c with its vertex, axis of symmetry and intercepts, and solve optimisation problems.
definitions: A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0.
The discriminant is Δ = b² − 4ac.
The vertex of a parabola is its highest or lowest point.
keyResults: Quadratic formula: x = (−b ± √Δ)/(2a) when Δ ≥ 0.
There are two distinct real roots if Δ > 0, one repeated real root if Δ = 0, and no real roots if Δ < 0.
Vieta: the roots r and s satisfy r + s = −b/a and rs = c/a.
Completing the square: ax² + bx + c = a(x + b/(2a))² − Δ/(4a).
misconceptions: Dividing both sides by x and losing the root x = 0.
Misapplying the zero-product property, e.g. concluding from (x − 1)(x − 2) = 6 that x − 1 = 6 or x − 2 = 6.
Thinking Δ < 0 means there are no solutions in any number system; there are two complex solutions.

references.title: Algebra
references.author: I. M. Gelfand and A. Shen

topics.title: Euclidean geometry and proof
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: Axiomatic plane geometry: congruence criteria, parallel lines, triangle and circle theorems, and writing geometric proofs, with attention to what each axiom contributes.

discoveries.note: The parallel postulate is independent of the other axioms: hyperbolic geometry satisfies them while violating it. Tarski showed that elementary Euclidean geometry, formalised in first-order logic, is complete and decidable.
On a sphere of radius r the angles of a triangle sum to more than 180°, and the excess (in radians) equals the area divided by r² (Girard's theorem), a first case of Gauss–Bonnet.

objectives: Use the congruence criteria SAS, ASA and SSS to prove properties of triangles and quadrilaterals.
Prove, using the parallel postulate, that the angles of a triangle sum to 180°, and prove circle theorems such as the inscribed angle theorem.
Explain the role of the parallel postulate and how its independence led to non-Euclidean geometries.
definitions: Parallel postulate (Playfair's form): through a point not on a given line there is exactly one line parallel to the given line.
Two triangles are congruent if their corresponding sides and corresponding angles are equal.
An inscribed angle has its vertex on a circle and its sides along chords of the circle.
keyResults: The angles of a triangle sum to 180°; given the other axioms, this is equivalent to the parallel postulate.
Inscribed angle theorem: an inscribed angle is half the central angle subtending the same arc.
The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle meet in a single point, the circumcentre.
misconceptions: Arguing from the appearance of a diagram instead of from stated facts.
Treating SSA as a congruence criterion.
Believing the parallel postulate has been proved from Euclid's other axioms; it is independent of them.

references.title: Kiselev's Geometry, Book I: Planimetry
references.author: A. P. Kiselev, adapted by Alexander Givental

topics.title: Trigonometry
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: Sine, cosine and tangent from right triangles to the unit circle, radian measure, graphs and identities, and the laws of sines and cosines.

discoveries.note: Periodic signals can be built from sines and cosines: the idea behind Fourier series.

objectives: Define sine, cosine and tangent for acute angles via similar right triangles, and for all angles via the unit circle.
Convert between degrees and radians and sketch the graphs of sin, cos and tan.
Prove and apply sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, the addition formulas, and the laws of sines and cosines.
definitions: For an acute angle θ of a right triangle, sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite/adjacent.
On the unit circle, the point at angle θ measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis is (cos θ, sin θ).
An angle of one radian subtends an arc equal in length to the radius; 2π radians equal 360°.
keyResults: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
sin(α + β) = sin α cos β + cos α sin β and cos(α + β) = cos α cos β − sin α sin β.
Law of cosines: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C.
Law of sines: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C.
misconceptions: Reading sin θ as 'sin times θ'.
Using degree mode when radians are required, or vice versa.
Thinking sin(α + β) = sin α + sin β.

references.title: Trigonometry
references.author: I. M. Gelfand and Mark Saul

topics.title: Functions and their graphs (precalculus)
topics.subject: analysis
topics.summary: Families of real functions (linear, quadratic, polynomial, rational, absolute value, piecewise), their graphs and transformations, and composition and inverses of functions of a real variable.

discoveries.note: Composition of functions is associative and has identities, the first axioms of a category.

objectives: Sketch graphs of standard function families and of transformations y = a f(b(x − h)) + k.
Compose real functions, find natural domains, and find inverse functions on intervals where a function is injective.
Identify zeros, asymptotes, symmetry and end behaviour of polynomial and rational functions.
definitions: The graph of f is the set {(x, f(x)) : x in the domain of f}.
f is even if f(−x) = f(x), and odd if f(−x) = −f(x), for all x in a domain symmetric about 0.
An inverse of f : A → B is a function g : B → A with g(f(x)) = x for all x ∈ A and f(g(y)) = y for all y ∈ B.
keyResults: The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x.
A function has an inverse if and only if it is a bijection; a strictly monotone function on an interval is injective.
The graph of y = f(x − h) is the graph of y = f(x) shifted h units to the right.
misconceptions: Writing f⁻¹(x) = 1/f(x).
Thinking y = f(x − 2) shifts the graph to the left.
Believing composition is commutative; in general f ∘ g ≠ g ∘ f.

topics.title: Exponential and logarithmic functions
topics.subject: analysis
topics.summary: Exponential growth and decay, rational and real exponents, logarithms as inverse functions, the laws of logarithms and the number e.

discoveries.note: exp is an isomorphism from (ℝ, +) to (ℝ>0, ×), with inverse ln: it translates one structure exactly into the other.

objectives: Extend exponents to negative and rational values and justify the definitions from the laws of exponents.
Solve exponential equations with logarithms and apply the laws of logarithms.
Model growth and decay with exponential functions and compare exponential with polynomial growth.
definitions: For a > 0, a^(1/n) is the positive n-th root of a, and a^(m/n) = (a^(1/n))^m.
For a > 0 with a ≠ 1 and x > 0, log_a x is the number y with a^y = x.
e is the limit of (1 + 1/n)ⁿ as n grows without bound; e ≈ 2.71828.
keyResults: log_a(xy) = log_a x + log_a y and log_a(x^r) = r log_a x.
For a > 1, aˣ eventually exceeds every polynomial in x.
For a > 0 with a ≠ 1, x ↦ aˣ is a bijection from ℝ onto (0, ∞) whose inverse is log_a.
e^(x + y) = eˣ · eʸ: the exponential function turns addition into multiplication.
misconceptions: Writing log(x + y) = log x + log y.
Thinking a⁻ⁿ is negative.
Confusing exponential growth (multiplying by the same factor) with linear growth (adding the same amount).

topics.title: Sequences and series
topics.subject: analysis
topics.summary: Arithmetic and geometric sequences, summation notation, sums of finite series, recursive definitions, and an informal look at convergence of infinite geometric series.

discoveries.note: Rigorous analysis makes 'approach' precise with ε–N definitions.

objectives: Find formulas for the n-th term and the partial sums of arithmetic and geometric sequences, and prove them by induction.
Use recursive definitions and summation notation.
Explain why 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ⋯ = 2 and decide when an infinite geometric series converges.
definitions: A sequence of real numbers is a function from ℕ (or from the positive integers) to ℝ.
An arithmetic sequence has a constant difference between terms; a geometric sequence has a constant ratio.
An infinite series Σ aₙ converges to S if its partial sums approach S.
keyResults: For r ≠ 1, a + ar + ⋯ + arⁿ⁻¹ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r).
If |r| < 1 then Σ_{k≥0} ar^k = a/(1 − r); if |r| ≥ 1 and a ≠ 0, the series diverges.
The harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ⋯ diverges, although its terms tend to 0.
misconceptions: Thinking a series must converge if its terms tend to zero.
Believing an infinite sum must be infinite.
Forgetting that 0.999… is a geometric series whose sum is exactly 1.

topics.title: Introductory calculus
topics.subject: analysis
topics.summary: Limits as an intuitive idea, the derivative as instantaneous rate of change and slope of a tangent, basic differentiation, the definite integral as accumulated signed area, and the fundamental theorem of calculus, informally.

discoveries.note: Making limits precise took until the nineteenth century; the ε–δ definition is due largely to Cauchy and Weierstrass.
When no antiderivative can be written in closed form, integrals are computed numerically, for example by the trapezoidal rule or Simpson's rule.

objectives: Estimate limits from tables and graphs, and compute simple limits algebraically.
Differentiate polynomials and use derivatives to find tangent lines, rates of change and extrema.
Approximate areas under curves with rectangles, and relate integrals to antiderivatives through the fundamental theorem.
definitions: The derivative of f at a is f′(a) = lim_{h→0} (f(a + h) − f(a))/h, when this limit exists.
The definite integral ∫_a^b f(x) dx is the limit of Riemann sums: a signed area.
An antiderivative of f is a function F with F′ = f.
keyResults: (xⁿ)′ = nxⁿ⁻¹ for every positive integer n.
At an interior maximum or minimum of a differentiable function, f′ = 0.
Fundamental theorem of calculus: if f is continuous on [a, b] and F′ = f there, then ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a).
misconceptions: Thinking f′(a) = 0 guarantees a maximum or minimum; x³ at 0 is a counterexample.
Believing the limit at a point is always the value of the function there.
Thinking an integral always gives a positive area; integrals are signed.

topics.title: Combinatorics
topics.subject: discrete
topics.summary: Permutations and combinations, binomial coefficients and Pascal's triangle, the binomial theorem, the pigeonhole principle and inclusion–exclusion, with combinatorial proofs.

discoveries.note: Generating functions turn counting problems into algebra.

objectives: Compute binomial coefficients and prove identities such as C(n, k) = C(n − 1, k − 1) + C(n − 1, k) by counting in two ways.
Prove and apply the binomial theorem.
Apply the pigeonhole principle and inclusion–exclusion to counting and existence problems.
definitions: C(n, k), read 'n choose k', is the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set.
Pigeonhole principle: if more than n objects are placed in n boxes, some box contains at least two objects.
keyResults: C(n, k) = n!/(k!(n − k)!) for 0 ≤ k ≤ n.
Binomial theorem: (x + y)ⁿ = Σ_{k=0}^{n} C(n, k) xᵏ yⁿ⁻ᵏ.
Inclusion–exclusion: |A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A| + |B| + |C| − |A ∩ B| − |A ∩ C| − |B ∩ C| + |A ∩ B ∩ C|.
misconceptions: Using permutations when order does not matter.
Thinking a pigeonhole argument must say which box contains two objects.

topics.title: Graphs
topics.subject: discrete
topics.summary: Graphs as vertices and edges, degree and the handshake lemma, paths and connectivity, Euler circuits, trees and graph isomorphism.

discoveries.note: A graph isomorphism is a structure-preserving bijection whose inverse also preserves structure.
Directed graphs (quivers) give rise to path algebras, whose modules are the representations of the quiver.

objectives: Prove the handshake lemma and Euler's criterion for Eulerian circuits.
Prove that a tree with n vertices has n − 1 edges.
Decide whether two small graphs are isomorphic.
definitions: A simple graph consists of a set V of vertices and a set E of two-element subsets of V, called edges.
A tree is a connected graph with no cycles.
Graphs G and H are isomorphic if there is a bijection between their vertex sets that preserves adjacency in both directions.
keyResults: Handshake lemma: the sum of the degrees of all vertices is 2|E|.
A connected graph has an Eulerian circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree.
A tree on n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges, and any two of its vertices are joined by a unique path.
misconceptions: Thinking a particular drawing determines the graph; very different drawings can show the same graph.
Confusing Euler circuits (using each edge once) with Hamiltonian cycles (visiting each vertex once).

references.title: Graph Theory with Applications
references.author: J. A. Bondy and U. S. R. Murty

topics.title: Conditional probability and independence
topics.subject: probability
topics.summary: Addition and multiplication rules, conditional probability, independence, Bayes' theorem in simple cases, and probabilities computed by counting.

discoveries.note: Bayesian statistics uses Bayes' theorem to update beliefs about unknown quantities in the light of data.

objectives: Compute conditional probabilities from two-way tables and tree diagrams.
Decide whether events are independent, and distinguish independence from mutual exclusivity.
Apply Bayes' theorem to problems such as diagnostic testing with base rates.
definitions: For P(B) > 0, the conditional probability of A given B is P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B).
Events A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).
Events A and B are mutually exclusive if they cannot both occur, that is, A ∩ B = ∅.
keyResults: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
Bayes' theorem: P(A | B) = P(B | A)P(A)/P(B) when P(B) > 0.
Law of total probability: if B₁, …, Bₙ partition the sample space, P(A) = Σ P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ).
Two mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are never independent.
misconceptions: Confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A) (the prosecutor's fallacy).
Ignoring base rates when interpreting a positive test result.
Thinking 'independent' means 'mutually exclusive'.

topics.title: Sampling and statistical reasoning
topics.subject: probability
topics.summary: Populations and samples, random sampling and bias, sampling variability, the normal distribution as a model, margin of error, correlation and regression lines, and why correlation is not causation.

discoveries.note: The central limit theorem explains why sample means are approximately normally distributed, even when the data are not.

objectives: Identify sources of bias in surveys and explain why random sampling helps.
Use simulation to see how sample statistics vary, and interpret a margin of error.
Fit and interpret a least-squares line and the correlation coefficient, distinguishing correlation from causation.
definitions: A population is the whole group of interest; a sample is the part that is observed.
In a simple random sample of size n, every subset of the population of size n is equally likely to be chosen.
The correlation coefficient r measures the strength and direction of a linear association; −1 ≤ r ≤ 1.
keyResults: Larger random samples give less variable estimates; for a sample mean, the spread shrinks in proportion to 1/√n.
Correlation, however strong, does not by itself establish causation; well-designed randomised experiments can provide evidence of causation.
r = 0 means no linear association, not necessarily no relationship.
misconceptions: Thinking a large biased sample is better than a smaller random one.
Misreading a 95% confidence interval: in the frequentist interpretation, 95% describes the long-run success rate of the method, not the probability that one computed interval contains the true value.

topics.title: Composition
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Composition of functions g ∘ f: why order matters, associativity, the identity laws, how injectivity, surjectivity and bijectivity behave under composition, and functions between sets as the motivating example of a category.

discoveries.note: Sets and functions, with composition and identity functions, are the motivating example of a category: the category Set.
A functor sends objects to objects and arrows to arrows, preserving composition and identities.
In an ∞-category, composites exist and are unique only up to a contractible space of choices, so associativity holds up to coherent homotopy rather than strictly.
Universal properties describe objects by how arrows compose with them; for example, a product is characterised by the maps into it.
The functions from a set to itself form a monoid under composition, and the bijections form a group.

objectives: Compute composites g ∘ f of functions given by formulas, tables and arrow diagrams, and determine when g ∘ f is defined.
Show by example that g ∘ f and f ∘ g can differ, and prove that composition is associative with identity functions as two-sided units.
Prove that composites of injections, surjections and bijections are injections, surjections and bijections, and that (g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹.
Explain why sets with functions, composition and identity functions satisfy the axioms that later define a category.
definitions: For f : A → B and g : B → C, the composite g ∘ f : A → C is defined by (g ∘ f)(a) = g(f(a)).
The identity function id_A : A → A is defined by id_A(a) = a.
f : A → B has an inverse if there is g : B → A with g ∘ f = id_A and f ∘ g = id_B.
keyResults: Associativity: h ∘ (g ∘ f) = (h ∘ g) ∘ f whenever the composites are defined.
Identity laws: f ∘ id_A = f = id_B ∘ f for every f : A → B.
Composites of injective (surjective, bijective) functions are injective (surjective, bijective).
If g ∘ f is injective then f is injective; if g ∘ f is surjective then g is surjective.
(g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹ when f and g are bijections.
misconceptions: Reading g ∘ f as 'do g first'; in g ∘ f, the function f is applied first.
Assuming composition is commutative.
Thinking that g ∘ f injective forces g to be injective; it forces only f to be injective.
Composing functions whose codomain and domain do not match.

references.title: Conceptual Mathematics: A First Introduction to Categories
references.author: F. William Lawvere and Stephen H. Schanuel

topics.title: Structure-preserving maps: homomorphisms and isomorphisms
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Concrete homomorphisms (maps that respect an operation, such as reduction modulo n, exp from (ℝ, +) to (ℝ>0, ×), linear maps and graph homomorphisms) and isomorphisms as structure-preserving bijections whose inverses also preserve structure, making 'the same structure' precise.

discoveries.note: The first isomorphism theorem identifies the image of any group homomorphism with a quotient of its domain.
Isomorphic structures satisfy the same first-order sentences, but structures satisfying the same sentences need not be isomorphic.

objectives: Check whether a given map preserves an operation, for example reduction modulo n from (ℤ, +) to clock arithmetic.
Show that composites of structure-preserving maps preserve structure, and that the inverse of a bijective homomorphism of groups is a homomorphism.
Decide whether two small structures (clock arithmetics, graphs, symmetry patterns) are isomorphic, and explain what an isomorphism transfers between them.
definitions: A map f from (A, ∗) to (B, ⋆) preserves the operation if f(x ∗ y) = f(x) ⋆ f(y) for all x and y in A.
An isomorphism is a structure-preserving bijection whose inverse is also structure-preserving.
Two structures are isomorphic if there is an isomorphism between them.
keyResults: exp : (ℝ, +) → (ℝ>0, ×) is an isomorphism, with inverse ln.
Reduction modulo n from ℤ to the integers mod n preserves addition and multiplication but is not injective.

For groups and rings, the inverse of a bijective homomorphism is automatically a homomorphism; for ordered sets or topological spaces a structure-preserving bijection can have an inverse that is not structure-preserving.
Isomorphic structures share every property that can be expressed purely in terms of their structure.
misconceptions: Thinking two structures are isomorphic just because they have the same number of elements: clock arithmetic mod 4 and the symmetries of a non-square rectangle are not isomorphic.
Treating isomorphism as equality; isomorphic structures can have entirely different elements.
Assuming every structure-preserving bijection has a structure-preserving inverse.

references.title: Conceptual Mathematics: A First Introduction to Categories
references.author: F. William Lawvere and Stephen H. Schanuel

topics.title: Products by maps: a first universal property
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: The Cartesian product A × B comes with projections to A and B, and every pair of functions X → A and X → B combines into exactly one function X → A × B compatible with the projections. This property characterises the product up to a unique compatible bijection.

discoveries.note: In any category, a product of A and B is defined by exactly this property; for groups it is the direct product, for topological spaces the product topology.
An object is determined up to isomorphism by the maps into it from all other objects; the Yoneda lemma makes this precise.

objectives: Given f : X → A and g : X → B, construct the unique h : X → A × B with π_A ∘ h = f and π_B ∘ h = g.
Draw the commuting diagram for this property and explain what 'exactly one' means.
Show that any set P with maps to A and B having the same property is in bijection with A × B by a unique bijection compatible with the maps.
definitions: The projections π_A : A × B → A and π_B : A × B → B send (a, b) to a and to b respectively.
The pairing ⟨f, g⟩ : X → A × B of f : X → A and g : X → B sends x to (f(x), g(x)).
A universal property describes an object by how it relates, through maps, to all other objects of the same kind.
keyResults: For every set X, functions X → A × B correspond one-to-one with pairs of functions X → A and X → B.
If a set P with maps p : P → A and q : P → B has the same property, there is exactly one bijection P → A × B compatible with the maps.
For finite sets this matches counting: |A × B|^|X| = |A|^|X| · |B|^|X|.
misconceptions: Thinking the universal property defines a different object from A × B; it describes A × B by its behaviour, up to a unique compatible bijection.
Forgetting the uniqueness part of the property.
Believing the set of ordered pairs is the only possible product; any set with the property serves equally well.

references.title: Conceptual Mathematics: A First Introduction to Categories
references.author: F. William Lawvere and Stephen H. Schanuel

topics.title: Algorithms, correctness and efficiency
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: Searching and sorting, proving algorithms correct with loop invariants, counting steps, and comparing growth rates such as logarithmic, linear and quadratic time.

discoveries.note: Some problems seem to require far more time than others; whether P equals NP is a famous open problem.

objectives: Implement linear search, binary search and a simple sort, and trace them on examples.
Prove an algorithm correct using a loop invariant, for example binary search or Euclid's algorithm.
Count the steps of simple algorithms and compare growth rates n, n log n and n².
definitions: A loop invariant is a statement that holds before the first iteration of a loop and is preserved by every iteration.
The running time of an algorithm is the number of basic steps it takes, as a function of the size of its input.
keyResults: Binary search on a sorted list of n items uses at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons.
Every comparison-based sorting algorithm needs at least log₂(n!) comparisons in the worst case, which grows like n log n.
An algorithm is correct if, for every valid input, it terminates and produces the specified output.
misconceptions: Thinking that testing on a few inputs proves an algorithm correct.
Believing faster computers make algorithmic efficiency irrelevant.

references.title: Introduction to Algorithms
references.author: Thomas H. Cormen, Charles E. Leiserson, Ronald L. Rivest and Clifford Stein

topics.title: First steps in Lean
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: Stating and proving simple results in the Lean 4 proof assistant: propositions and proofs, rewriting, induction on natural numbers and reading Mathlib statements, with attention to what a machine check does and does not guarantee.

discoveries.note: Lean's logic is a dependent type theory in which propositions are types and proofs are terms.

objectives: Write and check short Lean proofs of propositional tautologies and simple equalities using rfl, rw and simp.
Prove a statement about natural numbers by induction in Lean, such as 0 + n = n.
Read a Mathlib theorem statement, and distinguish applying a library theorem from proving a result independently.
definitions: A proof assistant is a program that checks proofs written in a formal language.
In Lean, a proposition is a type and a proof of it is a term of that type.
A tactic is a command that builds part of a proof, such as rw (rewrite) or induction.
keyResults: A Lean proof that compiles without sorry and without added axioms has been checked by Lean's kernel relative to Lean's logic.
A formal proof is only as meaningful as its formal statement: a mis-stated theorem can be proved correctly.
For Lean's natural numbers, n + 0 = n holds by definition (rfl), while 0 + n = n needs a proof by induction.
misconceptions: Believing a machine-checked proof guarantees that the statement says what was intended.
Thinking a proof containing sorry is finished.
Confusing the use of a Mathlib lemma with proving the result from more basic facts.

references.title: Theorem Proving in Lean 4
references.author: Jeremy Avigad, Leonardo de Moura, Soonho Kong and Sebastian Ullrich

topics.title: Mathematical modelling with functions
topics.subject: applied
topics.summary: The modelling cycle (simplify, formulate, solve, interpret, validate) with linear, quadratic and exponential models of real situations, and honest discussion of assumptions and limitations.

discoveries.note: Models of populations and epidemics are built from differential equations.

objectives: Formulate linear, quadratic and exponential models from situations and data.
Interpret the parameters of a model and use it to make predictions with stated assumptions.
Validate a model against data and explain where and why it fails.
definitions: A mathematical model is a simplified mathematical description of a real situation, together with its assumptions.
Validation compares a model's predictions with observations.
keyResults: A quantity growing continuously at rate r doubles every (ln 2)/r units of time.
Every model leaves out features of reality; it is judged by whether it serves its purpose.
Extrapolating far beyond the range of the data is risky.
misconceptions: Treating a model's output as fact rather than as a consequence of its assumptions.
Choosing the model that best fits past data regardless of whether it is plausible.

topics.title: Orders, lattices and well-orders
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Partial and total orders, Hasse diagrams, maximal elements and suprema, lattices and well-orders, with Zorn's lemma stated as a tool to be justified later.

discoveries.note: A preorder is exactly a category with at most one morphism between any two objects; order-preserving maps between preorders are then exactly functors.
A lattice can equivalently be described as a set with two operations ∧ and ∨ satisfying associative, commutative and absorption laws.

objectives: Verify the partial-order axioms and draw Hasse diagrams for finite posets such as divisibility on {1, …, 12} and inclusion on P({1, 2, 3}).
Distinguish maximal from greatest elements, and upper bounds from least upper bounds, with examples.
Define lattices and well-orders, and show that ℕ is well-ordered by ≤ while ℤ and ℚ are not.
definitions: A partial order on P is a relation ≤ that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive.
A lattice is a poset in which every pair of elements has a least upper bound (join) and a greatest lower bound (meet).
A well-order is a total order in which every non-empty subset has a least element.
Zorn's lemma: if every chain in a non-empty poset has an upper bound, then the poset has a maximal element.
keyResults: Every finite non-empty poset has a maximal element.
(P(A), ⊆) is a lattice with join ∪ and meet ∩.
Over ZF, Zorn's lemma is equivalent to the axiom of choice.
misconceptions: Treating 'maximal' and 'greatest' as synonyms.
Assuming every partial order is total.
Thinking a least upper bound of a subset must belong to that subset.

references.title: Introduction to Lattices and Order
references.author: B. A. Davey and H. A. Priestley

topics.title: First-order logic
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: The formal language of quantifiers: signatures, terms and formulas, structures and satisfaction, and a deductive system, with soundness proved and completeness stated.

discoveries.note: Church and Turing (1936) showed that no algorithm decides first-order validity, answering Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem negatively.
Categorical logic interprets first-order theories in categories other than the category of sets, such as toposes; models in sets are one special case.

objectives: Write first-order formulas in a given signature, such as the axioms for groups or for linear orders.
Decide whether a sentence is true in a given structure by unwinding the definition of satisfaction.
Prove soundness for a natural-deduction system and state Gödel's completeness theorem.
definitions: A signature specifies constant, function and relation symbols, each with an arity.
A structure for a signature is a non-empty set together with interpretations of its symbols.
M ⊨ φ means the sentence φ is true in M; Γ ⊨ φ means φ is true in every model of Γ.
Γ ⊢ φ means φ is derivable from Γ in a fixed proof system.
keyResults: Soundness: if Γ ⊢ φ then Γ ⊨ φ.
Isomorphic structures satisfy exactly the same first-order sentences.
Completeness (Gödel, 1929): if Γ ⊨ φ then Γ ⊢ φ.
misconceptions: Confusing ⊨ (truth in all models) with ⊢ (derivability) before the completeness theorem links them.
Quantifying over subsets of the domain in a first-order formula; that is second-order logic.
Thinking a first-order theory determines a unique structure; most theories have many non-isomorphic models.

topics.title: Congruences
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: Congruence modulo n as an equivalence relation compatible with addition and multiplication; linear congruences, inverses modulo n, the Chinese remainder theorem, and the theorems of Fermat, Euler and Wilson.

discoveries.note: The congruence classes modulo n are the elements of the quotient ring ℤ/nℤ, and reduction mod n is the quotient homomorphism ℤ → ℤ/nℤ.
(ℤ/nℤ, +) is the cyclic group of order n, and the invertible classes form the group of units of order φ(n); Euler's theorem then follows from Lagrange's theorem.
ℤ/nℤ is a finite commutative ring, and it is a field exactly when n is prime.
For p prime, ℤ/pℤ is the field 𝔽_p; every finite field has prime-power order pⁿ, and there is exactly one of each such order up to isomorphism.
In rings of integers of number fields one works modulo ideals rather than numbers; Kummer's ideal numbers and Dedekind's ideals grew out of attempts to restore unique factorisation.

objectives: Prove that congruence modulo n is an equivalence relation compatible with + and ×.
Solve linear congruences ax ≡ b (mod n) and systems of congruences using the Chinese remainder theorem.
Prove Fermat's little theorem and Euler's theorem and use them to compute large powers modulo n.
definitions: a ≡ b (mod n) means that n divides a − b.
Euler's totient φ(n) is the number of integers in {1, …, n} that are coprime to n.
An inverse of a modulo n is an integer b with ab ≡ 1 (mod n).
keyResults: a has an inverse modulo n if and only if gcd(a, n) = 1.
Chinese remainder theorem: if m and n are coprime, the system x ≡ a (mod m), x ≡ b (mod n) has a solution, unique modulo mn.
Fermat: if p is prime and p does not divide a, then a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p).
Euler: if gcd(a, n) = 1 then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n).
Wilson: (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p) for every prime p.
misconceptions: Cancelling a factor that is not coprime to n: 2 · 3 ≡ 2 · 9 (mod 12), but 3 ≢ 9 (mod 12).
Assuming the converse of Fermat's theorem: the Carmichael number 561 = 3 · 11 · 17 satisfies a^560 ≡ 1 (mod 561) for every a coprime to 561.

references.title: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory
references.author: Kenneth Ireland and Michael Rosen

topics.title: Constructing ℤ, ℚ and ℝ
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: Building the number systems from the natural numbers: ℤ from pairs of naturals, ℚ from pairs of integers, and ℝ from Dedekind cuts or Cauchy sequences, together with the uniqueness of the complete ordered field.

discoveries.note: Completeness of ℝ, established here by construction, is the property on which rigorous analysis rests.
The field of fractions has a universal property: every injective ring homomorphism from an integral domain into a field extends uniquely to its field of fractions.

objectives: Construct ℤ as equivalence classes of pairs of natural numbers and check that the operations are well defined.
Construct ℚ as the field of fractions of ℤ.
Construct ℝ by Dedekind cuts or Cauchy sequences and prove the least-upper-bound property.
definitions: On ℕ × ℕ, (a, b) ~ (c, d) if and only if a + d = b + c; the class of (a, b) represents a − b.
A Dedekind cut is a non-empty proper subset of ℚ that is closed downwards and has no greatest element.
A complete ordered field is an ordered field in which every non-empty subset that is bounded above has a supremum.
keyResults: Operations on equivalence classes are well defined: they do not depend on the chosen representatives.
Any two complete ordered fields are isomorphic by a unique order-preserving field isomorphism.
The Dedekind and Cauchy constructions produce isomorphic ordered fields.
misconceptions: Thinking well-definedness is automatic when operations are defined on equivalence classes.
Reading the constructions as saying what numbers 'really are', rather than as showing that structures with the required properties exist.

topics.title: Linear algebra
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Systems of linear equations and Gaussian elimination, matrices, vector spaces, linear maps, bases and dimension, rank–nullity, determinants, eigenvalues and diagonalisation.

discoveries.note: Vector spaces and linear maps form a category: composites of linear maps are linear and identity maps are linear.
A representation of a group is a homomorphism into the group of invertible linear maps of a vector space.

objectives: Solve linear systems by Gaussian elimination and describe solution sets as translates of null spaces.
Prove that all bases of a finite-dimensional vector space have the same size, and apply the rank–nullity theorem.
Represent linear maps by matrices, compose them by matrix multiplication and change basis.
Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors and decide whether a matrix is diagonalisable.
definitions: A vector space over a field k is a set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector-space axioms.
A linear map T : V → W satisfies T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(cv) = cT(v).
A basis is a linearly independent spanning set; dim V is the number of elements in a basis.
λ is an eigenvalue of T if Tv = λv for some non-zero vector v.
keyResults: Rank–nullity: dim V = dim ker T + dim im T for a linear map T : V → W with V finite-dimensional.
A composite of linear maps is linear, and corresponds to the product of their matrices.
A square matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is non-zero, if and only if its columns are linearly independent.
Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent.
misconceptions: Thinking matrix multiplication is commutative.
Assuming every square matrix is diagonalisable; the matrix with rows (0, 1) and (0, 0) is not.
Believing a linear map must send lines through the origin to lines; it may collapse them to a point.

topics.title: Algebraic structures: monoids, groups and rings
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Binary operations and the first algebraic structures (monoids, groups, rings and fields) with identities and inverses, examples from numbers, remainders, matrices and functions, and the homomorphisms between them.

discoveries.note: A monoid can be viewed as a category with one object, and a monoid homomorphism is then exactly a functor between such categories.
A monad is a monoid in a category of endofunctors, with composition as the product: the monoid idea reappears one level up.

objectives: Define monoids, groups, rings and fields, and test examples such as (ℕ, +), (ℤ, +), (ℤ, ×), ℤ/nℤ and 2 × 2 matrices.
Prove that identities and inverses are unique when they exist.
Explain why ℤ is a ring but not a field, while ℚ is a field.
Recognise structure-preserving maps (homomorphisms) between these structures.
definitions: A binary operation on a set S is a function S × S → S.
A monoid is a set with an associative binary operation and an identity element; a group is a monoid in which every element has an inverse.

A ring is a set with operations + and × such that (R, +) is an abelian group, (R, ×) is a monoid, and × distributes over +. A field is a commutative ring with 0 ≠ 1 in which every non-zero element has a multiplicative inverse.
A homomorphism is a function between structures of the same kind that preserves the operations and identity elements.
keyResults: In a monoid the identity element is unique, and each element has at most one inverse.
(ℕ, +) is a monoid but not a group, while (ℤ, +) is a group.
ℤ/nℤ is a field if and only if n is prime.
The functions from a set to itself form a monoid under composition, and the bijections form a group.
misconceptions: Thinking an identity element must be 0 or 1; for composition it is the identity function.
Assuming every operation is commutative; matrix multiplication and composition of functions are not.
Forgetting closure: the odd integers are not closed under addition.

topics.title: Transformation geometry and the Erlangen programme
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: Classifying the isometries of the plane, affine and projective transformations, and Klein's idea that a geometry is determined by a group of transformations and its invariants.

discoveries.note: Klein's idea can be recast categorically: a group is a one-object category in which every morphism is invertible, and a geometry studies what such morphisms preserve.
Plane patterns repeating in two independent directions fall into exactly 17 symmetry types (the wallpaper groups).

objectives: Prove that every isometry of the plane is a translation, a rotation, a reflection or a glide reflection.
Represent isometries and affine maps by matrices and compose them.
Explain Klein's Erlangen programme and compare Euclidean, affine and projective invariants.
definitions: An affine map of ℝⁿ has the form x ↦ Ax + b with A an invertible matrix.
A glide reflection is a reflection followed by a translation parallel to the mirror line.
Projective transformations of the real projective plane are induced by invertible 3 × 3 matrices, taken up to non-zero scalar multiples.
keyResults: Every isometry of ℝ² is a translation, a rotation, a reflection or a glide reflection.
Affine maps preserve parallelism and ratios of lengths along a line, but in general not lengths or angles.
Projective transformations preserve the cross-ratio of four collinear points.
misconceptions: Assuming every isometry fixes some point; translations and glide reflections do not.
Thinking affine maps preserve angles.

topics.title: Calculus of one variable
topics.subject: analysis
topics.summary: Calculus I–II: limits and continuity with ε–δ, derivatives and their applications, the mean value theorem, techniques of integration, improper integrals, series and convergence tests, and Taylor series.

discoveries.note: Why does the Taylor series of 1/(1 + x²) at 0 converge only for |x| < 1, although the function is smooth on all of ℝ? Its complex poles at ±i explain it.

objectives: Differentiate and integrate elementary functions using the chain rule, substitution and integration by parts.
State and apply the mean value theorem and L'Hôpital's rule.
Test series for convergence and compute Taylor polynomials with error bounds.
definitions: f is continuous at a if for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that |f(x) − f(a)| < ε whenever |x − a| < δ.
The Taylor series of f at a is Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(x − a)ⁿ/n!.
keyResults: Mean value theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a) for some c in (a, b).
Taylor's theorem with remainder.
eˣ = Σ xⁿ/n! for every real x.
An absolutely convergent series converges.
misconceptions: Assuming every smooth function equals its Taylor series; f(x) = e^(−1/x²) with f(0) = 0 is a counterexample at 0.
Applying L'Hôpital's rule to limits that are not indeterminate forms.

topics.title: Multivariable and vector calculus
topics.subject: analysis
topics.summary: Calculus III: partial derivatives, the derivative as a linear map, optimisation with Lagrange multipliers, multiple integrals and change of variables, line and surface integrals, and the theorems of Green, Stokes and Gauss.

discoveries.note: The chain rule says that taking derivatives respects composition; in categorical language, differentiation at a point is functorial.

objectives: Compute partial and directional derivatives, gradients and Jacobian matrices.
Solve constrained optimisation problems with Lagrange multipliers.
Evaluate multiple, line and surface integrals and apply Green's theorem, Stokes's theorem and the divergence theorem.
definitions: The derivative of f : ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ at a is the linear map Df(a) such that f(a + h) = f(a) + Df(a)h + o(|h|) as h → 0.
The gradient ∇f of a real-valued function collects its partial derivatives.
keyResults: Chain rule: D(g ∘ f)(a) = Dg(f(a)) ∘ Df(a).
Change of variables in multiple integrals uses the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant.
Divergence theorem: the flux of F out of a bounded region V with smooth boundary equals ∭_V div F dV.
If all partial derivatives of f exist and are continuous near a, then f is differentiable at a.
misconceptions: Thinking the existence of partial derivatives implies differentiability.
Forgetting the Jacobian factor when changing variables.

references.title: Vector Calculus, Linear Algebra, and Differential Forms
references.author: John H. Hubbard and Barbara Burke Hubbard

topics.title: Ordinary differential equations
topics.subject: analysis
topics.summary: First-order equations, linear equations with constant coefficients, linear systems and phase portraits via eigenvalues, existence and uniqueness theorems, and qualitative behaviour.

discoveries.note: Adding random noise to differential equations leads to stochastic differential equations.

objectives: Solve separable equations, linear first-order equations and constant-coefficient linear equations.
Solve linear systems x′ = Ax using eigenvalues and sketch their phase portraits.
State the Picard–Lindelöf theorem and give an example of non-uniqueness when its hypotheses fail.
definitions: An ordinary differential equation of order n relates an unknown function of one variable to its first n derivatives.
An equilibrium of x′ = f(x) is a point where f vanishes.
keyResults: Picard–Lindelöf: if f is continuous and locally Lipschitz in x, then x′ = f(t, x), x(t₀) = x₀ has a unique solution on some interval around t₀.
The solution of x′ = Ax with initial value x(0) is x(t) = e^(tA) x(0).
x′ = √|x| with x(0) = 0 has more than one solution, e.g. x ≡ 0 and x(t) = t²/4 for t ≥ 0 (and 0 for t < 0).
misconceptions: Assuming solutions exist for all time; solutions of x′ = x² can blow up in finite time.
Thinking every differential equation has a solution in closed form.

references.title: Differential Equations, Dynamical Systems, and an Introduction to Chaos
references.author: Morris W. Hirsch, Stephen Smale and Robert L. Devaney

topics.title: Recurrences and generating functions
topics.subject: discrete
topics.summary: Recurrence relations such as the Fibonacci recurrence, solving linear recurrences, ordinary generating functions and asymptotic notation.

discoveries.note: Recurrences describe the running time of recursive algorithms; mergesort satisfies T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), so T(n) = O(n log n).

objectives: Solve linear recurrences with constant coefficients using characteristic polynomials.
Use generating functions to solve recurrences and counting problems.
Compare growth rates using O, Ω and Θ notation.
definitions: The ordinary generating function of a sequence (aₙ) is the formal power series Σ aₙxⁿ.
f(n) = O(g(n)) means |f(n)| ≤ C|g(n)| for some constant C and all sufficiently large n.
keyResults: Binet's formula: with F₀ = 0 and F₁ = 1, Fₙ = (φⁿ − ψⁿ)/√5 where φ = (1 + √5)/2 and ψ = (1 − √5)/2.
The Catalan numbers C(2n, n)/(n + 1) count, among many other things, balanced sequences of n pairs of brackets.
misconceptions: Thinking formal power series must converge to be useful.
Reading big-O as an exact count rather than an upper bound up to a constant.

references.title: Concrete Mathematics
references.author: Ronald L. Graham, Donald E. Knuth and Oren Patashnik

topics.title: Probability theory
topics.subject: probability
topics.summary: Random variables, discrete and continuous distributions, expectation and variance, joint distributions and independence, the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem.

discoveries.note: Making 'random variable' fully rigorous, especially for continuous distributions, requires measure theory.

objectives: Compute expectations and variances for the binomial, geometric, Poisson, uniform, exponential and normal distributions.
Use linearity of expectation and indicator variables, including for dependent events.
Prove the weak law of large numbers via Chebyshev's inequality, state the central limit theorem, and use the normal approximation.
definitions: A random variable is a numerical quantity determined by the outcome of a random experiment.
E[X] = Σ x P(X = x) in the discrete case and ∫ x f(x) dx in the continuous case, when the sum or integral converges absolutely.
Var(X) = E[(X − E[X])²].
keyResults: Linearity of expectation holds for all random variables with finite expectation, whether or not they are independent.
Chebyshev: P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k² for k > 0.
Central limit theorem: for independent identically distributed variables with finite positive variance, the standardised sums converge in distribution to the standard normal distribution.
Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) when X and Y are uncorrelated, in particular when they are independent.
misconceptions: Assuming E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] for all random variables; it requires X and Y to be uncorrelated.
Believing the central limit theorem says the data themselves become normally distributed.

references.title: An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Volume I
references.author: William Feller

topics.title: Statistical inference
topics.subject: probability
topics.summary: Estimators and their properties, likelihood and maximum likelihood, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and p-values, linear regression, and an introduction to Bayesian inference.

discoveries.note: Statistical analyses should be reproducible, with code, data and random seeds recorded so that others can rerun them.

objectives: Derive maximum likelihood estimators and assess their bias and variance.
Construct confidence intervals and perform hypothesis tests, interpreting p-values correctly.
Fit linear regression models and check their assumptions using residuals.
definitions: An estimator is a function of the data used to estimate an unknown parameter.
A p-value is the probability, computed assuming the null hypothesis, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed.
The likelihood L(θ) is the probability or density of the observed data, regarded as a function of the parameter θ.
keyResults: For an independent sample from a population with mean μ and variance σ², the sample mean is unbiased for μ and has variance σ²/n.
Least-squares regression coefficients satisfy the normal equations XᵀXβ = Xᵀy.
Performing many tests inflates the chance of false positives unless the analysis corrects for multiplicity.
misconceptions: Reading a p-value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
Treating a non-significant result as proof that there is no effect.

references.title: Statistical Inference
references.author: George Casella and Roger L. Berger

topics.title: Categories
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Categories as objects and morphisms with associative composition and identities; the categories of sets, groups, vector spaces, topological spaces and posets; monoids and preorders as categories; isomorphisms; and opposite categories with the duality principle.

discoveries.note: Once there are maps between categories (functors), one can ask for maps between functors: natural transformations.
Categories themselves, with functors and natural transformations, form a 2-category, the starting point of higher category theory.
Categories can also model logic and computation, with types or propositions as objects and programs or proofs as morphisms.

objectives: State the axioms of a category and verify them for Set, Grp, Vect_k, Top and a poset regarded as a category.
Recognise a monoid as a one-object category, and a preorder as a category with at most one morphism between any two objects.
Define isomorphisms in a category and prove that inverses are unique.
Form the opposite category and dualise simple statements, for example exchanging monomorphisms and epimorphisms.
definitions: A category C consists of objects; morphisms f : A → B between them; a composite g ∘ f for each pair of composable morphisms; and an identity morphism id_A for each object, such that composition is associative and identities are two-sided units.
A morphism f : A → B is an isomorphism if there is g : B → A with g ∘ f = id_A and f ∘ g = id_B.
The opposite category Cᵒᵖ has the same objects as C and one morphism B → A for each morphism A → B of C, with composition reversed.
f is a monomorphism if f ∘ g = f ∘ h implies g = h; epimorphisms are defined dually.
keyResults: Inverses in a category are unique when they exist.
In Set, the monomorphisms are the injections and the epimorphisms are the surjections.
In the category of rings with identity, the inclusion ℤ → ℚ is an epimorphism but is not surjective.
Duality principle: if a statement holds in every category, so does the dual statement obtained by reversing all arrows.
misconceptions: Thinking morphisms must be functions; in a poset regarded as a category, a morphism is just the fact that x ≤ y.
Assuming epimorphisms are always surjective.
Believing the objects of a category must have elements.

topics.title: Functors
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Functors as structure-preserving maps between categories: covariant and contravariant functors, forgetful and free functors, power-set and hom functors, and functoriality as a tool for proving that things are impossible.

discoveries.note: π₁ is a functor, and functoriality gives a short proof of the Brouwer fixed-point theorem for the disc.
Hom functors are the raw material of the Yoneda lemma.

objectives: Verify that the power-set, forgetful and hom functors are functors, and that a contravariant functor from C to D is the same as a functor Cᵒᵖ → D.
Explain why functors preserve isomorphisms and use this to show that objects are not isomorphic.
Describe the free monoid on a set (finite lists) and the free vector space on a set as functors.
definitions: A functor F : C → D assigns to each object A of C an object F(A) of D and to each morphism f : A → B a morphism F(f) : F(A) → F(B), such that F(g ∘ f) = F(g) ∘ F(f) and F(id_A) = id_{F(A)}.
A contravariant functor from C to D is a functor Cᵒᵖ → D.
For an object A of a locally small category C, the hom functor Hom(A, −) : C → Set sends each object B to the set of morphisms A → B.
keyResults: Functors preserve isomorphisms: if f is an isomorphism, so is F(f).
Functors compose, and small categories with functors form a category Cat.
The fundamental group is a functor from pointed spaces to groups; functoriality shows there is no retraction of the disc onto its boundary circle.
misconceptions: Thinking a functor must be injective on objects or on morphisms.
Believing every functor reflects isomorphisms, so that F(f) invertible would force f invertible; this fails in general.

topics.title: Universal properties
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Describing objects by their relationships rather than their elements: universal properties of products, quotients, free objects and fields of fractions, and the fact that an object with a universal property is unique up to unique isomorphism.

discoveries.note: Products, equalisers, pullbacks and their duals are all limits or colimits: one universal property covering many constructions.
Limits and colimits are themselves special Kan extensions, along the functor to the category with one object and one morphism.

objectives: State the universal properties of products in Set, Grp and Top, of quotient sets and quotient groups, and of free monoids and free groups.
Prove that any two objects with the same universal property are isomorphic by a unique isomorphism compatible with the structure maps.
Recognise when a familiar construction, such as the tensor product or the field of fractions, is best defined by a universal property.
definitions: A universal arrow from an object X of C to a functor U : D → C is an object F of D with a morphism η : X → U(F) such that every morphism X → U(E) equals U(g) ∘ η for a unique g : F → E.
A free monoid on a set S is a monoid F(S) with a map S → F(S) through which every map from S to a monoid factors uniquely via a monoid homomorphism.
keyResults: Objects defined by a universal property are unique up to a unique isomorphism compatible with the structure maps.
The free monoid on S is the monoid of finite words in the elements of S under concatenation.
The quotient map X → X/~ is universal among maps out of X that are constant on equivalence classes.
misconceptions: Thinking a universal property constructs an object; it characterises one, and existence must be proved separately. For example, the fields 𝔽₂ and 𝔽₃ have no product in the category of fields.
Forgetting the uniqueness clause, which is what makes the object unique up to isomorphism.

topics.title: Numerical methods
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: Floating-point arithmetic and rounding error, root finding by bisection and Newton's method, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration, and error analysis and rates of convergence.

discoveries.note: Gradient descent and Newton's method for minimisation are close relatives of root-finding methods.

objectives: Explain floating-point representation, machine epsilon and catastrophic cancellation.
Implement bisection and Newton's method and compare their rates of convergence.
Implement the trapezoidal and Simpson's rules and estimate their errors.
definitions: Machine epsilon is the gap between 1 and the next larger floating-point number.
An iterative method converges with order p if its errors satisfy eₙ₊₁ ≈ C eₙᵖ for some constant C.
keyResults: Newton's method converges quadratically to a simple root of a twice continuously differentiable function when started close enough to the root.
Bisection halves the error bound at each step and always converges for a continuous function with a sign change.
For smooth integrands, the composite trapezoidal rule has error O(h²) and the composite Simpson's rule O(h⁴).
misconceptions: Assuming that printing more digits means more accuracy.
Expecting Newton's method to converge from every starting point.

references.title: Numerical Analysis
references.author: Richard L. Burden and J. Douglas Faires

references.title: An Introduction to Numerical Analysis
references.author: Endre Süli and David F. Mayers

references.title: Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms
references.author: Nicholas J. Higham

topics.title: Algorithm design and analysis
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: Recursion and divide and conquer, greedy algorithms, dynamic programming, graph algorithms (breadth- and depth-first search, shortest paths, spanning trees), asymptotic analysis and correctness proofs.

discoveries.note: Matching and network-flow algorithms are algorithmic counterparts of theorems such as Hall's and Menger's.

objectives: Design divide-and-conquer algorithms and analyse them with recurrences, as for mergesort.
Prove the correctness of greedy algorithms such as Kruskal's algorithm and Dijkstra's algorithm with non-negative weights.
Design dynamic-programming algorithms for problems such as longest common subsequence.
definitions: Divide and conquer splits a problem into smaller instances, solves them recursively and combines the results.
Dynamic programming solves a problem by combining solutions of overlapping subproblems, storing them to avoid recomputation.
keyResults: Mergesort runs in O(n log n) time.
Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from a source vertex when all edge weights are non-negative.
Kruskal's algorithm finds a minimum spanning tree of a connected weighted graph.
misconceptions: Using Dijkstra's algorithm when some edge weights are negative.
Assuming a greedy algorithm is correct without a proof.

references.title: Introduction to Algorithms
references.author: Thomas H. Cormen, Charles E. Leiserson, Ronald L. Rivest and Clifford Stein

topics.title: Formalising mathematics in Lean and Mathlib
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: Formalising undergraduate mathematics in Lean 4 with Mathlib: structures and type classes, sets and functions, quantifier reasoning, algebraic structures, and searching and contributing to a large library.

discoveries.note: The type theory beneath Lean explains how types, universes and definitional equality behave.

objectives: Formalise definitions and proofs about sets, functions and quantifiers, such as the fact that a composite of injections is injective.
Use Mathlib's algebraic hierarchy to state and prove results about groups and rings.
Search Mathlib for existing results and explain the trade-off between using library lemmas and proving from scratch.
definitions: Mathlib is the community-maintained mathematical library for Lean 4.
A type class packages structure, such as a group operation, which Lean then finds automatically by instance search.
A structure in Lean is a type whose elements bundle several fields, such as the carrier operations and laws of a monoid.
keyResults: Mathlib's Function.Injective.comp states that a composite of injective functions is injective.
Lean's #print axioms command lists the axioms on which a proof depends.
A formal library is useful only if its definitions match standard mathematical usage, which people must check.
misconceptions: Thinking formalisation is mere translation; it often exposes hidden assumptions and edge cases.
Believing Lean's convention x / 0 = 0 changes mathematics; it is a definitional convenience, and theorems carry hypotheses such as x ≠ 0 where needed.

references.title: Theorem Proving in Lean 4
references.author: Jeremy Avigad, Leonardo de Moura, Soonho Kong and Sebastian Ullrich

topics.title: Classical mechanics
topics.subject: applied
topics.summary: Newton's laws as differential equations, conservation of energy and momentum, oscillators, central forces and Kepler's laws, and an introduction to Lagrangian mechanics.

discoveries.note: Configuration spaces are manifolds, and Hamiltonian mechanics lives on cotangent bundles with their symplectic structure.

objectives: Solve the equations of motion of projectiles and of harmonic oscillators, with and without damping.
Use conservation of energy and angular momentum to analyse motion under a central force and derive Kepler's laws.
Derive equations of motion from a Lagrangian using the Euler–Lagrange equations.
definitions: Newton's second law: F = ma, where the acceleration a is the second derivative of position.
A force field F is conservative if F = −∇V for some potential V.
The Lagrangian of a system is L = T − V, kinetic energy minus potential energy.
keyResults: For conservative forces the total energy T + V is conserved.
Under a central force, angular momentum is conserved and the motion stays in a plane.
Bound orbits under an inverse-square attractive force are ellipses (Kepler's first law).
misconceptions: Thinking a force is needed to keep an object moving at constant velocity.
Confusing mass with weight.

topics.title: Cryptography
topics.subject: applied
topics.summary: The mathematics of modern cryptography: symmetric and public-key systems, RSA, Diffie–Hellman key exchange, discrete logarithms, digital signatures, and the unproved hardness assumptions on which security rests.

discoveries.note: The existence of one-way functions would imply P ≠ NP, which remains unproved.
Shannon proved that the one-time pad achieves perfect secrecy, and that perfect secrecy requires a key with at least as much entropy as the message.

objectives: Implement RSA key generation, encryption and decryption, and prove correctness using Euler's theorem and the Chinese remainder theorem.
Carry out Diffie–Hellman key exchange and explain its reliance on the hardness of discrete logarithms.
Explain why fast modular exponentiation makes these systems practical, and why their security claims are conditional.
definitions: In RSA, n = pq for large primes p and q, and exponents e and d satisfy ed ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)); a message m is encrypted as mᵉ mod n.
The discrete logarithm problem asks, given g and h = gˣ in a group, to find x.
A one-way function is easy to compute but believed to be hard to invert.
keyResults: RSA decryption works: (mᵉ)ᵈ ≡ m (mod n) for every integer m, by Euler's theorem and the Chinese remainder theorem.
Modular exponentiation by repeated squaring uses O(log e) multiplications.
Shor's algorithm would factor integers and compute discrete logarithms in polynomial time on a sufficiently large quantum computer.
misconceptions: Thinking RSA's security has been proved; it rests on unproved assumptions about factoring.
Believing encryption alone guarantees authenticity; that needs signatures or message authentication codes.
Using 'textbook' RSA without padding in practice.

references.title: An Introduction to Mathematical Cryptography
references.author: Jeffrey Hoffstein, Jill Pipher and Joseph H. Silverman

topics.title: ZFC: axiomatic set theory
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: The Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms with choice as a first-order theory (extensionality, pairing, union, power set, separation, replacement, infinity, foundation, choice) and how pairs, relations, functions and numbers are encoded as sets.

discoveries.note: Lawvere's Elementary Theory of the Category of Sets (ETCS) axiomatises sets through functions instead of membership; without an added replacement axiom it is strictly weaker than ZFC.
Iterating 'sets of sets' transfinitely builds the cumulative hierarchy V_α; with the axiom of foundation, every set appears at some stage.
If ZFC is consistent, it cannot prove that an inaccessible cardinal exists; at an inaccessible κ, the stage V_κ of the hierarchy is itself a model of ZFC.
Lean is founded not on ZFC but on a dependent type theory. Each foundation can model the other given suitable assumptions, but they are not interchangeable.

objectives: State the ZFC axioms and explain what each one contributes.
Encode ordered pairs, relations, functions and the natural numbers as sets, and prove the characteristic property of Kuratowski pairs.
Explain the difference between proving a theorem in ZFC and proving that ZFC is consistent.
definitions: ZFC is the first-order theory in the language {∈} with the axioms of extensionality, pairing, union, power set, separation (a schema), replacement (a schema), infinity, foundation and choice.
The Kuratowski ordered pair is (a, b) = {{a}, {a, b}}.
The von Neumann natural numbers are 0 = ∅ and n + 1 = n ∪ {n}; ω is the least set containing 0 and closed under n ↦ n + 1.
keyResults: For Kuratowski pairs, (a, b) = (c, d) if and only if a = c and b = d.
ZF proves that there is no set of all sets.
If ZFC is consistent, it cannot prove its own consistency (Gödel's second incompleteness theorem).
Most of ordinary mathematics, including analysis, algebra and topology, can be formalised in ZFC.
misconceptions: Thinking ZFC says what sets 'really are'; it is a list of assumptions from which theorems are derived.
Believing natural numbers 'are' von Neumann ordinals; that is one convenient encoding among several.
Assuming ZFC has been proved consistent; its consistency is assumed, and cannot be proved within ZFC itself if it is consistent.

references.title: Set Theory: An Introduction to Independence Proofs
references.author: Kenneth Kunen

topics.title: Ordinals and cardinals
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Von Neumann ordinals, transfinite induction and recursion, cardinals as initial ordinals, the Schröder–Bernstein theorem and the first facts of cardinal arithmetic.

discoveries.note: ZFC does not decide the value of 2^ℵ₀: Cohen's forcing shows that, if ZFC is consistent, so is ZFC + 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂, and many other values are possible.
Beyond the alephs lie inaccessible, measurable and larger cardinals whose existence ZFC cannot prove.

objectives: Define ordinals as transitive sets well-ordered by ∈, and prove that every well-order is isomorphic to exactly one ordinal.
Use transfinite induction and transfinite recursion to prove statements about, and define functions on, the ordinals.
Prove the Schröder–Bernstein theorem and compute basic cardinal sums and products.
definitions: An ordinal is a transitive set that is well-ordered by ∈.
A cardinal is an ordinal that is not in bijection with any smaller ordinal; ℵ₀ = ω, and ℵ_{α+1} is the least cardinal greater than ℵ_α.
|A| ≤ |B| means that there is an injection from A to B.
keyResults: Schröder–Bernstein (provable in ZF): if |A| ≤ |B| and |B| ≤ |A| then |A| = |B|.
Every well-ordered set is order-isomorphic to exactly one ordinal.
For every infinite aleph κ, κ + κ = κ · κ = κ.
Ordinal addition is not commutative: 1 + ω = ω, but ω + 1 ≠ ω.
misconceptions: Confusing ordinal and cardinal arithmetic: ω and ω + 1 are different ordinals with the same cardinality.
Assuming every set has an aleph as its cardinality without the axiom of choice; in ZF this holds exactly for well-orderable sets.
Believing 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₁ is a theorem; it is the continuum hypothesis, which ZFC neither proves nor refutes (if ZFC is consistent).

references.title: Set Theory: An Introduction to Independence Proofs
references.author: Kenneth Kunen

topics.title: The axiom of choice and its equivalents
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: The axiom of choice, its equivalents Zorn's lemma and the well-ordering theorem, typical applications in algebra and analysis, and its non-constructive consequences.

discoveries.note: Vitali's construction of a non-measurable set uses AC; this is one reason Lebesgue measure is defined on a σ-algebra of sets rather than on all subsets of ℝ.
The Hahn–Banach theorem is usually proved with Zorn's lemma, although it follows from the strictly weaker ultrafilter lemma.
Over ZF, 'every vector space has a basis' is equivalent to the axiom of choice (Blass, 1984).

objectives: Prove, over ZF, that the axiom of choice, Zorn's lemma and the well-ordering theorem are equivalent.
Use Zorn's lemma to prove that every vector space has a basis and that every non-zero commutative ring with identity has a maximal ideal.
Describe results, such as the existence of a non-measurable set of reals, that are provable with choice but not in ZF alone (relative to the consistency of an inaccessible cardinal).
definitions: Axiom of choice (AC): every family of non-empty sets has a choice function.
Well-ordering theorem: every set admits a well-order.
Countable choice and dependent choice (DC) are weaker principles that suffice for much of classical analysis.
keyResults: Over ZF, AC, Zorn's lemma and the well-ordering theorem are equivalent.
Gödel: if ZF is consistent, so is ZFC. Cohen (1963): if ZF is consistent, so is ZF + ¬AC.

AC implies that some subset of ℝ is not Lebesgue measurable (Vitali). Solovay showed that, if an inaccessible cardinal is consistent with ZFC, then ZF + DC is consistent with every set of reals being Lebesgue measurable.
misconceptions: Thinking choice is only needed for uncountable families; choosing from countably many two-element sets can already require it.
Believing the Banach–Tarski paradox refutes AC; it shows that some sets cannot be assigned a volume invariant under rigid motions.
Assuming every proof that uses Zorn's lemma can easily be made constructive.

references.title: Set Theory: An Introduction to Independence Proofs
references.author: Kenneth Kunen

topics.title: Completeness, compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Gödel's completeness theorem and its consequences: compactness, the Löwenheim–Skolem theorems, nonstandard models and the limits of first-order axiomatisation.

discoveries.note: Compactness yields ordered fields elementarily equivalent to ℝ that contain infinitesimals, the basis of Robinson's nonstandard analysis.

objectives: Prove the completeness theorem for countable languages by a Henkin construction.
Use compactness to show that some classes, such as torsion groups or finite structures, are not first-order axiomatisable.
State the Löwenheim–Skolem theorems and explain Skolem's paradox.
definitions: A theory is consistent if it does not prove a contradiction, and satisfiable if it has a model.
Compactness: a set of sentences has a model whenever every finite subset of it has a model.
keyResults: Completeness: a first-order theory is consistent if and only if it has a model.
The compactness theorem holds for first-order logic.
Löwenheim–Skolem: a theory in a countable language with an infinite model has a model of every infinite cardinality.
Peano arithmetic has nonstandard models.
misconceptions: Thinking the completeness and incompleteness theorems contradict each other; one concerns truth in all models, the other provability of truths about one intended model.
Reading Skolem's paradox as an inconsistency: a countable model of ZFC contains no bijection between ω and its version of ℝ, although one exists outside the model.

topics.title: Type theory and propositions as types
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Simply typed and dependent type theories, the Curry–Howard correspondence between proofs and programs, inductive types, and the type theory behind proof assistants such as Lean, compared with axiomatic set theory.

discoveries.note: Normalisation of typed λ-terms corresponds to removing detours in natural-deduction proofs, a central theme of proof theory.
Dependent types let programs carry machine-checked proofs of their own specifications.

objectives: Type-check terms of the simply typed λ-calculus and read them as proofs in intuitionistic propositional logic.
Explain dependent function (Π) and dependent pair (Σ) types and use them to express ∀ and ∃.
Define the natural numbers and lists as inductive types and derive their induction principles.
Contrast a type-theoretic foundation, where every term has a type, with ZFC, where everything is a set and membership is global.
definitions: A typing judgement t : A asserts that the term t has type A.
Curry–Howard correspondence: propositions correspond to types and proofs to terms; implication corresponds to function types.
An element of a dependent function type Π (x : A), B(x) sends each a : A to an element of B(a).
An inductive type is freely generated by its constructors; for example ℕ is generated by zero and succ.
keyResults: The simply typed λ-calculus is strongly normalising.
Normalisation of proofs in intuitionistic natural deduction corresponds to β-reduction of typed λ-terms.
Lean's logic is a dependent type theory in the tradition of the calculus of inductive constructions, with a hierarchy of universes; classical principles such as choice are added as explicit axioms.
misconceptions: Thinking type theory and set theory are interchangeable; they have different primitive notions and are related by interpretations, not identical.
Treating types as sets: a term has its type as part of its meaning, whereas a set may belong to many unrelated sets.
Assuming every program is a meaningful proof; in a consistent type theory, non-terminating terms are excluded.

references.title: Theorem Proving in Lean 4
