references.author: Jeremy Avigad, Leonardo de Moura, Soonho Kong and Sebastian Ullrich

references.title: Proofs and Types
references.author: Jean-Yves Girard, Yves Lafont and Paul Taylor

references.title: Type Theory and Formal Proof: An Introduction
references.author: Rob Nederpelt and Herman Geuvers

topics.title: Mathematical writing
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Writing mathematics that others can read and check: structure, definitions before use, notation, examples, LaTeX, and honest statements of what has and has not been proved.

discoveries.note: Formalisation blueprints link each informal statement to its formal counterpart, which forces precision in writing.

objectives: Rewrite a correct but unclear proof so that its structure, assumptions and key steps are explicit.
Typeset definitions, theorems and proofs in LaTeX with consistent notation.
Write a short expository note that states precisely which results are proved, which are cited and which are conjectured.
definitions: A theorem is a principal result, a lemma an auxiliary result, and a corollary a result that follows quickly from another.
Exposition is writing whose purpose is explanation rather than the announcement of new results.
keyResults: Every symbol should be defined before it is used, and every cited result should be identifiable by the reader.
A proof is written for a reader who will check it against the stated hypotheses.
misconceptions: Thinking a shorter proof is always a clearer one.
Using 'standard' notation without defining it.
Leaving the status of a claim (proved, cited or conjectured) for the reader to guess.

references.title: Mathematical Writing
references.author: Donald E. Knuth, Tracy Larrabee and Paul M. Roberts

references.title: Handbook of Writing for the Mathematical Sciences
references.author: Nicholas J. Higham

topics.title: Number theory
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: Primitive roots, quadratic residues and quadratic reciprocity, arithmetic functions and Möbius inversion, sums of two squares and Pell's equation.

discoveries.note: Diffie–Hellman key exchange works in a large cyclic group, such as the units modulo a prime with a primitive root as generator.
Quadratic reciprocity can be proved with Gauss sums and cyclotomic fields.

objectives: Prove that (ℤ/pℤ)ˣ is cyclic for p prime and find primitive roots.
Compute Legendre symbols and apply the law of quadratic reciprocity.
Characterise the primes that are sums of two squares, and solve Pell's equation using continued fractions.
definitions: a is a quadratic residue modulo p if x² ≡ a (mod p) has a solution.
The Legendre symbol (a/p) is 0, 1 or −1 according as p divides a, a is a non-zero quadratic residue, or a is a non-residue.
A primitive root modulo n is a generator of the group (ℤ/nℤ)ˣ.
keyResults: Quadratic reciprocity: for distinct odd primes p and q, (p/q)(q/p) = (−1)^(((p−1)/2)((q−1)/2)).
An odd prime p is a sum of two squares if and only if p ≡ 1 (mod 4).
Primitive roots modulo n exist exactly when n is 1, 2, 4, pᵏ or 2pᵏ for an odd prime p.
For every positive integer d that is not a square, x² − dy² = 1 has infinitely many integer solutions.
misconceptions: Assuming every modulus has a primitive root; modulo 8 there is none.
Treating quadratic reciprocity as an isolated trick; it has many proofs and far-reaching generalisations.

references.title: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory
references.author: Kenneth Ireland and Michael Rosen

references.title: An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers
references.author: G. H. Hardy and E. M. Wright

topics.title: Groups
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Groups and subgroups, cyclic, dihedral and symmetric groups, cosets and Lagrange's theorem, homomorphisms and normal subgroups, and group actions with the orbit–stabiliser theorem.

discoveries.note: An action of G on a set X is the same thing as a functor from the one-object category BG to the category of sets.
Diffie–Hellman and elliptic-curve cryptography work in finite abelian groups in which discrete logarithms are believed to be hard to compute.

objectives: Work with cyclic, dihedral and symmetric groups, computing orders of elements and subgroups.
Prove Lagrange's theorem using cosets as equivalence classes.
Identify kernels and images of homomorphisms and recognise normal subgroups.
Apply the orbit–stabiliser theorem and Burnside's lemma to counting problems.
definitions: A subgroup is a subset that contains the identity and is closed under the operation and under inverses.
The left coset of H containing g is gH = {gh : h ∈ H}.
A subgroup N is normal if gNg⁻¹ = N for every g in the group.
An action of G on a set X is a map G × X → X with e · x = x and g · (h · x) = (gh) · x.
keyResults: Lagrange: the order of a subgroup of a finite group divides the order of the group.
Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic; up to isomorphism the cyclic groups are ℤ and ℤ/nℤ.
The kernels of group homomorphisms are exactly the normal subgroups.
Orbit–stabiliser: for a finite group, |G · x| = |G| / |G_x|.
Cayley: every group is isomorphic to a group of permutations of some set.
misconceptions: Believing the converse of Lagrange's theorem: A₄ has order 12 but no subgroup of order 6.
Thinking every subgroup is normal.
Assuming groups are commutative.

references.title: Abstract Algebra
references.author: David S. Dummit and Richard M. Foote

topics.title: Rings, ideals and fields
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Rings and ring homomorphisms, ideals, integral domains and fields, polynomial rings, and the hierarchy of Euclidean domains, principal ideal domains and unique factorisation domains.

discoveries.note: Ideals of polynomial rings correspond to geometric shapes cut out by equations, the starting point of commutative algebra and algebraic geometry.

objectives: Verify the ring axioms and find ideals, units and zero divisors in examples such as ℤ, ℤ/nℤ, ℤ[i] and k[x].
Prove that Euclidean domains are principal ideal domains and that principal ideal domains are unique factorisation domains.
Show that ℤ[√−5] is not a unique factorisation domain.
definitions: An ideal of a commutative ring R is an additive subgroup I such that ra ∈ I for all r ∈ R and a ∈ I.
An integral domain is a commutative ring with 0 ≠ 1 and no zero divisors.
A principal ideal domain is an integral domain in which every ideal is generated by a single element.
keyResults: Euclidean domain ⇒ principal ideal domain ⇒ unique factorisation domain, and neither implication reverses.
If k is a field, the polynomial ring k[x] is a Euclidean domain.
Every finite integral domain is a field.
The kernels of ring homomorphisms are exactly the two-sided ideals.
misconceptions: Assuming every ring is commutative or has a multiplicative identity; conventions differ, so state them.
Confusing subrings with ideals.
Assuming irreducible and prime elements coincide in every integral domain.

references.title: Abstract Algebra
references.author: David S. Dummit and Richard M. Foote

topics.title: Quotient groups and quotient rings
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Collapsing a group by a normal subgroup or a ring by an ideal: cosets as elements, well-defined operations, the isomorphism theorems, ℤ/nℤ as ℤ modulo nℤ, and fields built as quotients of polynomial rings.

discoveries.note: The quotient G → G/N is a coequaliser in the category of groups (of the inclusion N → G and the trivial homomorphism); quotients in general are colimits.

objectives: Construct G/N and R/I and prove that the operations are well defined exactly when N is normal, respectively when the additive subgroup I is an ideal.
Prove the first isomorphism theorem and use it to identify quotients such as ℤ/nℤ, ℝ[x]/(x² + 1) ≅ ℂ and GLₙ(k)/SLₙ(k) ≅ kˣ.
Show that R/I is a field if and only if I is maximal, and an integral domain if and only if I is prime.
definitions: For a normal subgroup N of G, G/N is the set of cosets gN with (gN)(hN) = ghN.
For an ideal I of a ring R, R/I is the set of cosets a + I with the induced addition and multiplication.
The quotient map G → G/N sends g to gN.
keyResults: First isomorphism theorem: for a homomorphism φ : G → H, G/ker φ ≅ im φ, and likewise for rings.
ℤ/nℤ, the quotient of ℤ by the ideal nℤ, is the ring of congruence classes modulo n.
For a commutative ring R with identity, R/I is a field if and only if I is a maximal ideal.
Universal property: every homomorphism G → H whose kernel contains N factors uniquely through the quotient map G → G/N.
misconceptions: Thinking G/N is a subgroup of G.
Defining operations on cosets without checking that they are independent of the chosen representatives.
Assuming every non-zero quotient ℤ/nℤ is a field.

references.title: Abstract Algebra
references.author: David S. Dummit and Richard M. Foote

topics.title: Fields and Galois theory
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Field extensions and degrees, algebraic elements and minimal polynomials, splitting fields, finite fields, the fundamental theorem of Galois theory, and the unsolvability of the general quintic by radicals.

discoveries.note: The Galois correspondence is an instance of a Galois connection, which is an adjunction between partially ordered sets (one taken with the opposite order).

objectives: Compute degrees of extensions with the tower law and find minimal polynomials.
Construct the finite fields 𝔽_{pⁿ} and prove that there is exactly one of each prime-power order up to isomorphism.
State and apply the fundamental theorem of Galois theory, and outline why the general quintic is not solvable by radicals.
definitions: The degree [L : K] of a field extension is the dimension of L as a vector space over K.
The Galois group Gal(L/K) is the group of field automorphisms of L that fix K pointwise.
A finite extension is Galois if it is normal and separable.
keyResults: Tower law: [M : K] = [M : L][L : K].
For a finite Galois extension L/K, intermediate fields correspond bijectively, reversing inclusion, to subgroups of Gal(L/K).
Abel–Ruffini: the general polynomial of degree n ≥ 5 is not solvable by radicals.
With straightedge and compass one cannot trisect a general angle or double the cube.
misconceptions: Reading Abel–Ruffini as saying that no quintic has roots expressible by radicals; specific quintics such as x⁵ − 2 do.
Confusing the ring ℤ/p²ℤ with the field of p² elements.

topics.title: Advanced linear algebra
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Inner product spaces and the spectral theorem, dual spaces, Jordan and rational canonical forms, multilinear algebra and tensor products of vector spaces.

discoveries.note: The isomorphism V → V** is natural in V while V ≅ V* is not; making this distinction precise was a motivation for Eilenberg and Mac Lane's definition of natural transformation.
Vector spaces with the tensor product form a symmetric monoidal category.

objectives: Prove the spectral theorem for real symmetric and complex normal operators.
Compute Jordan normal forms and minimal polynomials.
Define dual spaces and tensor products by universal properties and compute with bases.
definitions: An inner product on a real vector space is a symmetric, positive-definite bilinear form.
The dual space V* is the space of linear maps from V to the field k.
The tensor product V ⊗ W comes with a bilinear map V × W → V ⊗ W through which every bilinear map out of V × W factors uniquely via a linear map.
keyResults: Spectral theorem: every real symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalisable.
Over an algebraically closed field every square matrix is similar to a Jordan normal form, unique up to the order of the blocks.
Cayley–Hamilton: a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial.
dim(V ⊗ W) = dim V · dim W, and for finite-dimensional V the map V → V** is a natural isomorphism.
misconceptions: Thinking V ≅ V* canonically; such an isomorphism depends on a choice (of basis or inner product), whereas V ≅ V** is natural.
Believing every element of V ⊗ W has the form v ⊗ w.

topics.title: Metric spaces and point-set topology
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: From metric spaces to topological spaces: open and closed sets, continuity, homeomorphism, connectedness, compactness, product and quotient topologies, and separation axioms.

discoveries.note: Product and quotient topologies are characterised by universal properties: they are the coarsest, respectively finest, topologies making the relevant maps continuous.

objectives: Prove that ε–δ continuity between metric spaces agrees with the open-set definition.
Prove the Heine–Borel theorem, and that continuous images of compact (respectively connected) spaces are compact (connected).
Construct quotient spaces such as the circle, torus and Möbius band from intervals and squares.
definitions: A metric on X is a function d : X × X → [0, ∞) with d(x, y) = 0 exactly when x = y, d(x, y) = d(y, x), and the triangle inequality.
A topology on X is a collection of subsets (the open sets) containing ∅ and X and closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections.
A space is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover.
A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection whose inverse is continuous.
keyResults: Heine–Borel: a subset of ℝⁿ is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
A continuous real-valued function on a non-empty compact space attains a maximum and a minimum.
Tychonoff: every product of compact spaces is compact; over ZF this is equivalent to the axiom of choice.
The interval [0, 1] is connected.
misconceptions: Thinking 'closed' means 'not open'; a set can be both, or neither.
Assuming a continuous bijection is a homeomorphism; t ↦ (cos t, sin t) from [0, 2π) to the circle is not.
Believing that closed and bounded implies compact in every metric space.

topics.title: Differential geometry of curves and surfaces
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: Curvature and torsion of space curves, the first and second fundamental forms of surfaces, Gaussian and mean curvature, Gauss's Theorema Egregium, geodesics and the Gauss–Bonnet theorem.

discoveries.note: The Theorema Egregium motivates intrinsic geometry, which is studied on abstract manifolds with no surrounding space.

objectives: Compute curvature and torsion using the Frenet–Serret frame.
Compute the first and second fundamental forms and the Gaussian curvature of standard surfaces.
State the Theorema Egregium and the Gauss–Bonnet theorem and check them on spheres and tori.
definitions: The curvature of a unit-speed curve γ is κ = |γ″|.
The Gaussian curvature K of a surface at a point is the product of its principal curvatures.
A geodesic on a surface is a curve whose acceleration is everywhere normal to the surface.
keyResults: Theorema Egregium: Gaussian curvature depends only on the first fundamental form, so it is intrinsic.
Gauss–Bonnet: for a compact oriented surface S without boundary, ∫_S K dA = 2πχ(S).
No map from an open region of a sphere to the plane preserves all distances, because their Gaussian curvatures differ.
misconceptions: Thinking a cylinder is curved in the Gaussian sense; its Gaussian curvature is zero.
Confusing the curvature of a curve with the Gaussian curvature of a surface.

references.title: Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces
references.author: Manfredo P. do Carmo

topics.title: Homotopy and the fundamental group
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: Homotopy of maps and paths, the fundamental group, covering spaces, the computation π₁(S¹) ≅ ℤ, the Seifert–van Kampen theorem and applications such as the two-dimensional Brouwer fixed-point theorem.

discoveries.note: In homotopy type theory the circle is a higher inductive type, and π₁(S¹) ≅ ℤ has a synthetic proof.

objectives: Define homotopy and the fundamental group, and prove that the fundamental group is a homotopy invariant.
Compute π₁(S¹) ≅ ℤ using covering spaces and deduce the Brouwer fixed-point theorem for the disc.
Use the Seifert–van Kampen theorem to compute fundamental groups of wedges of circles and of surfaces.
definitions: A homotopy between maps f, g : X → Y is a continuous map H : X × [0, 1] → Y with H(x, 0) = f(x) and H(x, 1) = g(x).
π₁(X, x₀) is the group of homotopy classes of loops based at x₀, with concatenation as the operation.
A covering map p : E → B is a continuous surjection such that each point of B has an open neighbourhood U whose preimage is a disjoint union of open sets, each mapped homeomorphically onto U.
keyResults: π₁(S¹) ≅ ℤ.
Brouwer: every continuous map from the closed disc to itself has a fixed point.
The fundamental group of a wedge of two circles is the free group on two generators.
For path-connected, locally path-connected and semilocally simply connected spaces, connected covering spaces correspond to conjugacy classes of subgroups of π₁.
misconceptions: Thinking fundamental groups are always abelian.
Believing spaces with isomorphic fundamental groups are homeomorphic; S² and a point both have trivial fundamental group.

topics.title: Real analysis
topics.subject: analysis
topics.summary: Rigorous analysis on the real line: completeness, sequences and series, limits and continuity, uniform convergence, differentiation and the Riemann integral, with proofs of the theorems calculus relies on.

discoveries.note: Mathlib formalises much of undergraduate analysis, so theorems such as these can be stated and checked in Lean.

objectives: Prove the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem and the intermediate and extreme value theorems from completeness.
Distinguish pointwise from uniform convergence and prove that uniform limits of continuous functions are continuous.
Prove the fundamental theorem of calculus for the Riemann integral.
definitions: aₙ → L if for every ε > 0 there is N such that |aₙ − L| < ε for all n ≥ N.
fₙ → f uniformly on S if sup_{x∈S} |fₙ(x) − f(x)| → 0.
A sequence is Cauchy if for every ε > 0 there is N such that |aₘ − aₙ| < ε for all m, n ≥ N.
keyResults: In ℝ, a sequence converges if and only if it is Cauchy.
Bolzano–Weierstrass: every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence.
Uniform limits of continuous functions are continuous.
There are continuous functions that are differentiable nowhere (Weierstrass).
misconceptions: Interchanging limits without justification; a pointwise limit of continuous functions need not be continuous.
Thinking every bounded function on [0, 1] is Riemann integrable; the indicator function of ℚ is not.

topics.title: Complex analysis
topics.subject: analysis
topics.summary: Holomorphic functions and the Cauchy–Riemann equations, contour integration and Cauchy's theorem, power series, Liouville's theorem, the residue theorem and conformal maps.

discoveries.note: Compact Riemann surfaces correspond to smooth projective complex algebraic curves.

objectives: Check holomorphy using the Cauchy–Riemann equations.
Prove Cauchy's integral formula and deduce that holomorphic functions are analytic.
Evaluate real integrals by residues, and prove the fundamental theorem of algebra from Liouville's theorem.
definitions: f is holomorphic on an open set U ⊆ ℂ if it is complex-differentiable at every point of U.
The residue of f at an isolated singularity a is the coefficient of (z − a)⁻¹ in its Laurent expansion about a.
keyResults: Cauchy's integral formula.
Holomorphic functions are infinitely differentiable and are locally equal to their Taylor series.
Liouville: every bounded entire function is constant.
Fundamental theorem of algebra: every non-constant complex polynomial has a complex root.
misconceptions: Assuming every real-differentiable function of two variables is holomorphic; z ↦ z̄ is not.
Thinking a function holomorphic except at one point always extends holomorphically to that point; 1/z does not.

references.title: Complex Analysis
references.author: Elias M. Stein and Rami Shakarchi

topics.title: Partial differential equations and Fourier series
topics.subject: analysis
topics.summary: The heat, wave and Laplace equations, separation of variables, Fourier series and their convergence, boundary value problems and the maximum principle.

discoveries.note: Fourier series are expansions in an orthonormal basis of the Hilbert space L².

objectives: Solve the heat and wave equations on an interval by separation of variables and Fourier series.
State convergence results for Fourier series and compute examples, including the Gibbs phenomenon.
Use the maximum principle and energy methods to prove uniqueness of solutions.
definitions: The heat equation is u_t = k u_xx, the wave equation is u_tt = c² u_xx, and Laplace's equation is Δu = 0.
The Fourier series of an integrable 2π-periodic function f is Σ cₙ e^(inx) with cₙ = (1/2π) ∫_{−π}^{π} f(x) e^(−inx) dx.
keyResults: Parseval: for square-integrable f, Σ |cₙ|² = (1/2π) ∫_{−π}^{π} |f(x)|² dx.
Harmonic functions have the mean value property and satisfy the maximum principle.
d'Alembert: every twice continuously differentiable solution of the wave equation on ℝ has the form f(x − ct) + g(x + ct).
misconceptions: Thinking the Fourier series of every continuous function converges at every point; du Bois-Reymond constructed a counterexample.
Assuming a Fourier series can always be differentiated term by term.

references.title: Fourier Analysis: An Introduction
references.author: Elias M. Stein and Rami Shakarchi

topics.title: Graph theory
topics.subject: discrete
topics.summary: Connectivity, matchings and Hall's theorem, colouring, planarity and Euler's formula, extremal results such as Turán's theorem, and Ramsey theory.

discoveries.note: Deciding whether a graph is 3-colourable is NP-complete.

objectives: Prove Hall's marriage theorem and apply it.
Prove Euler's formula V − E + F = 2 for connected plane graphs and deduce that K₅ and K₃,₃ are not planar.
Prove that R(3, 3) = 6 and establish upper bounds for Ramsey numbers.
definitions: A matching is a set of edges no two of which share a vertex.
A proper k-colouring assigns one of k colours to each vertex so that adjacent vertices receive different colours.
The Ramsey number R(s, t) is the least n such that every red–blue colouring of the edges of Kₙ contains a red K_s or a blue K_t.
keyResults: Hall: a bipartite graph with parts A and B has a matching covering A if and only if |N(S)| ≥ |S| for every S ⊆ A.
Four colour theorem (Appel and Haken, 1976): every planar graph is 4-colourable; the proof relies on computer verification.
Kuratowski: a graph is planar if and only if it contains no subdivision of K₅ or K₃,₃.
misconceptions: Thinking a graph is planar only if a given drawing has no crossings; it is planar if some drawing has none.
Assuming the four colour theorem has a short proof checkable by hand; known proofs use computers, and one has been formally verified in Coq.

references.title: Graph Theory with Applications
references.author: J. A. Bondy and U. S. R. Murty

topics.title: Enumerative combinatorics
topics.subject: discrete
topics.summary: Generating functions in depth, integer partitions, exponential generating functions, Burnside's lemma and Pólya counting, and the combinatorics of permutations.

discoveries.note: Partitions of n index the irreducible complex representations of the symmetric group Sₙ.

objectives: Use exponential generating functions to count labelled structures such as set partitions and derangements.
Prove Euler's theorem that partitions into odd parts are equinumerous with partitions into distinct parts.
Count colourings up to symmetry with Burnside's lemma and Pólya's theorem.
definitions: A partition of n is a way of writing n as an unordered sum of positive integers.
The exponential generating function of (aₙ) is Σ aₙxⁿ/n!.
Burnside's lemma: a finite group G acting on a finite set X has (1/|G|) Σ_{g∈G} |Fix(g)| orbits.
keyResults: The number of partitions of n into odd parts equals the number of partitions of n into distinct parts.
The number of derangements of n objects is n! Σ_{k=0}^{n} (−1)ᵏ/k!.
Burnside's lemma (also called the Cauchy–Frobenius lemma).
misconceptions: Counting colourings up to symmetry by dividing by the size of the group; this fails when some colourings are themselves symmetric.

topics.title: Markov chains
topics.subject: probability
topics.summary: Discrete-time Markov chains: transition matrices, classification of states, stationary distributions, convergence to equilibrium, hitting times and random walks.

discoveries.note: Stochastic models of populations and of genetic drift, such as the Wright–Fisher model, are Markov chains.

objectives: Model processes with transition matrices and compute n-step transition probabilities.
Classify states as recurrent or transient and find stationary distributions.
Prove convergence to equilibrium for irreducible aperiodic finite chains.
definitions: A Markov chain is a sequence of random variables in which the conditional distribution of the next state, given the past, depends only on the current state.
A probability distribution π (as a row vector) is stationary for transition matrix P if πP = π.
A chain is irreducible if every state can be reached from every other state.
keyResults: An irreducible Markov chain on a finite state space has a unique stationary distribution.
If it is also aperiodic, the distribution at time n converges to the stationary distribution from any starting distribution.
Pólya: simple random walk is recurrent on ℤ and ℤ² and transient on ℤ³.
misconceptions: Reading 'memoryless' as 'forgets everything'; it means the future depends on the past only through the present.

topics.title: Natural transformations
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Natural transformations as morphisms between functors: naturality squares, natural isomorphisms, functor categories, equivalence of categories, and examples such as the double-dual embedding and the determinant.

discoveries.note: Eilenberg and Mac Lane introduced categories, functors and natural transformations (1945) to make precise the naturality of constructions in algebraic topology, such as homology.

objectives: Verify naturality for examples such as V → V** and the determinant GLₙ(R) → Rˣ, natural in the commutative ring R.
Explain why V ≅ V** is natural, while V ≅ V* cannot even be stated as a natural transformation between functors of the same variance.
Define equivalence of categories and prove that a functor is an equivalence if and only if it is full, faithful and essentially surjective.
definitions: A natural transformation α : F ⇒ G between functors F, G : C → D consists of morphisms α_A : F(A) → G(A), one for each object A, such that G(f) ∘ α_A = α_B ∘ F(f) for every morphism f : A → B.
A natural isomorphism is a natural transformation all of whose components are isomorphisms.
An equivalence of categories is a functor F : C → D together with a functor G : D → C and natural isomorphisms G ∘ F ≅ id_C and F ∘ G ≅ id_D.
keyResults: Functors C → D and the natural transformations between them form a functor category [C, D].
A functor is an equivalence if and only if it is fully faithful and essentially surjective (the 'if' direction uses the axiom of choice in general).
The category of finite-dimensional vector spaces over k is equivalent to its full subcategory on the spaces kⁿ, whose morphisms are matrices.
misconceptions: Thinking 'natural' means 'obvious' or 'canonical-looking'; it is a precise commuting condition.
Believing equivalent categories must be isomorphic.

topics.title: Products, coproducts, initial and terminal objects
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Initial and terminal objects, products and coproducts in a general category, their computation in Set, Grp, Ab, Top and posets, and the duality between them.

discoveries.note: Product and sum types in programming languages correspond to products and coproducts.

objectives: Identify initial and terminal objects in Set, Grp, rings and posets, or show that none exist.
Compute products and coproducts in Set (disjoint union), Grp (free product), Ab (direct sum), Top and a poset (meet and join).
Prove that products are unique up to unique isomorphism and that coproducts in C are products in Cᵒᵖ.
definitions: An object T is terminal if every object has exactly one morphism to T; an initial object is defined dually.
A product of A and B is an object A × B with morphisms π₁ : A × B → A and π₂ : A × B → B such that for every f : X → A and g : X → B there is a unique h : X → A × B with π₁ ∘ h = f and π₂ ∘ h = g.
A coproduct in C is a product in Cᵒᵖ.
keyResults: In Set, ∅ is initial, every one-element set is terminal, and coproducts are disjoint unions.
In Grp the trivial group is both initial and terminal, and the coproduct of two groups is their free product.
In a poset regarded as a category, products are greatest lower bounds and coproducts are least upper bounds, when they exist.
In the category of rings with identity, ℤ is initial.
A product of A and B is a terminal object in the category of cones over the pair (A, B).
misconceptions: Assuming coproducts look like products: in Grp, ℤ ∗ ℤ is non-abelian, unlike ℤ × ℤ.
Thinking every category has products.

topics.title: Limits and colimits
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Diagrams, cones and limits: equalisers, pullbacks and inverse limits and their duals, completeness of Set, Grp and Top, the construction of all limits from products and equalisers, and preservation of limits by functors.

discoveries.note: Limits are right adjoints: taking limits of J-shaped diagrams is right adjoint to the diagonal functor C → [J, C], and right adjoints preserve all limits.

objectives: Compute equalisers, pullbacks and pushouts in Set, Grp and Top.
Prove that a category with all small products and equalisers has all small limits.
Show that hom functors Hom(A, −) preserve limits, and describe the p-adic integers as an inverse limit.
definitions: A diagram of shape J in C is a functor D : J → C.
A cone over D with apex X is a natural transformation from the constant functor at X to D; a limit of D is a terminal cone.
A colimit is a limit in the opposite category, that is, an initial cocone.
keyResults: A category with all small products and equalisers has all small limits.
Set, Grp, Ab, Top and Vect_k have all small limits and colimits.
Hom(A, −) sends limits in C to limits in Set.
The p-adic integers are the inverse limit of the rings ℤ/pⁿℤ.
misconceptions: Identifying categorical limits with limits of sequences. They are related (the supremum of an increasing sequence of reals is a colimit in the poset (ℝ, ≤)) but they are different notions.
Expecting forgetful functors to preserve colimits as they preserve limits; Grp → Set preserves products but not coproducts.

topics.title: Adjunctions
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Adjoint functors F ⊣ G via natural bijections Hom(FA, B) ≅ Hom(A, GB), units and counits, free–forgetful adjunctions, Galois connections, currying and the tensor–hom adjunction, and the preservation of limits by right adjoints.

discoveries.note: A functor G : D → C has a left adjoint if and only if, for each object A of C, the functor Hom_C(A, G(−)) : D → Set is representable; the Yoneda lemma then assembles the representing objects into a functor.
Currying, the adjunction − × B ⊣ (−)^B, is the basis of function types in the typed λ-calculus.

objectives: Verify adjunctions such as free monoid ⊣ forgetful, − × B ⊣ (−)^B in Set, and the tensor–hom adjunction.
Pass between the hom-set and the unit–counit definitions of an adjunction using the triangle identities.
Prove that right adjoints preserve limits and left adjoints preserve colimits, and use this to show that some functors have no adjoint.
definitions: F : C → D is left adjoint to G : D → C, written F ⊣ G, if there are bijections Hom_D(FA, B) ≅ Hom_C(A, GB) natural in A and B.
The unit η : id_C ⇒ GF and counit ε : FG ⇒ id_D of an adjunction satisfy the triangle identities εF ∘ Fη = id_F and Gε ∘ ηG = id_G.
A Galois connection is an adjunction between posets regarded as categories.
keyResults: A left (or right) adjoint of a functor is unique up to unique natural isomorphism.
Right adjoints preserve all limits that exist, and left adjoints preserve all colimits that exist.
Every adjunction F ⊣ G induces a monad GF.
In Set, − × B ⊣ (−)^B: functions A × B → C correspond to functions A → C^B (currying).
misconceptions: Thinking every functor has an adjoint.
Mixing up left and right; in a free–forgetful adjunction the free functor is the left adjoint.
Assuming an adjunction is an equivalence; its unit and counit need not be isomorphisms.

topics.title: Representable functors
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Functors naturally isomorphic to Hom(A, −) or Hom(−, A): the forgetful functor on groups (represented by ℤ), the power-set functor (represented by a two-element set), and representing objects as solutions of universal problems.

discoveries.note: Grothendieck's functor of points views a scheme X through the functor Hom(−, X); many moduli problems ask whether a given functor is representable.
In a topos, the functor sending an object to its set of subobjects is represented by the subobject classifier Ω, generalising the representation of power sets by {0, 1}.

objectives: Show that the forgetful functor Grp → Set is represented by ℤ, and that the contravariant power-set functor on Set is represented by {0, 1}.
Prove that a representing object, together with its universal element, is unique up to unique isomorphism.
Express products, free objects and quotients as representing objects of suitable functors.
definitions: A functor F : C → Set is representable if F ≅ Hom(A, −) for some object A; a functor F : Cᵒᵖ → Set is representable if F ≅ Hom(−, A).
A universal element of F : C → Set is a pair (A, x) with x ∈ F(A) such that for every object B and y ∈ F(B) there is a unique f : A → B with F(f)(x) = y.
keyResults: The forgetful functor Grp → Set is represented by ℤ, with universal element 1.
The contravariant power-set functor is isomorphic to Hom(−, {0, 1}): subsets correspond to characteristic functions.
Representations of F correspond to universal elements of F.
misconceptions: Thinking every functor to Set is representable.
Confusing covariant with contravariant representability.

topics.title: The Yoneda lemma
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: The Yoneda lemma, Nat(Hom(A, −), F) ≅ F(A); the full and faithful Yoneda embedding of a category into presheaves; and the principle that an object is determined up to isomorphism by the morphisms into it.

discoveries.note: An ∞-categorical Yoneda lemma also holds and is a basic tool of higher category theory.
In homotopy type theory, path induction can be seen as a type-theoretic analogue of the Yoneda lemma for identity types.

objectives: State and prove the Yoneda lemma, including its naturality in A and F.
Deduce that the Yoneda embedding C → [Cᵒᵖ, Set] is full and faithful, and that Hom(−, A) ≅ Hom(−, B) implies A ≅ B.
Apply the Yoneda lemma in familiar settings, for example to recover Cayley's theorem for groups.
definitions: For a locally small category C, the Yoneda embedding y : C → [Cᵒᵖ, Set] sends A to Hom(−, A).
A presheaf on C is a functor Cᵒᵖ → Set.
keyResults: Yoneda lemma: for every functor F : C → Set and object A, natural transformations Hom(A, −) ⇒ F correspond bijectively to elements of F(A), via α ↦ α_A(id_A).
The Yoneda embedding is full and faithful; hence A ≅ B whenever Hom(−, A) ≅ Hom(−, B).
Applied to a group regarded as a one-object category, the Yoneda lemma yields Cayley's theorem.
Every presheaf on a small category is a colimit of representable presheaves.
misconceptions: Reading Yoneda as saying an object 'is' its set of elements; it says an object is determined by the morphisms into it from all objects.
Expecting the lemma to be hard to prove; its proof is short, and its power lies in how widely it applies.

topics.title: Computability
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: Turing machines and other models of computation, the Church–Turing thesis, decidable and recursively enumerable sets, the undecidability of the halting problem, reductions and Rice's theorem.

discoveries.note: Church's λ-calculus computes exactly the same functions as Turing machines.

objectives: Design simple Turing machines and simulate them.
Prove that the halting problem is undecidable by a diagonal argument.
Use reductions to prove undecidability, and state Rice's theorem.
definitions: A Turing machine is a finite-state machine with an unbounded tape that it can read, write and move along.
A set is decidable if some algorithm always halts and correctly decides membership, and recursively enumerable if some algorithm halts exactly on its members.
The Church–Turing thesis states that every effectively computable function is computable by a Turing machine.
keyResults: The halting problem is undecidable (Turing, 1936).
A set is decidable if and only if both it and its complement are recursively enumerable.
Rice's theorem: every non-trivial property of the functions computed by programs is undecidable.
There are only countably many Turing machines, so most functions ℕ → ℕ are not computable.
misconceptions: Treating the Church–Turing thesis as a theorem; it concerns the informal notion of effective computability and is supported by the equivalence of many models.
Thinking undecidability means no instance can be solved; it means no single algorithm solves every instance.

references.title: Introduction to the Theory of Computation
references.author: Michael Sipser

references.title: Computability and Logic
references.author: George S. Boolos, John P. Burgess and Richard C. Jeffrey

topics.title: The λ-calculus
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: The untyped λ-calculus (terms, β-reduction, Church encodings, fixed-point combinators, confluence) and the simply typed λ-calculus with normalisation.

discoveries.note: The simply typed λ-calculus with products is an internal language for cartesian closed categories (Lambek).

objectives: Reduce λ-terms and encode booleans, pairs and natural numbers (Church numerals).
Use a fixed-point combinator to define recursive functions, and explain why untyped terms need not terminate.
State the Church–Rosser theorem and explain why every simply typed term has a normal form.
definitions: λ-terms are built from variables by application (M N) and abstraction (λx. M).
β-reduction rewrites (λx. M) N to M[N/x], using capture-avoiding substitution.
A term is in normal form if no β-reduction applies to it.
keyResults: Church–Rosser: β-reduction is confluent, so a term has at most one normal form.
The untyped λ-calculus computes exactly the partial recursive functions.
Every simply typed λ-term has a normal form; in fact the simply typed λ-calculus is strongly normalising.
misconceptions: Substituting without renaming bound variables (variable capture).
Thinking every λ-term has a normal form; (λx. x x)(λx. x x) does not.

references.title: The Lambda Calculus: Its Syntax and Semantics
references.author: H. P. Barendregt

references.title: Lambda-Calculus and Combinators: An Introduction
references.author: J. Roger Hindley and Jonathan P. Seldin

topics.title: Computational complexity
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: Time and space complexity classes, P and NP, polynomial-time reductions, NP-completeness and the Cook–Levin theorem, and the status of the P versus NP problem.

discoveries.note: Proof complexity asks how long proofs of propositional tautologies must be; NP ≠ coNP holds if and only if no propositional proof system has polynomial-size proofs of all tautologies (Cook–Reckhow).

objectives: Define P and NP and place standard problems in them.
Prove NP-completeness of problems such as 3-SAT, vertex cover or graph 3-colouring by reductions.
Explain what is known and unknown about P versus NP, and why cryptography relies on unproved hardness assumptions.
definitions: P is the class of decision problems solvable in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine.
NP is the class of decision problems whose yes-instances have certificates that can be verified in polynomial time.
A problem is NP-complete if it is in NP and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time.
keyResults: Cook–Levin: Boolean satisfiability (SAT) is NP-complete.
P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME, and P ≠ EXPTIME by the time hierarchy theorem.
Whether P = NP is open; it is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems.
misconceptions: Thinking NP stands for 'not polynomial'; it stands for nondeterministic polynomial time.
Believing NP-complete problems cannot be solved in practice; many large instances are solved routinely.

references.title: Introduction to the Theory of Computation
references.author: Michael Sipser

topics.title: Numerical analysis
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: Numerical linear algebra (LU and QR factorisations, conditioning, least squares, eigenvalue algorithms), numerical solution of ODEs (Euler and Runge–Kutta methods, stiffness), and convergence and stability analysis.
objectives: Solve linear systems by LU factorisation with partial pivoting and analyse their conditioning.
Solve least-squares problems via QR factorisation and compute eigenvalues with the QR algorithm.
Implement Euler and Runge–Kutta methods and analyse their order and stability, including for stiff problems.
definitions: The condition number κ(A) = ‖A‖ ‖A⁻¹‖ measures how sensitive the solution of Ax = b is to perturbations of the data.
An algorithm is backward stable if it computes the exact answer to a slightly perturbed problem.
A one-step method for ODEs has order p if its global error is O(hᵖ) for step size h.
keyResults: The relative error in the solution of Ax = b is bounded, to first order, by κ(A) times the relative error in the data.
Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting is backward stable in practice, although its worst-case growth factor is 2ⁿ⁻¹.
The classical Runge–Kutta method has order 4.
Explicit methods applied to stiff problems need very small steps, whereas some implicit methods are A-stable.
misconceptions: Computing A⁻¹ in order to solve Ax = b.
Assuming a smaller step size always reduces the total error; rounding error eventually grows.

references.title: Numerical Linear Algebra
references.author: Lloyd N. Trefethen and David Bau III

references.title: An Introduction to Numerical Analysis
references.author: Endre Süli and David F. Mayers

topics.title: Optimisation
topics.subject: applied
topics.summary: Linear programming and duality, convex sets and functions, Lagrange multipliers and the KKT conditions, gradient descent and Newton's method, and applications to data fitting.

discoveries.note: Least squares and maximum likelihood estimation are optimisation problems.

objectives: Formulate and solve linear programs with the simplex method, and interpret the dual problem.
Prove that local minima of convex functions are global, and apply the KKT conditions.
Implement gradient descent and analyse its convergence for smooth convex functions.
definitions: A set C is convex if it contains the line segment between any two of its points.
A function f is convex if f(tx + (1 − t)y) ≤ t f(x) + (1 − t) f(y) for all x, y and 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.
A linear program optimises a linear function subject to finitely many linear inequalities.
keyResults: Strong duality for linear programming: if the primal problem has an optimal solution, so does the dual, with the same optimal value.
Every local minimum of a convex function on a convex set is a global minimum.
For a convex function with L-Lipschitz gradient, gradient descent with step size 1/L reduces the gap to the optimal value at rate O(1/k).
misconceptions: Assuming every critical point is a minimum.
Thinking every linear program has an optimal solution; it may be infeasible or unbounded.

references.title: Numerical Optimization
references.author: Jorge Nocedal and Stephen J. Wright

topics.title: Information theory
topics.subject: applied
topics.summary: Entropy and information, Shannon's source coding theorem, prefix codes and Huffman coding, mutual information, channel capacity and the noisy-channel coding theorem.
objectives: Compute entropy, joint and conditional entropy, and mutual information.
Construct Huffman codes and prove Kraft's inequality.
State the source coding and noisy-channel coding theorems and compute the capacity of the binary symmetric channel.
definitions: The entropy of a discrete random variable X is H(X) = −Σ p(x) log₂ p(x).
The mutual information of X and Y is I(X; Y) = H(X) − H(X | Y).
The capacity of a channel is the maximum of I(X; Y) over all input distributions.
keyResults: The expected length of an optimal binary prefix code for X lies between H(X) and H(X) + 1 bits.
Kraft: a binary prefix code with codeword lengths ℓᵢ exists if and only if Σ 2^(−ℓᵢ) ≤ 1.
The binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p has capacity 1 − H(p).
Noisy-channel coding theorem: reliable communication is possible at every rate below capacity and impossible at rates above it.
misconceptions: Equating information with meaning; Shannon information measures uncertainty.
Thinking a compression method can shrink every file.

references.title: Elements of Information Theory
references.author: Thomas M. Cover and Joy A. Thomas

references.title: Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms
references.author: David J. C. MacKay

topics.title: Mathematical biology
topics.subject: applied
topics.summary: Mathematical models in biology: population growth and the logistic equation, predator–prey and competition models, epidemic models such as SIR, stability analysis by linearisation, and the limits of models.
objectives: Analyse the logistic equation and discrete-time population models, including the onset of chaos in the logistic map.
Find the equilibria of predator–prey and SIR models and classify their stability using the Jacobian.
Interpret the basic reproduction number R₀ and the assumptions behind it.
definitions: The logistic equation is dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K).
The SIR model is S′ = −βSI/N, I′ = βSI/N − γI, R′ = γI.
In the simple SIR model, R₀ = β/γ is the expected number of new infections caused by one infected individual in a fully susceptible population.
keyResults: In the SIR model the number of infected individuals initially grows if and only if R₀ S(0)/N > 1.
An equilibrium at which every eigenvalue of the Jacobian has negative real part is locally asymptotically stable.
The Lotka–Volterra predator–prey model has a conserved quantity, so its orbits are closed curves.
misconceptions: Treating model predictions as forecasts independent of their assumptions.
Thinking R₀ is a fixed biological constant; it depends on behaviour and environment.

topics.title: Model theory
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Structures and their theories: elementary equivalence and elementary embeddings, types, ultraproducts and Łoś's theorem, and quantifier elimination, with examples from orders, fields and algebraic geometry.

discoveries.note: Quantifier elimination for algebraically closed fields gives a logical proof that projections of constructible sets are constructible.
Forcing builds new models of ZFC from old ones, a model-theoretic method at the heart of independence proofs.

objectives: Prove Łoś's theorem and use ultraproducts to give a second proof of compactness.
Prove quantifier elimination for dense linear orders without endpoints, and state it for algebraically closed fields.
Use the theory of algebraically closed fields to explain the Lefschetz principle and the Ax–Grothendieck theorem.
definitions: Structures are elementarily equivalent if they satisfy the same first-order sentences.
An elementary embedding preserves the truth of every formula with parameters.
A theory has quantifier elimination if every formula is equivalent, modulo the theory, to a quantifier-free formula.
An ultraproduct ∏ Mᵢ / U is the quotient of a product of structures by an ultrafilter U on the index set.
keyResults: Łoś's theorem: a formula holds in ∏ Mᵢ / U exactly when the set of indices i at which it holds in Mᵢ belongs to U.
The theory of dense linear orders without endpoints is ℵ₀-categorical and has quantifier elimination.
The theory of algebraically closed fields has quantifier elimination, a result closely related to Chevalley's theorem on constructible sets.
Ax–Grothendieck: every injective polynomial map ℂⁿ → ℂⁿ is surjective.
misconceptions: Thinking elementarily equivalent structures must be isomorphic: (ℚ, <) and (ℝ, <) are elementarily equivalent but not isomorphic.
Taking the existence of many models as a sign that a theory is vague; it is typical of first-order theories with infinite models.

references.title: Model Theory
references.author: C. C. Chang and H. J. Keisler

topics.title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Arithmetisation of syntax, representability of computable functions, the diagonal lemma, Gödel's first and second incompleteness theorems and Tarski's undefinability of truth.

discoveries.note: If ZFC is consistent it cannot prove that an inaccessible cardinal exists, because such a cardinal κ would give a model V_κ of ZFC and hence prove Con(ZFC).

objectives: Explain how formulas and proofs are coded by natural numbers and why provability is expressible in arithmetic.
Prove the diagonal lemma and derive the first incompleteness theorem, in Rosser's form, for consistent recursively axiomatised theories extending Robinson arithmetic Q.
State the second incompleteness theorem and Tarski's theorem, and explain precisely what they do and do not say.
definitions: A theory is recursively axiomatised if its set of axioms is decidable.
Robinson arithmetic Q is a weak, finitely axiomatised fragment of Peano arithmetic (PA) without the induction schema.
Diagonal lemma: for every formula φ(x) there is a sentence G such that the theory proves G ↔ φ(⌜G⌝), where ⌜G⌝ is the numeral of G's code.
keyResults: First incompleteness theorem (Gödel 1931; Rosser 1936): every consistent, recursively axiomatised theory extending Q is incomplete.
Second incompleteness theorem: a consistent, recursively axiomatised theory extending PA does not prove its own (standard) consistency statement.
Tarski: the set of true sentences of arithmetic is not definable in arithmetic.
Presburger arithmetic (addition only) and the theory of real closed fields are complete and decidable, so incompleteness needs enough arithmetic.
misconceptions: Claiming Gödel showed that 'some truths can never be known'; the theorems concern provability in a fixed formal theory.
Applying the theorems to theories that are not recursively axiomatised or cannot interpret enough arithmetic.
Thinking the second theorem leaves PA's consistency wholly unsupported; it can be proved in stronger systems, for example by Gentzen's method using induction up to ε₀.

references.title: Computability and Logic
references.author: George S. Boolos, John P. Burgess and Richard C. Jeffrey

topics.title: Proof theory
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Proofs as mathematical objects: natural deduction and sequent calculus, cut elimination and normalisation, consistency proofs and ordinal analysis, and the link to computation through Curry–Howard.

discoveries.note: Proofs modulo normalisation can be organised into categories: proofs in the conjunction–implication fragment of intuitionistic logic correspond to morphisms of free cartesian closed categories.

objectives: Present classical and intuitionistic sequent calculi and prove cut elimination for propositional logic.
Derive the subformula property and consistency from cut elimination.
Explain the idea of Gentzen's consistency proof for PA using transfinite induction up to ε₀.
definitions: A sequent Γ ⊢ Δ asserts that the conjunction of the formulas in Γ entails the disjunction of those in Δ.
The cut rule combines proofs of Γ ⊢ A, Δ and Γ′, A ⊢ Δ′ into a proof of Γ, Γ′ ⊢ Δ, Δ′.
ε₀ is the least ordinal ε with ω^ε = ε.
keyResults: Gentzen's Hauptsatz: the cut rule is admissible in the sequent calculus for first-order logic.
Cut-free proofs have the subformula property.
Gentzen (1936): the consistency of PA is provable in primitive recursive arithmetic together with quantifier-free transfinite induction up to ε₀.
PA does not prove transfinite induction up to ε₀ (for a standard notation system), although it proves it for every smaller ordinal in that system.
misconceptions: Thinking Gentzen's proof is circular; it relies on a principle not available in PA but different in kind from PA's consistency.
Believing cut elimination shortens proofs; it can increase their length enormously (non-elementarily).

references.title: Basic Proof Theory
references.author: A. S. Troelstra and H. Schwichtenberg

references.title: Proofs and Types
references.author: Jean-Yves Girard, Yves Lafont and Paul Taylor

topics.title: Axiomatic set theory: hierarchy, cardinal arithmetic and L
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Graduate set theory: the cumulative hierarchy, transfinite recursion, cofinality and cardinal arithmetic, reflection, and Gödel's constructible universe L, which shows that AC and GCH are consistent relative to ZF.

discoveries.note: Inner models such as L, and reflection arguments, are model-theoretic tools used inside set theory.

objectives: Define the cumulative hierarchy V_α by transfinite recursion and show, using foundation, that every set lies in some V_α.
Compute with cofinality and prove König's theorem that cf(2^κ) > κ.
Outline Gödel's proof that if ZF is consistent then so is ZFC + GCH, using the constructible universe L.
definitions: V₀ = ∅, V_{α+1} = P(V_α), and V_λ = ⋃_{α<λ} V_α for limit ordinals λ.
The cofinality cf(κ) is the least order type of a cofinal subset of κ; κ is regular when cf(κ) = κ.
L is the union of levels L_α, where L_{α+1} consists of the subsets of L_α definable over L_α with parameters.
The generalised continuum hypothesis (GCH) states that 2^κ = κ⁺ for every infinite cardinal κ.
keyResults: König: cf(2^κ) > κ for every infinite cardinal κ; in particular 2^ℵ₀ ≠ ℵ_ω.
Gödel: L satisfies ZFC + GCH, so if ZF is consistent then so is ZFC + GCH.
Reflection: for each finite set of formulas, ZF proves that some V_α reflects them.
misconceptions: Thinking L is the universe of all sets; V = L is an extra axiom, consistent with ZFC but not provable from it (if ZFC is consistent).
Confusing a relative consistency proof with an absolute consistency proof.

references.title: Set Theory: An Introduction to Independence Proofs
references.author: Kenneth Kunen

topics.title: Forcing and independence
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Relative consistency and independence: countable transitive models, posets of conditions, generic filters and the forcing relation, leading to Cohen's proof that the continuum hypothesis is independent of ZFC.

discoveries.note: Many independent statements concern sets of reals, where descriptive set theory gives a finer classification of which sets are well behaved.
Cohen's construction can be presented as passing to a topos of sheaves on a poset of conditions, as in Mac Lane and Moerdijk's treatment of the independence of CH.

objectives: Explain what it means for a statement to be independent of ZFC and why independence proofs are relative-consistency proofs.
Construct a generic extension M[G] by Cohen forcing and verify that it satisfies ZFC + ¬CH, given a countable transitive model M of ZFC.
State Easton's theorem and give other examples of statements shown independent by forcing, such as Suslin's hypothesis.
definitions: A statement φ is independent of ZFC if neither φ nor ¬φ is provable from ZFC.
A forcing notion is a poset (P, ≤) of conditions; a filter G ⊆ P is M-generic if it meets every dense subset of P that belongs to M.
The forcing relation p ⊩ φ means that φ holds in every generic extension M[G] with p ∈ G.
keyResults: Cohen (1963): if ZFC is consistent, so is ZFC + ¬CH. Together with Gödel's work on L, CH is independent of ZFC.
Truth lemma: φ holds in M[G] if and only if some p ∈ G forces φ.
Easton (1970): on regular cardinals, the function κ ↦ 2^κ can consistently be any non-decreasing function F with cf(F(κ)) > κ.
misconceptions: Thinking independence makes a question meaningless; it means ZFC does not settle it.
Believing forcing requires a countable transitive model of ZFC to exist; formal treatments avoid this with Boolean-valued models or by working with finite fragments of ZFC.

references.title: Set Theory: An Introduction to Independence Proofs
references.author: Kenneth Kunen

references.title: Set Theory and the Continuum Hypothesis
references.author: Paul J. Cohen

topics.title: Descriptive set theory
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Definable sets of reals and of Polish spaces: the Borel hierarchy, analytic and coanalytic sets, Suslin's theorem and the perfect set property, where topology, set theory and logic meet.

discoveries.note: Martin and Steel showed that infinitely many Woodin cardinals imply projective determinacy, which settles many classical questions about projective sets of reals.
Analytic sets are universally measurable (Lusin), so measure theory extends beyond the Borel sets in a controlled way.

objectives: Define Polish spaces and the Borel hierarchy, and locate standard sets within it.
Prove that every uncountable analytic set contains a perfect set and hence has cardinality 2^ℵ₀.
State Suslin's theorem that a subset of a Polish space is Borel if and only if it is both analytic and coanalytic.
definitions: A Polish space is a separable, completely metrisable topological space.
The Borel sets form the smallest σ-algebra containing the open sets.
A subset of a Polish space is analytic if it is a continuous image of a Polish space (or is empty), and coanalytic if its complement is analytic.
keyResults: Suslin: in a Polish space, the Borel sets are exactly the sets that are both analytic and coanalytic.
Analytic sets have the perfect set property, so no analytic set is a counterexample to the continuum hypothesis.
There are analytic sets that are not Borel; Suslin found this while correcting an error of Lebesgue about projections of Borel sets.
misconceptions: Assuming the projection of a Borel set is always Borel.
Thinking 'definable' means 'computable'; the effective hierarchies refine the classical ones but are different notions.

topics.title: Reading the mathematical literature
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Finding, reading and reconstructing research mathematics: navigating arXiv and review databases, reading notation and conventions, reconstructing omitted steps, and judging the status of results and open problems.

discoveries.note: Computation can test conjectures from the literature and search for counterexamples, provided the results are reported as evidence rather than proof.

objectives: Locate primary sources and surveys for a topic using arXiv, zbMATH Open or MathSciNet, and follow a chain of citations.
Reconstruct the omitted steps of a published proof and list the results it depends on.
Classify the claims in a paper as proved, cited, conjectured or heuristic, and judge what is genuinely open.
definitions: A preprint is a paper made public before, or without, peer review.
A survey summarises a field and its literature; a research article claims new results.
A conjecture is a statement believed but not proved; an open problem is a question with no accepted resolution.
keyResults: Peer review lowers but does not remove the chance of error; published proofs are sometimes corrected or withdrawn.
Computational evidence is not proof: Goldbach's conjecture has been verified for all even numbers up to 4 × 10¹⁸ and remains unproved.
misconceptions: Treating a preprint's claims as established before the community has checked them.
Expecting to understand every line of a paper on a first, linear reading.
Assuming a conjecture with strong numerical support must be true: the Mertens conjecture was disproved in 1985 although it holds for every n that has been checked.

topics.title: Algebraic number theory
topics.subject: number
topics.summary: Number fields and their rings of integers: Dedekind domains, unique factorisation of ideals, the ideal class group, Dirichlet's unit theorem and the splitting of primes in extensions.

discoveries.note: Spec 𝒪_K is a one-dimensional scheme, and the analogy between number fields and function fields of curves guides much of arithmetic geometry.

objectives: Compute rings of integers and discriminants of quadratic and cyclotomic fields.
Prove unique factorisation of ideals in Dedekind domains and use it to factor rational primes in quadratic fields.
State the finiteness of the class number and Dirichlet's unit theorem, and compute small examples.
definitions: A number field is a finite extension K of ℚ; its ring of integers 𝒪_K consists of the elements of K that are roots of monic polynomials with integer coefficients.
A Dedekind domain is a Noetherian, integrally closed domain in which every non-zero prime ideal is maximal.
The ideal class group of K is the group of fractional ideals of 𝒪_K modulo the principal ones.
keyResults: In a Dedekind domain every non-zero ideal factors uniquely as a product of prime ideals.
The ideal class group of a number field is finite.
Dirichlet's unit theorem: 𝒪_Kˣ is isomorphic to μ_K × ℤ^(r₁ + r₂ − 1), where μ_K is the finite group of roots of unity in K and r₁, r₂ count the real embeddings and pairs of complex embeddings.
𝒪_K is a unique factorisation domain if and only if its class number is 1.
misconceptions: Assuming unique factorisation of elements holds in every ring of integers; ℤ[√−5] fails it, although its ideals still factor uniquely.

topics.title: Modules
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Modules over rings, submodules and quotients, exact sequences, free, projective and injective modules, tensor products, and the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a principal ideal domain.

discoveries.note: The tensor–hom adjunction Hom(M ⊗ N, P) ≅ Hom(M, Hom(N, P)), natural in all three variables, is a basic example of an adjunction.

objectives: Work with module homomorphisms, kernels, cokernels and exact sequences.
Prove the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID, and deduce the classification of finitely generated abelian groups and the Jordan normal form.
Compute tensor products of modules and describe their effect on exact sequences.
definitions: A module over a ring R is an abelian group with an action of R satisfying the distributive and associative laws.
A sequence A → B → C is exact at B if the image of the first map equals the kernel of the second.
A module P is projective if Hom(P, −) carries surjections to surjections.
keyResults: A finitely generated module over a PID R is isomorphic to a direct sum R/(d₁) ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ R/(dₖ) with d₁ | d₂ | ⋯ | dₖ.
Free modules are projective, and over a PID every submodule of a free module is free.
M ⊗_R − is right exact but in general not exact.
misconceptions: Expecting modules to behave like vector spaces: ℤ/2ℤ is a ℤ-module with no basis.
Assuming tensoring preserves injectivity: multiplication by 2 on ℤ is injective, but becomes zero after tensoring with ℤ/2ℤ.

references.title: Abstract Algebra
references.author: David S. Dummit and Richard M. Foote

topics.title: Commutative algebra
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Commutative rings and their modules: prime and maximal ideals, localisation, Noetherian rings and Hilbert's basis theorem, integral extensions, the Nullstellensatz, primary decomposition and dimension.

discoveries.note: Regular local rings are characterised homologically, as the Noetherian local rings of finite global dimension (Auslander–Buchsbaum–Serre).

objectives: Localise rings and modules, and use localisation to reduce problems to local rings.
Prove Hilbert's basis theorem and Nakayama's lemma.
State and use the Nullstellensatz to relate ideals and algebraic sets.
definitions: The spectrum Spec R is the set of prime ideals of R.
A ring is Noetherian if every ascending chain of ideals stabilises.
The localisation S⁻¹R formally inverts the elements of a multiplicative subset S.
keyResults: Hilbert's basis theorem: if R is Noetherian then so is R[x].
Nullstellensatz: over an algebraically closed field k, the maximal ideals of k[x₁, …, xₙ] correspond to the points of kⁿ.
Nakayama's lemma for finitely generated modules over local rings.
The Krull dimension of k[x₁, …, xₙ] is n.
misconceptions: Thinking every ring is Noetherian; k[x₁, x₂, x₃, …] is not.
Confusing prime ideals with maximal ideals.

references.title: Introduction to Commutative Algebra
references.author: M. F. Atiyah and I. G. Macdonald

references.title: Commutative Algebra with a View Toward Algebraic Geometry
references.author: David Eisenbud

topics.title: Representation theory of finite groups
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Representations of finite groups over ℂ: Maschke's theorem, Schur's lemma, characters and orthogonality, character tables, induced representations and Frobenius reciprocity.

discoveries.note: A representation of G is a functor from the one-object category BG to the category of vector spaces, and intertwining maps are natural transformations between such functors.
Symmetry groups act on quantum state spaces, and irreducible representations organise energy levels and quantum numbers.

objectives: Decompose representations of small finite groups into irreducibles using characters.
Prove Maschke's theorem and Schur's lemma and derive the orthogonality relations.
Construct the character tables of S₃, S₄, D₄ and Q₈, and use Frobenius reciprocity for induced representations.
definitions: A representation of G on a vector space V is a homomorphism ρ : G → GL(V).
A representation is irreducible if it is non-zero and has no invariant subspaces other than 0 and V.
The character of ρ is the function χ(g) = tr ρ(g).
keyResults: Maschke: every finite-dimensional representation of a finite group over a field whose characteristic does not divide |G| is a direct sum of irreducible representations.
The number of irreducible complex representations of G equals the number of conjugacy classes of G.
The squares of the dimensions of the irreducible complex representations sum to |G|.
Non-isomorphic groups can have the same character table: D₄ and Q₈ do.
misconceptions: Assuming complete reducibility when the characteristic divides |G|.
Thinking the character table determines the group up to isomorphism.

topics.title: Homological algebra
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Chain complexes and homology, long exact sequences, projective and injective resolutions, the derived functors Ext and Tor, and their first applications in algebra and topology.

discoveries.note: Abelian categories axiomatise the setting in which homological algebra works; Grothendieck's Tôhoku paper (1957) developed derived functors in that generality.
Singular homology is the homology of the singular chain complex of a space.

objectives: Compute homology of chain complexes and derive the long exact sequence of a short exact sequence of complexes via the snake lemma.
Construct projective and injective resolutions and compute Ext and Tor over ℤ and k[x].
Explain derived functors as measuring the failure of a functor to be exact.
definitions: A chain complex is a sequence of modules with maps dₙ satisfying dₙ ∘ dₙ₊₁ = 0; its homology is Hₙ = ker dₙ / im dₙ₊₁.
A quasi-isomorphism is a chain map that induces isomorphisms on all homology groups.
Ext and Tor are the derived functors of Hom and of the tensor product.
keyResults: The snake lemma, and the long exact sequence in homology.
Ext and Tor do not depend, up to canonical isomorphism, on the resolutions chosen.
Ext¹(A, B) classifies extensions 0 → B → E → A → 0 up to equivalence.
misconceptions: Thinking every quasi-isomorphism has an inverse chain map; in general it does not.
Believing a complex is determined up to isomorphism by its homology.

topics.title: Quivers and path algebras
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Quivers and their path algebras: paths as a basis, multiplication by concatenation, representations of quivers as modules over the path algebra, and simple, projective and indecomposable representations.

discoveries.note: The paths in a quiver form the free category generated by that quiver, and the path algebra is its linearisation.

objectives: Compute the path algebra kQ of a small quiver and show that it is finite-dimensional exactly when Q is finite with no oriented cycles.
Prove that representations of Q correspond to kQ-modules, giving an equivalence of categories.
Classify the indecomposable representations of a linearly oriented quiver of type Aₙ.
definitions: A quiver Q is a directed graph, possibly with loops and multiple arrows.
The path algebra kQ has a basis consisting of all paths in Q, including a trivial path at each vertex, with product given by concatenation when the paths compose and zero otherwise.
A representation of Q assigns a vector space to each vertex and a linear map to each arrow.
keyResults: For a finite quiver, the category of representations of Q is equivalent to the category of kQ-modules.
For a finite quiver Q, kQ is finite-dimensional if and only if Q has no oriented cycles.
The path algebra of a finite acyclic quiver is hereditary: submodules of projective modules are projective.
misconceptions: Mixing conventions: texts compose paths left-to-right or right-to-left, which interchanges left and right modules.
Treating a quiver as an undirected graph; orientation and multiple arrows matter.

references.title: Elements of the Representation Theory of Associative Algebras, Volume 1
references.author: Ibrahim Assem, Daniel Simson and Andrzej Skowroński

topics.title: Algebraic topology
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: Singular and cellular homology, CW complexes, exact sequences and Mayer–Vietoris, homotopy invariance, cohomology and cup products, with applications such as invariance of dimension and the Lefschetz fixed-point theorem.
objectives: Compute homology of spheres, projective spaces and surfaces using cellular homology and Mayer–Vietoris.
Prove that homology is a homotopy-invariant functor and deduce that ℝᵐ and ℝⁿ are not homeomorphic for m ≠ n.
Compute cohomology rings of simple spaces and use cup products to distinguish spaces with the same homology.
definitions: The singular chain complex of X has as n-chains the formal integer combinations of continuous maps from the standard n-simplex into X.
A CW complex is a space built by successively attaching cells of increasing dimension.
Singular cohomology Hⁿ(X; R) is the cohomology of the dual cochain complex with coefficients in R.
keyResults: Hₙ(Sⁿ) ≅ ℤ for n ≥ 1, and the reduced homology of Sⁿ vanishes in all other degrees.
Mayer–Vietoris gives a long exact sequence relating the homology of a union to that of its pieces.
ℝᵐ and ℝⁿ are homeomorphic only if m = n.
Cup products distinguish ℂP² from S² ∨ S⁴, although the two spaces have isomorphic homology groups.
misconceptions: Thinking homology determines homotopy type.
Confusing homology groups with homotopy groups; the higher homotopy groups of spheres are far more complicated.

topics.title: Smooth manifolds
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: Smooth manifolds, tangent and cotangent bundles, vector fields and flows, differential forms, de Rham cohomology, Stokes's theorem and an introduction to Riemannian metrics.

discoveries.note: The tangent construction is a functor from smooth manifolds to vector bundles, and the chain rule is precisely the statement that it preserves composition.

objectives: Show that spheres, projective spaces and matrix groups are smooth manifolds, using the regular value theorem.
Compute with tangent vectors, vector fields, differential forms and pullbacks.
Prove Stokes's theorem for manifolds with boundary and compute the de Rham cohomology of simple manifolds.
definitions: A smooth n-manifold is a second-countable Hausdorff space with a maximal atlas of charts to ℝⁿ whose transition maps are smooth.
The tangent space TₚM can be defined as the space of derivations at p.
A differential k-form is a smooth section of the k-th exterior power of the cotangent bundle.
keyResults: Regular value theorem: the preimage of a regular value of a smooth map is an embedded submanifold.
Stokes: ∫_M dω = ∫_{∂M} ω for a compactly supported (n − 1)-form ω on an oriented n-manifold M with boundary.
Whitney: every smooth n-manifold embeds in ℝ²ⁿ.
de Rham: de Rham cohomology is isomorphic to singular cohomology with real coefficients.
misconceptions: Thinking every manifold comes with a preferred embedding in some ℝᴺ.
Confusing vectors and covectors when changing coordinates.

topics.title: Algebraic geometry
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: Affine and projective varieties, the Zariski topology, coordinate rings, morphisms and rational maps, dimension, and a first look at sheaves and schemes.

discoveries.note: Derived categories arose in Grothendieck and Verdier's work on duality theory in algebraic geometry.

objectives: Pass between ideals and affine varieties using the Nullstellensatz.
Work with projective varieties, homogeneous coordinates and Bézout's theorem for plane curves.
Explain why schemes generalise varieties, using Spec of a ring and its structure sheaf.
definitions: An affine algebraic set is the common zero set in kⁿ of a set of polynomials; a variety is often required in addition to be irreducible.
The Zariski topology has the algebraic sets as its closed sets.
Spec R, with the Zariski topology and its structure sheaf, is an affine scheme.
keyResults: Over an algebraically closed field, radical ideals of k[x₁, …, xₙ] correspond bijectively, reversing inclusion, to algebraic subsets of kⁿ.
Bézout: over an algebraically closed field, two projective plane curves of degrees d and e with no common component meet in exactly de points counted with multiplicity.
Over an algebraically closed field, the category of affine varieties is equivalent to the opposite of the category of finitely generated reduced k-algebras.
misconceptions: Thinking the Zariski topology is Hausdorff; on any infinite irreducible variety it is not.
Treating a variety as just a set of points; its coordinate ring carries the structure.

references.title: Ideals, Varieties, and Algorithms
references.author: David Cox, John Little and Donal O'Shea

topics.title: Sheaves
topics.subject: geometry
topics.summary: Presheaves and sheaves on a topological space, stalks and sheafification, sheaves of functions and of sections, and a preview of sheaf cohomology.

discoveries.note: Sheaves on a space form a Grothendieck topos, a central example of an elementary topos.

objectives: Define presheaves as functors from the opposite of the poset of open sets to sets, and state the sheaf condition as an equaliser condition.
Compute stalks and sheafify simple presheaves, such as constant presheaves.
Explain how sheaves of continuous, smooth and holomorphic functions encode local-to-global structure.
definitions: A presheaf on X is a functor O(X)ᵒᵖ → Set, where O(X) is the poset of open subsets of X.
A presheaf F is a sheaf if, for every open cover {Uᵢ} of an open set U, the diagram F(U) → ∏ F(Uᵢ) ⇉ ∏ F(Uᵢ ∩ Uⱼ) is an equaliser.
The stalk F_x is the colimit of the sets F(U) over open neighbourhoods U of x.
keyResults: Sheafification is left adjoint to the inclusion of sheaves into presheaves.
A morphism of sheaves is an isomorphism if and only if it induces isomorphisms on all stalks.
The category of sheaves of sets on a topological space is a Grothendieck topos.
misconceptions: Thinking every presheaf is a sheaf; constant presheaves usually are not.
Believing a sheaf is determined by its global sections.

references.title: Sheaves in Geometry and Logic
references.author: Saunders Mac Lane and Ieke Moerdijk

topics.title: Measure theory and integration
topics.subject: analysis
topics.summary: σ-algebras and measures, Lebesgue measure, measurable functions and the Lebesgue integral, the monotone and dominated convergence theorems, product measures and Fubini–Tonelli, and Lᵖ spaces.
objectives: Construct Lebesgue measure from outer measure using Carathéodory's criterion.
Prove and apply the monotone and dominated convergence theorems.
Apply the Fubini–Tonelli theorem, and prove that Lᵖ spaces are complete.
definitions: A σ-algebra on X is a collection of subsets of X that contains X and is closed under complements and countable unions.
A measure is a countably additive function μ from a σ-algebra to [0, ∞] with μ(∅) = 0.
Lᵖ(μ) consists of measurable functions f with ∫ |f|ᵖ dμ < ∞, with functions equal almost everywhere identified.
keyResults: Dominated convergence theorem.
Fubini–Tonelli theorem for σ-finite measure spaces.
Lᵖ(μ) is a Banach space for 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞ (Riesz–Fischer).
Every Riemann-integrable function on [a, b] is Lebesgue integrable, with the same integral.
misconceptions: Thinking sets of measure zero must be countable; the Cantor set is uncountable and has measure zero.
Interchanging limits and integrals without a domination or monotonicity hypothesis.

references.title: Real Analysis: Modern Techniques and Their Applications
references.author: Gerald B. Folland

references.title: Real Analysis: Measure Theory, Integration, and Hilbert Spaces
references.author: Elias M. Stein and Rami Shakarchi

topics.title: Functional analysis
topics.subject: analysis
topics.summary: Normed, Banach and Hilbert spaces, bounded operators, the Hahn–Banach, open mapping, closed graph and uniform boundedness theorems, weak topologies, and the spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators.
objectives: Prove the Riesz representation theorem for Hilbert spaces and work with orthonormal bases.
State and apply the Hahn–Banach, open mapping and uniform boundedness theorems.
Prove the spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators.
definitions: A Banach space is a complete normed vector space; a Hilbert space is a complete inner product space.
A linear operator T between normed spaces is bounded if ‖Tx‖ ≤ C‖x‖ for some constant C and all x.
A bounded operator is compact if it maps bounded sets to sets with compact closure.
keyResults: Riesz: every bounded linear functional on a Hilbert space H has the form x ↦ ⟨x, y⟩ for a unique y ∈ H.
Uniform boundedness principle.
Spectral theorem: a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors for the closure of its range, and its non-zero eigenvalues can only accumulate at 0.
The closed unit ball of an infinite-dimensional normed space is not compact in the norm topology.
misconceptions: Assuming every linear map between normed spaces is continuous.
Thinking all norms on an infinite-dimensional vector space are equivalent.

references.title: Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations
references.author: Haim Brezis

references.title: Methods of Modern Mathematical Physics I: Functional Analysis
references.author: Michael Reed and Barry Simon

topics.title: The probabilistic method
topics.subject: discrete
topics.summary: Proving existence by showing that a random object has the desired property with positive probability: Erdős's lower bound for Ramsey numbers, linearity of expectation, the second-moment method, the Lovász local lemma and concentration inequalities.
