discoveries.note: Derandomisation asks when random constructions can be replaced by efficient deterministic ones; the algorithmic local lemma of Moser and Tardos is one success.

objectives: Prove Erdős's bound R(k, k) > 2^(k/2) for k ≥ 3 using a random colouring.
Use linearity of expectation and deletion arguments to prove existence results.
Apply the Lovász local lemma and Chernoff bounds.
definitions: First-moment method: if X takes non-negative integer values and E[X] < 1, then P(X = 0) > 0.

Lovász local lemma (symmetric form): if each of a collection of bad events has probability at most p and is mutually independent of all but at most d of the others, and ep(d + 1) ≤ 1, then with positive probability none of the bad events occurs.
keyResults: R(k, k) > 2^(k/2) for every k ≥ 3 (Erdős, 1947).
There are graphs with arbitrarily large girth and arbitrarily large chromatic number (Erdős, 1959).
misconceptions: Thinking a probabilistic existence proof gives an efficient construction; explicit constructions are often unknown.

references.title: The Probabilistic Method
references.author: Noga Alon and Joel H. Spencer

topics.title: Measure-theoretic probability
topics.subject: probability
topics.summary: Probability on measure-theoretic foundations: probability spaces, independence, modes of convergence, conditional expectation, martingales, and proofs of the strong law of large numbers and the central limit theorem.
objectives: Prove the Borel–Cantelli lemmas and the strong law of large numbers.
Define conditional expectation via the Radon–Nikodym theorem and use its properties.
Prove the central limit theorem using characteristic functions, and apply the martingale convergence theorem.
definitions: A probability space is a measure space (Ω, F, P) with P(Ω) = 1.
For an integrable X and a sub-σ-algebra G, the conditional expectation E[X | G] is the (almost surely unique) G-measurable random variable whose integral over every set in G equals that of X.
An adapted integrable sequence (Xₙ) is a martingale if E[Xₙ₊₁ | Fₙ] = Xₙ almost surely.
keyResults: Strong law of large numbers: for independent identically distributed integrable Xᵢ, the sample means converge almost surely to E[X₁].
Lévy's continuity theorem relates convergence in distribution to convergence of characteristic functions.
Doob's martingale convergence theorem: an L¹-bounded martingale converges almost surely.
misconceptions: Confusing almost sure convergence with convergence in probability.
Treating a conditional expectation as a number rather than as a random variable.

topics.title: Stochastic processes
topics.subject: probability
topics.summary: Continuous-time processes: Poisson processes, continuous-time Markov chains, Brownian motion and its path properties, continuous-time martingales, and an introduction to Itô calculus and stochastic differential equations.
objectives: Construct the Poisson process and derive its basic properties.
State the defining properties of Brownian motion and use its basic path properties.
Apply Itô's formula and solve simple stochastic differential equations such as that of geometric Brownian motion.
definitions: Standard Brownian motion is a process B with B₀ = 0, continuous paths, and independent increments with B_t − B_s normally distributed with mean 0 and variance t − s for s < t.
The Itô integral ∫ H dB is defined as a limit in L² of sums in which the integrand is evaluated at the left endpoint of each interval.
keyResults: Brownian paths are almost surely continuous and nowhere differentiable.
Itô's formula: for twice continuously differentiable f, df(B_t) = f′(B_t) dB_t + ½ f″(B_t) dt.
The equation dS = μS dt + σS dB has the solution S_t = S₀ exp((μ − σ²/2)t + σB_t).
misconceptions: Applying the ordinary chain rule to Itô integrals.
Thinking Brownian paths are differentiable because they are continuous.

references.title: Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus
references.author: Ioannis Karatzas and Steven E. Shreve

topics.title: Monads
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Monads and their algebras, the Kleisli and Eilenberg–Moore categories, the correspondence between monads and adjunctions, monadicity, and monads in the semantics of programming languages.

discoveries.note: Moggi (1991) showed that monads structure the semantics of computational effects; they are central in languages such as Haskell.

objectives: Verify the monad axioms for the list (free monoid) monad, the power-set monad and the 'maybe' (exception) monad on Set.
Construct the Kleisli and Eilenberg–Moore categories and show that each gives an adjunction inducing the monad.
Explain how monads model computational effects, and state Beck's monadicity theorem.
definitions: A monad on C is an endofunctor T with natural transformations η : id ⇒ T and μ : TT ⇒ T satisfying associativity and unit laws.
An algebra for T is an object A with a morphism a : TA → A such that a ∘ η_A = id_A and a ∘ Ta = a ∘ μ_A.
The Kleisli category of T has the same objects as C, with morphisms A → TB in C serving as its morphisms from A to B.
keyResults: Every adjunction F ⊣ G induces the monad GF; every monad arises from an adjunction, and the Kleisli and Eilenberg–Moore adjunctions are initial and terminal among those inducing it.
Algebras for the list monad on Set are exactly monoids.
The category of groups is monadic over Set.
misconceptions: Thinking monads come from programming; they arose in algebra and topology (as Godement's 'standard constructions', later called triples).
Believing the Kleisli and Eilenberg–Moore categories of a monad are always equivalent.

topics.title: Monoidal categories
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Monoidal, braided and symmetric monoidal categories, coherence, monoid objects, closed monoidal categories and string diagrams, with examples from vector spaces, sets and representations.

discoveries.note: Symmetric monoidal categories with duals, such as finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, are the setting of categorical quantum mechanics (Abramsky and Coecke).

objectives: Verify that (Vect_k, ⊗, k), (Set, ×, 1) and (Set, ⊔, ∅) are symmetric monoidal categories.
State Mac Lane's coherence theorem and compute with string diagrams.
Define monoid objects and identify them in examples: monoids, k-algebras, and monads as monoids in a category of endofunctors.
definitions: A monoidal category is a category with a functor ⊗ : C × C → C, a unit object I, and natural isomorphisms expressing associativity and unit laws that satisfy the pentagon and triangle axioms.
A braiding is a natural isomorphism A ⊗ B ≅ B ⊗ A satisfying the hexagon axioms; it is symmetric if braiding twice gives the identity.
A monoid object is an object M with morphisms μ : M ⊗ M → M and η : I → M satisfying associativity and unit laws.
keyResults: Mac Lane's coherence theorem: every monoidal category is monoidally equivalent to a strict one, and all formal diagrams built from associators and unitors commute.
Monoid objects in (Ab, ⊗_ℤ, ℤ) are rings, and in (Vect_k, ⊗, k) they are k-algebras.
Monads on C are monoid objects in the monoidal category of endofunctors of C under composition.
misconceptions: Assuming every braided monoidal category is symmetric; categories of representations of quantum groups are braided but not symmetric.
Thinking the monoidal product must be a cartesian product.

references.title: Tensor Categories
references.author: Pavel Etingof, Shlomo Gelaki, Dmitri Nikshych and Victor Ostrik

topics.title: Abelian categories
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Additive and abelian categories, kernels and cokernels, exact sequences and exact functors, categories of modules and of sheaves of abelian groups, and the Freyd–Mitchell embedding theorem.

discoveries.note: Sheaves of abelian groups form an abelian category, the setting for sheaf cohomology.

objectives: Verify that R-Mod and the category of sheaves of abelian groups on a space are abelian, and explain why the category of free abelian groups is additive but not abelian.
Prove the snake lemma and the five lemma in an abelian category.
State the Freyd–Mitchell embedding theorem and explain what it does and does not allow.
definitions: An additive category is a category enriched in abelian groups with a zero object and all finite biproducts.
An abelian category is an additive category with all kernels and cokernels in which every monomorphism is a kernel and every epimorphism is a cokernel.
A functor between abelian categories is exact if it preserves short exact sequences.
keyResults: R-Mod is abelian for every ring R.
Freyd–Mitchell: every small abelian category admits a full, faithful and exact functor into R-Mod for some ring R.
Sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space form an abelian category with enough injectives (Grothendieck).
In the category of free abelian groups, multiplication by 2 on ℤ is both monic and epic but not an isomorphism, so that category is not abelian.
misconceptions: Thinking every additive category is abelian.
Applying Freyd–Mitchell to large categories without care; it is a theorem about small abelian categories.

topics.title: Enriched categories
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Categories enriched in a monoidal category V, with hom-objects in place of hom-sets: additive categories as Ab-enriched, strict 2-categories as Cat-enriched, Lawvere's metric spaces as [0, ∞]-enriched, and enriched functors and natural transformations.

discoveries.note: Strict 2-categories are categories enriched in Cat; weakening their laws gives bicategories.

objectives: Define V-enriched categories, functors and natural transformations.
Show that Lawvere metric spaces are categories enriched in ([0, ∞], ≥, +, 0), with the triangle inequality as composition.
Explain why additive categories are Ab-enriched and strict 2-categories are Cat-enriched.
definitions: For a monoidal category (V, ⊗, I), a V-category has hom-objects C(A, B) in V, composition morphisms C(B, C) ⊗ C(A, B) → C(A, C) and identities I → C(A, A), satisfying associativity and unit axioms.
A Lawvere metric space is a set with distances d(x, y) ∈ [0, ∞] such that d(x, x) = 0 and d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z); it is exactly a category enriched in ([0, ∞], ≥, +, 0).
keyResults: Locally small categories are exactly the categories enriched in (Set, ×, 1).
Preorders are exactly the categories enriched in the two-element poset of truth values with conjunction.
Ab-enriched categories with one object are exactly rings.
misconceptions: Thinking enrichment adds arbitrary extra structure to hom-sets; composition must itself be a morphism of V.
Assuming Lawvere metric spaces are symmetric; enrichment does not force d(x, y) = d(y, x).

references.title: Basic Concepts of Enriched Category Theory
references.author: G. M. Kelly

references.title: Metric spaces, generalized logic, and closed categories
references.author: F. William Lawvere

topics.title: Categorical logic
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Logic and type theory interpreted in categories: cartesian closed categories and the simply typed λ-calculus (Curry–Howard–Lambek), quantifiers as adjoints, and Heyting algebras as models of intuitionistic logic.

discoveries.note: Dependent type theories with identity types have models in homotopical and higher-categorical structures, which led to homotopy type theory.

objectives: Interpret the simply typed λ-calculus with products in any cartesian closed category, and show that Set is cartesian closed.
Express ∃ and ∀ as left and right adjoints to pulling back predicates along a projection (Lawvere).
Use Heyting algebras to model intuitionistic propositional logic, and show that P ∨ ¬P fails in some models.
definitions: A cartesian closed category has finite products and, for every object B, a right adjoint (−)^B to the functor − × B.
A Heyting algebra is a bounded lattice with an operation → such that c ≤ (a → b) if and only if c ∧ a ≤ b.
For a projection π : X × Y → X, pulling back subsets π* has a left adjoint ∃_π and a right adjoint ∀_π (Lawvere).
keyResults: Curry–Howard–Lambek: the simply typed λ-calculus with products serves as an internal language for cartesian closed categories.
Quantifiers are adjoints to substitution.
Intuitionistic propositional logic is sound and complete with respect to Heyting algebras.
The open subsets of ℝ form a Heyting algebra that is not Boolean.
misconceptions: Thinking categorical semantics replaces set-theoretic semantics; models in Set are one important case among many.
Believing intuitionistic logic asserts the negation of excluded middle; it merely does not assume excluded middle, and it proves ¬¬(P ∨ ¬P).

references.title: Introduction to Higher Order Categorical Logic
references.author: J. Lambek and P. J. Scott

topics.title: Elementary topos theory
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Elementary toposes as categories that behave like categories of sets (finite limits, exponentials and a subobject classifier); presheaf and sheaf toposes; internal intuitionistic logic; and Lawvere's ETCS as a categorical axiomatisation of sets.

discoveries.note: ∞-toposes extend topos theory to homotopy theory, and they model homotopy type theory.

objectives: Verify the topos axioms for Set and for presheaf categories [Cᵒᵖ, Set], computing their subobject classifiers.
Show that the internal logic of a topos is intuitionistic, and give a presheaf topos whose logic is not Boolean.
State the axioms of ETCS and compare them with ZFC.
definitions: An elementary topos is a category with finite limits, exponentials and a subobject classifier.
A subobject classifier is a morphism true : 1 → Ω such that every monomorphism is the pullback of true along a unique morphism to Ω.
A Grothendieck topos is a category equivalent to the category of sheaves on a site.
keyResults: Every presheaf category [Cᵒᵖ, Set] on a small category C is a topos.
The subobjects of any object of a topos form a Heyting algebra.
Set is a Boolean topos, while the topos of presheaves on the poset {0 < 1} is not Boolean.
ETCS without a replacement axiom is strictly weaker than ZFC in consistency strength.
misconceptions: Thinking a topos is a kind of topological space; every space gives a topos of sheaves, but many toposes do not arise in this way.
Believing the internal logic of every topos is classical because that of Set is.

references.title: Sheaves in Geometry and Logic
references.author: Saunders Mac Lane and Ieke Moerdijk

references.title: Topoi: The Categorial Analysis of Logic
references.author: Robert Goldblatt

references.title: Sketches of an Elephant: A Topos Theory Compendium
references.author: Peter T. Johnstone

topics.title: Kan extensions
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Left and right Kan extensions, their pointwise formulas via limits and colimits, and Mac Lane's slogan that 'all concepts are Kan extensions': limits, adjoints and representability as instances.

discoveries.note: Kan extensions, limits and adjunctions all have ∞-categorical versions that are central to modern homotopy theory.

objectives: Define left and right Kan extensions by universal properties and compute them by pointwise formulas when the target has the necessary colimits or limits.
Express limits, colimits and adjoint functors as Kan extensions.
Use left Kan extension along the Yoneda embedding to extend a functor from representables to all presheaves.
definitions: A left Kan extension of F : C → E along K : C → D is a functor Lan_K F : D → E with a natural transformation F ⇒ (Lan_K F) ∘ K that is universal among such pairs.
Right Kan extensions are defined dually.
keyResults: Pointwise formula: (Lan_K F)(d) is the colimit of F over the comma category (K ↓ d), when these colimits exist.
The limit of F : J → C is the right Kan extension of F along the unique functor from J to the terminal category.
A functor G has a left adjoint if and only if the right Kan extension of the identity along G exists and is preserved by G; that Kan extension is then the left adjoint.
misconceptions: Thinking Kan extensions always exist; they do when the source is small and the target has enough colimits (or limits).
Confusing left and right Kan extensions; pointwise left Kan extensions are computed by colimits.

topics.title: Formal methods
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: Mathematical methods for specifying and verifying software and hardware: operational and denotational semantics, Hoare logic, model checking, type soundness, and proof assistants for verified programs.
objectives: Give an operational semantics for a small imperative language and prove properties by induction on derivations.
Verify programs with Hoare triples and loop invariants.
Model-check finite-state systems against temporal-logic specifications.
definitions: A Hoare triple {P} C {Q} asserts that if P holds before command C runs and C terminates, then Q holds afterwards.
Model checking algorithmically decides whether a finite model satisfies a temporal-logic formula.
A type system is sound if well-typed programs cannot reach a stuck state (progress and preservation).
keyResults: Hoare logic is sound, and it is relatively complete for suitable languages (Cook).
CTL model checking can be done in time linear in the product of the sizes of the model and the formula.
By Rice's theorem, verifying arbitrary properties of arbitrary programs cannot be fully automated.
misconceptions: Thinking a verified program is correct in every sense; it is correct relative to its specification and its trusted base.
Believing partial correctness implies termination.

references.title: The Formal Semantics of Programming Languages
references.author: Glynn Winskel

topics.title: Computational reproducibility
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: Making computational mathematics checkable by others: version control, pinned environments, tests, notebooks, random seeds and data provenance, and reporting results honestly as exact, numerical, statistical or experimental evidence.

discoveries.note: Formal verification is the strongest form of reproducibility for proofs, including computer-assisted ones.

objectives: Package a computation with pinned dependencies, tests and a single command that reproduces its results.
Classify a computational claim as exact, numerical, statistical or experimental, and state its limitations.
Archive code and data with persistent identifiers, and cite software properly.
definitions: A computation is reproducible if others can obtain the same results from the same code, data and environment.
A pinned environment fixes the exact versions of all software dependencies.
Exact computation (integer or symbolic arithmetic) differs from floating-point approximation, whose results need error bounds to be meaningful.
keyResults: Floating-point results can differ between hardware and library versions, so tolerances must be stated.
A computer-assisted proof depends on the correctness of its code; formal verification or independent reimplementation strengthens the claim.
misconceptions: Thinking a notebook that ran once is reproducible.
Reporting agreement to many digits as if it were proof.

topics.title: Experimental mathematics: conjectures and counterexamples
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: Using computation to discover patterns, generate conjectures and search for counterexamples: integer sequences and the OEIS, integer-relation algorithms such as PSLQ, exhaustive search, and computer-assisted proofs, with honest reporting of evidence.

discoveries.note: Experimental results must be reported honestly, with code and bounds, and credited properly.

objectives: Generate and test conjectures numerically, and design a counterexample search with clearly stated bounds.
Use high-precision arithmetic and integer-relation detection to guess closed forms, and then look for proofs.
Assess computer-assisted proofs, such as those of the four colour theorem and the Kepler conjecture, and how they were verified.
definitions: An integer relation among real numbers x₁, …, xₙ is a non-zero integer vector (a₁, …, aₙ) with a₁x₁ + ⋯ + aₙxₙ = 0.
A counterexample search is exhaustive up to a bound if it checks every case below that bound.
keyResults: The Bailey–Borwein–Plouffe formula for π was found with the help of the PSLQ integer-relation algorithm.
Hales's proof of the Kepler conjecture was formally verified by the Flyspeck project, completed in 2014.
Numerical evidence can mislead: π(x) < li(x) for every x that has been checked, yet Littlewood proved that the inequality reverses infinitely often.
misconceptions: Treating a pattern that holds in many cases as established.
Reporting a search as exhaustive without stating its bounds.

references.title: Mathematics by Experiment: Plausible Reasoning in the 21st Century
references.author: Jonathan Borwein and David Bailey

topics.title: Mathematical foundations of quantum mechanics
topics.subject: applied
topics.summary: Quantum mechanics in the language of functional analysis: states as unit vectors in Hilbert space, observables as self-adjoint operators, the spectral theorem, the Schrödinger equation and unitary evolution, and the harmonic oscillator.
objectives: Explain why observables are modelled by self-adjoint, possibly unbounded, operators and measurement outcomes by their spectra.
Solve the quantum harmonic oscillator using ladder operators.
Derive the Robertson–Heisenberg uncertainty relation from commutators.
definitions: A pure state is a unit vector in a Hilbert space H, determined up to a phase.
An observable is a self-adjoint operator A on H; measuring it gives values in the spectrum of A.
Time evolution is ψ(t) = e^(−itH/ℏ) ψ(0), where H is the Hamiltonian.
keyResults: Stone's theorem: strongly continuous one-parameter unitary groups correspond to self-adjoint generators.
Robertson's inequality: σ_A σ_B ≥ ½ |⟨[A, B]⟩|.
The harmonic oscillator has energy levels ℏω(n + ½) for n = 0, 1, 2, ….
The canonical commutation relation [x, p] = iℏ has no solution in bounded operators.
misconceptions: Treating unbounded operators as if they were bounded; their domains matter.
Interpreting the uncertainty principle only as a statement about clumsy measurement.

topics.title: Large cardinals
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Optional advanced material: inaccessible, measurable and larger cardinals, elementary embeddings of the universe, and the hierarchy of consistency strength that organises much of modern set theory.

discoveries.note: Grothendieck universes, which correspond to inaccessible cardinals, are a common way of handling size issues in category theory.

objectives: Define inaccessible and measurable cardinals and show that V_κ satisfies ZFC when κ is inaccessible.
Explain why ZFC cannot prove that an inaccessible cardinal exists (if ZFC is consistent), and what 'consistency strength' means.
Describe how measurable cardinals correspond to non-trivial elementary embeddings j : V → M.
definitions: κ is (strongly) inaccessible if it is uncountable, regular, and 2^λ < κ for every λ < κ.
κ is measurable if there is a κ-complete non-principal ultrafilter on κ.
A theory T has at least the consistency strength of S if the consistency of T implies the consistency of S, provably in a weak base theory.
keyResults: If κ is inaccessible then V_κ is a model of ZFC.
Scott (1961): if a measurable cardinal exists, then V ≠ L.
Every measurable cardinal is inaccessible and is a limit of inaccessible cardinals.
misconceptions: Thinking large cardinals are merely very big numbers; their significance lies in consistency strength and their consequences, for instance for sets of reals.
Assuming large-cardinal axioms are known to be consistent; their consistency cannot be proved in ZFC and rests on mathematical evidence and judgement.

topics.title: Homotopy type theory
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Homotopy type theory reads types as spaces (∞-groupoids) and equalities as paths. Voevodsky's univalence axiom identifies equivalent types, and higher inductive types make synthetic homotopy theory possible.

discoveries.note: Shulman (2019) showed that every Grothendieck (∞,1)-topos gives a model of homotopy type theory with univalent universes.

objectives: Explain identity types and their path interpretation, including transport and path induction.
State the univalence axiom and explain why it is incompatible with uniqueness of identity proofs for the universe.
Define the circle as a higher inductive type and outline the synthetic proof that its loop space is equivalent to ℤ.
definitions: For a, b : A, the identity type a =_A b has elements thought of as paths from a to b.
An equivalence of types is a function with contractible fibres, equivalently one with a two-sided homotopy inverse.
Univalence: for types A and B in a universe, the canonical map (A = B) → (A ≃ B) is an equivalence.
A higher inductive type has constructors for paths as well as points, such as base : S¹ and loop : base = base.
keyResults: In homotopy type theory the loop space of the circle is equivalent to ℤ (Licata and Shulman).
Univalence implies function extensionality.
Univalent type theory has a model in Kan simplicial sets (Kapulkin and Lumsdaine, after Voevodsky).
misconceptions: Thinking HoTT replaces set theory or category theory wholesale; it is one foundation among several, with its own strengths and open questions.
Reading univalence as a statement about sets in ZFC; it is an axiom about identity types inside type theory.
Identifying HoTT with ∞-category theory; they are connected through models, not the same subject.

references.title: Homotopy Type Theory: Univalent Foundations of Mathematics
references.author: The Univalent Foundations Program

topics.title: Research ethics and attribution
topics.subject: foundations
topics.summary: Honest research practice: attribution and citation, priority and authorship, plagiarism, disclosure of computational and AI assistance, handling errors, and clearly separating established results from conjecture.
objectives: Cite sources accurately, including results learned from talks, software, databases and AI systems.
Decide authorship and acknowledgements fairly in a collaborative project, knowing that mathematics commonly lists authors alphabetically.
Respond appropriately when an error is found in one's own published work or in someone else's.
definitions: Plagiarism is presenting another person's words, ideas or results as one's own.
Attribution credits the origin of an idea, result, proof, code or data set.
An erratum or corrigendum is a published correction.
keyResults: Mathematical truth does not depend on who discovers it, but credit for a discovery belongs to those who made it.
Agreement among several AI systems is not evidence that a proof is correct; proofs must be checked by people or by verified formal methods.
misconceptions: Thinking well-known results need no citation.
Treating AI-generated text or proofs as exempt from attribution and verification.
Believing that admitting an error does more harm than concealing it.

topics.title: Quiver representations
topics.subject: algebra
topics.summary: Optional research direction: Gabriel's theorem on quivers of finite representation type, Auslander–Reiten theory, Kac's theorem, and links with Lie theory, cluster algebras and geometric representation theory.

discoveries.note: Lusztig used the geometry of spaces of quiver representations to construct canonical bases of quantum groups, an important source of categorification.

objectives: State Gabriel's theorem and verify it for small Dynkin quivers using reflection functors.
Compute Auslander–Reiten quivers of path algebras of Dynkin type.
Read a recent survey on quiver representations and separate established results from open questions.
definitions: A quiver has finite representation type if it has only finitely many indecomposable representations up to isomorphism.
The Tits form of Q is q(x) = Σᵢ xᵢ² − Σ_{arrows i→j} xᵢxⱼ.
An Auslander–Reiten sequence is a non-split short exact sequence 0 → A → B → C → 0 with A and C indecomposable, such that every map into C that is not a split epimorphism factors through B → C.
keyResults: Gabriel (1972): a connected quiver has finite representation type if and only if its underlying graph is a Dynkin diagram of type A, D or E, and then dimension vectors give a bijection between indecomposables and positive roots.
Kac: over an algebraically closed field, the dimension vectors of indecomposable representations of any quiver are exactly the positive roots of the associated Kac–Moody root system.
Auslander–Reiten sequences exist for finite-dimensional algebras, ending in any indecomposable non-projective module.
misconceptions: Thinking Gabriel's theorem depends on the orientation of the arrows; finite type depends only on the underlying graph.
Confusing finite representation type with having finitely many representations; there are always infinitely many decomposable ones over an infinite field.

references.title: Representation Theory of Artin Algebras
references.author: Maurice Auslander, Idun Reiten and Sverre O. Smalø

topics.title: Higher categories
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Optional research direction: strict 2-categories and bicategories, the 2-category of categories, functors and natural transformations, pseudofunctors and coherence, and an overview of approaches to n-categories.

discoveries.note: Higher-dimensional structure also appears in type theory: the iterated identity types of a type form a weak ∞-groupoid (Lumsdaine; van den Berg and Garner).

objectives: Define strict 2-categories and bicategories, and show that a bicategory with one object is a monoidal category.
Work in the 2-category Cat with vertical and horizontal composition and the interchange law.
Describe the difficulties of defining weak n-categories and the main approaches, separating established theory from open questions.
definitions: A strict 2-category has objects, 1-morphisms and 2-morphisms with vertical and horizontal compositions satisfying associativity, unit and interchange laws.
A bicategory weakens the associativity and unit laws for 1-morphisms to coherent invertible 2-morphisms.
A pseudofunctor preserves composition and identities up to coherent invertible 2-morphisms.
keyResults: Categories, functors and natural transformations form a strict 2-category Cat.
A bicategory with one object is the same thing as a monoidal category.
Every bicategory is biequivalent to a strict 2-category.
Not every tricategory is triequivalent to a strict 3-category; Gordon, Power and Street showed that Gray-categories are needed.
misconceptions: Assuming strictification works in every dimension.
Thinking there is one agreed definition of weak n-category for all n; several definitions exist, and comparing them is ongoing research.

topics.title: ∞-categories
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Optional research direction: (∞,1)-categories as quasi-categories and other models, ∞-groupoids and the homotopy hypothesis, limits, adjunctions and the Yoneda lemma in the ∞-setting, and applications in homotopy theory and algebraic geometry.
objectives: Define simplicial sets and quasi-categories, and recognise nerves of categories and Kan complexes as examples.
Explain why composition in a quasi-category is defined only up to a contractible space of choices.
Survey the models of (∞,1)-categories (quasi-categories, complete Segal spaces, simplicial categories) and how they are compared.
definitions: A simplicial set is a functor Δᵒᵖ → Set.
A quasi-category is a simplicial set in which every inner horn Λᵏ[n] → X with 0 < k < n extends to the simplex Δ[n].
A Kan complex is a simplicial set in which every horn extends; Kan complexes model ∞-groupoids.
keyResults: The nerve of a category is a quasi-category, and a simplicial set is isomorphic to the nerve of a category if and only if its inner horns have unique fillers.
Joyal and Lurie developed category theory inside quasi-categories, including limits, adjunctions and a Yoneda lemma.
The main models of (∞,1)-categories are related by Quillen equivalences of model categories (Bergner, Joyal–Tierney, Lurie).
misconceptions: Thinking ∞-categories are just categories with more arrows; their composition and coherence are homotopical.
Treating the homotopy hypothesis as a single theorem in every formulation; it is a guiding principle, established for particular definitions.

topics.title: Derived categories
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Optional research direction: the homotopy category of complexes, localisation at quasi-isomorphisms, the derived category D(A) of an abelian category, total derived functors, and why derived categories have become a standard language in algebra and geometry.

discoveries.note: Happel described the bounded derived category of the path algebra of a Dynkin quiver Q in terms of the repetitive quiver ℤQ.

objectives: Construct K(A) and D(A), and explain why localising at quasi-isomorphisms needs care.
Compute derived functors such as RHom and the derived tensor product in examples, and recover Ext as morphisms in D(A).
Read about derived equivalences, such as those from tilting theory and Fourier–Mukai transforms, and separate established results from open problems.
definitions: K(A) has chain complexes as objects and homotopy classes of chain maps as morphisms.
D(A) is obtained from the category of complexes by formally inverting the quasi-isomorphisms.
A total right derived functor RF extends a left exact functor F to derived categories; when A has enough injectives it is computed with injective resolutions.
keyResults: Extⁿ_A(M, N) ≅ Hom_{D(A)}(M, N[n]).
If A has enough injectives, D⁺(A) is equivalent to the homotopy category of bounded-below complexes of injective objects.
Non-isomorphic algebras can have equivalent derived categories, for example via tilting theory.
misconceptions: Thinking D(A) is abelian; it is triangulated and in general not abelian.
Believing every object of D(A) is determined by its homology; this holds over fields and, more generally, for hereditary abelian categories, but fails in general.

references.title: Methods of Homological Algebra
references.author: Sergei I. Gelfand and Yuri I. Manin

topics.title: Triangulated categories
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Optional research direction: additive categories with a shift functor and distinguished triangles satisfying Verdier's axioms, including the octahedral axiom; examples from derived and stable homotopy categories; t-structures and their hearts.
objectives: State Verdier's axioms and derive basic consequences, such as long exact Hom sequences.
Show that K(A) and D(A) are triangulated.
Define t-structures and identify A with the heart of the standard t-structure on D(A).
definitions: A triangulated category is an additive category with an autoequivalence [1] and a class of distinguished triangles X → Y → Z → X[1] satisfying Verdier's axioms, including the octahedral axiom.
A t-structure is a pair of full subcategories (D^{≤0}, D^{≥0}) satisfying truncation axioms; its heart D^{≤0} ∩ D^{≥0} is an abelian category.
keyResults: Hom(W, −) sends distinguished triangles to long exact sequences of abelian groups.
The heart of every t-structure is abelian (Beilinson, Bernstein and Deligne).
Cones are unique only up to non-unique isomorphism, a defect that motivates enhancements such as dg-categories and stable ∞-categories.
misconceptions: Thinking the cone construction is functorial in a triangulated category; in general it is not.
Believing every triangulated category is the homotopy category of a stable ∞-category; Muro, Schwede and Strickland found triangulated categories without such models.

references.title: Methods of Homological Algebra
references.author: Sergei I. Gelfand and Yuri I. Manin

topics.title: Stable ∞-categories
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Optional research direction: stable ∞-categories, in which fibre and cofibre sequences coincide, as enhancements of triangulated categories; spectra; and the passage from a stable ∞-category to its triangulated homotopy category.
objectives: Define stable ∞-categories and give examples, including derived ∞-categories of rings and the ∞-category of spectra.
Explain why the homotopy category of a stable ∞-category is triangulated.
Explain how stable ∞-categories resolve the non-functoriality of cones.
definitions: An ∞-category is stable if it has a zero object, every morphism has a fibre and a cofibre, and a triangle is a fibre sequence if and only if it is a cofibre sequence.
Spectra form the stable ∞-category Sp, the stabilisation of the ∞-category of pointed spaces.
keyResults: The homotopy category of a stable ∞-category is canonically triangulated (Lurie, Higher Algebra).
In a stable ∞-category, cofibres are functorial.
The derived category of a ring is the homotopy category of a stable ∞-category.
misconceptions: Thinking stable ∞-categories are triangulated categories under a new name; they carry strictly more information.

references.author: Jacob Lurie

topics.title: Categorical representation theory
topics.subject: category
topics.summary: Optional research direction: representations on categories rather than vector spaces, including tensor and fusion categories, module categories, categorical actions and categorification, such as Chuang–Rouquier sl₂-categorification and Khovanov homology.
objectives: Explain categorification through examples: from natural numbers to finite sets, from Euler characteristic to homology, and from the Jones polynomial to Khovanov homology.
Define tensor and fusion categories and module categories over them, with Rep(G) as an example.
Read a survey on categorical actions and separate established results from open problems.
definitions: Categorification replaces a set-based structure by a category-based one from which the original can be recovered, often by passing to a Grothendieck group.
A fusion category is a rigid semisimple k-linear monoidal category with finitely many simple objects and a simple unit object.
The Grothendieck group K₀(A) of an abelian category is generated by classes [X] of objects, with [B] = [A] + [C] for every short exact sequence 0 → A → B → C → 0.
keyResults: For a finite group G, Rep(G) over ℂ is a fusion category whose Grothendieck ring is the representation ring of G.
Khovanov homology is a link invariant whose graded Euler characteristic is the (unnormalised) Jones polynomial.
Chuang and Rouquier used sl₂-categorification to prove Broué's abelian defect group conjecture for symmetric groups.
misconceptions: Thinking categorification is a single construction; it is a family of methods, and a structure may have many categorifications or none known.
Assuming the Grothendieck group remembers everything about a category; much information is lost.

references.title: Tensor Categories
references.author: Pavel Etingof, Shlomo Gelaki, Dmitri Nikshych and Victor Ostrik

topics.title: Formalising published mathematics
topics.subject: computation
topics.summary: Optional research direction: turning published mathematics into machine-checked proofs, using blueprints that link informal statements to formal ones, collaborating on large projects, and contributing to libraries such as Mathlib.
objectives: Write a blueprint that breaks a published theorem into formalisable lemmas and records their dependencies.
Formalise a short published result, recording any gaps or implicit assumptions found along the way.
Describe completed large formalisations and what they did and did not verify.
definitions: A blueprint is a document linking each informal definition and lemma to its formal counterpart and recording the dependencies between them.
The trusted base of a formal proof is what must be trusted for the check to be meaningful: the proof checker's kernel, the axioms used and the formal statement.
keyResults: The Liquid Tensor Experiment formalised a central theorem of Clausen and Scholze's condensed mathematics in Lean; it was completed in 2022.
The Feit–Thompson odd order theorem was formalised in Coq by Gonthier and collaborators (2012).
Formalisation verifies the proof of the formal statement; whether that statement faithfully captures the published theorem must be checked by people.
misconceptions: Thinking formalisation makes peer review unnecessary.
Believing a formal proof follows the informal paper line by line; formal proofs often reorganise the argument substantially.

references.author: Jeremy Avigad, Leonardo de Moura, Soonho Kong and Sebastian Ullrich
